World.title: From the archive: Are Mexicans really always late?
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in December 2024 — is a humorous look at a stereotype regarding Mexicans and punctuality.

Before we get into the nuts and bolts regarding Mexican punctuality — or lack thereof — it’s important to clarify one thing. Mexicans are not actually always late.

That said, all stereotypes have to come from somewhere, don’t they? But like everything in life, there’s nuance to it.

Just like people all over the world, there’s room for a great deal of variety. Some people are always on time, and some people never are. Most people are punctual for certain activities, and unpunctual for others.

My dad, for instance, has never been punctual; I remember my mother saying she was terrified he wouldn’t make it to their wedding on time. My ex-husband also has challenges with punctuality, as does one of my best friends; I’ve spent great chunks of my adult life waiting hours.

I’m always super duper on time for everything, though I might let myself get to a party up to an hour late. My kid is leaning unpunctual, but I’m doing my damnedest to lecture it out of her. Because if there’s one thing kids love and respond to, it’s a good lecture.

Linguistic flexibility

One of the problems about even defining “late” is the language around defining time. For a deep dive into this, check out Joseph Sorrentino’s excellent piece on this specific type of vocabulary. Ahorita, al ratito, mañana … None of these words specify an actual time, you see? So “ahorita” could mean right this minute, and it could mean in five hours, or never. Al ratito (in a while) might mean in a couple of hours, or it might mean in a few years, depending on who’s saying it. You get the idea.

And really, this kind of language is useful because it allows for flexibility. In this way at least, Mexico is a flexible country.

Really, it has to be. Things come up that need tending to. Public transportation can be unpredictable. The opportunity to have a meal or talk to a pretty girl might come up. Your mom tells you to go fetch some things from the store, and you don’t tell her, “Sorry, I have plans.” Really, you just never know what can happen!

Life is unpredictable, and Mexicans have a fairly high tolerance for it being unpredictable, which is lucky for all of us.

Sometimes, though, there are things you must be on time for. And a good indicator of what those things are is whether or not there’s a specific time attached to them.

The meaning of ‘tolerancia’

School is one of those things. At my daughter’s school, for example, 8 a.m. is the official time kids have to be in the door. As a courtesy to the perpetually-late parents, there’s a “tolerance” of 10 minutes. To me, this means my daughter must be there before 8 a.m. if we’re not to be seen as rude and irresponsible. To others, it means 8:10 or even 8:11 is the limit. If kids aren’t in by that time, they must wait to enter the 9 a.m. class.

It was like this when I taught school here, too; some things, I suppose, are non-negotiable.

The same goes for official appointment times, even if the official or doctor you’re meeting isn’t exactly on time. So if you have a meeting with, say, immigration, you’d better be there at your appointment time! Some places will let you know that they have a tolerancia (literally, tolerance) of 10-15 minutes. This means that if you’re more than that amount of time late, you lose the appointment!

For other things, usually involving celebrations, arrival and start times are more flexible. This is especially true of parties, to which you can show up rather late without causing a fuss. Unless you’ve promised to bring something essential for the party, they’re just glad to have you there at some point. This doesn’t mean they’ll wait for you to start in on the cake and piñatas, though, so beware!

Clocks vs. cultural norms

Concerts and plays typically start within 15 to 30 minutes of their “official” start time; rock concerts might start hours after they’re meant to. Oh, well!

And if you’re meeting friends, it might depend on the specific circumstances. Are you meeting someone busy who only has a few minutes? Are you meeting them alone? In my group of mom friends, we always know that things can come up. “I’ll text you when I leave” is a good, flexible bridge that keeps people updated but keeps plans flexible.

In my own conservative and somewhat strict view, being on time means showing respect for the other person. If you are not on time, then you do not care about them or their time. And if you are on time, not only are you showing respect for them, but you’re making things easier for yourself, avoiding fluster. My cultural chauvinism is showing, I know.

But for plenty of people here, that’s a ridiculous notion. Why stress so much about being on time when literally anything can happen to make you not on time? Perhaps there’s a message here too about avoiding blame and responsibility. “Se me durmió el gallo” (The rooster went to sleep on me; as in, the rooster didn’t wake me up).

But that’s for another article. For now, I’ll leave you with a cute little proverb, as well as its juxtaposed, more truthful meme:

“Al que madruga, Dios le ayuda.” (The one who rises early receives God’s help.) It rhymes!

“Al que madruga, encuentra todo cerrado.” (The one who rises early finds everything closed.)

Truer words were never spoken.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, https://sarahedevries.substack.com/

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Exports and gas production hit record highs as patriotic spirit swells
World.content:
Listen to this article

Bilateral communications were front and center in Mexico the week of Sept. 7, with developments running the gamut from encouraging to combative. U.S. President Donald Trump’s remark that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs beyond “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” caught fire over the weekend, unleashing a fresh round of provocations from Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the days that followed.

Mexico, however, continued to highlight trade and security collaboration with its northern neighbor, though the PISA test results and next year’s midterm elections sparked more conversations at home. Meanwhile, the annual inflation rate ticked up to 3.26% — as expected according to Banxico, which forecasts inflation of 3.5% by the end of 2026. President Claudia Sheinbaum remained optimistic through it all, especially as her administration makes its plans for 2027. Overhead, punishing heat baked Mexico’s northern border states even as monsoon rains drenched the Pacific coast and center of the country.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

2027 budget takes shape

On Monday, Finance Minister Édgar Amador Zamora submitted a 10.6-trillion-peso (US $627.8 billion) budget proposal for 2027 to Congress, an increase of about 1% in real terms over this year. Amador framed the package around “five pillars” — economic growth, protecting government priorities, strengthening revenue, more efficient spending and fiscal discipline. The government is banking on those pillars to shrink the budget deficit to 3.9% of GDP next year from an estimated 4.1% in 2026, even as public debt climbs to 55% of GDP. No new taxes or fuel-price hikes are planned.

Health care gets a 10.9% real-terms boost to 1.1 trillion pesos, largely for IMSS-Bienestar infrastructure and medicine supply, while education rises about 7% to 1.3 trillion pesos to fund new schools. Pension and welfare programs get just over 1 trillion pesos, and debt servicing alone eats up 1.6 trillion pesos — roughly one of every seven pesos the government spends. Security agencies see an 11.6% bump to 331.4 billion pesos, while Pemex funding falls 69.2% as the state oil company pushes toward self-sufficiency.

The National Electoral Institute (INE) is the biggest percentage winner of all, with an 87.5% real-terms increase ahead of 2027 midterm elections, while the Energy Ministry, the National Human Rights Commission and the Federal Electricity Commission absorb the steepest cuts. Sheinbaum said the following day that she is “very satisfied” with the package and that growth could exceed the official forecast of 1.5-2.5%, citing anticipated stability in trade relations with the U.S. and Canada.

Homicides continue to fall

Security officials reported this week that daily homicides fell 53% in August compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration, making it the least violent August since 2015.

More than 67,000 people have been arrested for high-impact crimes since Sheinbaum took office, though Security Minister Omar García Harfuch cautioned that “the job is not done.” Days later, from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the president highlighted a 63% drop in Chiapas’s homicide rate since Gov. Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar took office, alongside nearly 10,000 arrests in the southern state. The same briefing revealed the discovery of a clandestine hospital the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) used to treat injured members.

Olmeca Refinery notches record month

Pemex’s Olmeca Refinery in Tabasco posted its best month yet for fuel production in July, averaging 252,498 barrels per day, a 78.8% jump over June. Gasoline output rose even more sharply, up nearly 128% month-over-month, after equipment fires forced repairs earlier in the year. Despite the milestone, the plant — which began operating approximately two years ago — is still running at roughly two-thirds of its 340,000-bpd capacity.

Fox and PRI’s Alito Moreno join forces

In a striking political reunion, former President Vicente Fox met with PRI leader Alejandro “Alito” Moreno to discuss “the need to build a strong opposition” ahead of 2027 midterms — 26 years after Fox became the first opposition candidate to sweep the once-dominant PRI out of the presidency, and years after he called the party “black vipers, vermin and tadpoles.”

Morena, for its part, dismissed the pairing as “the reorganization of the power elite,” saying in a statement that “they change the names, they invent new organizations, but behind the facade, it’s the same old faces.” The PRI, which ruled Mexico for 71 years, now holds just two of the country’s 32 governorships — the same number as the much smaller Citizens Movement (MC) party.

At her Monday press conference, Sheinbaum branded the reunion “PRIAN” politics dating to the “neoliberal” era of former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, and called Fox a “traitor of democracy” — a jab tied to his role in Mexico’s disputed 2006 election.

Bilateral high points

Trade and security cooperation produced some of the week’s more encouraging bilateral news. Mexico’s exports to the U.S. hit a monthly record in July: US $60.55 billion worth of goods were sent north, pushing Mexico’s share of the $332.92 billion U.S. import market above 18%.

Along the border, Mexican and U.S. forces carried out “High Eagle,” a binational operation to detect and disable drones cartels use to surveil authorities near Tijuana and San Diego. And though bad weather grounded Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s flight to Mexico City on Wednesday, he and Sheinbaum still held a video call on USMCA negotiations that Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard described as “cordial” and “very useful,” with talks on steel, aluminum and automotive tariffs continuing ahead of a fourth bilateral review round.

Bilateral low points

Other exchanges were considerably more combative. Over the weekend, Trump proposed to rename New Mexico “New America,” despite having no legal authority to rename a U.S. state, drawing pushback from the state’s Democratic leaders. Later in the week, from Ecuador, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio doubled down on claims that cartels control “vast territories” of Mexico, hinting the threat may eventually have to be “confronted one way or the other.” Sheinbaum shot back on Thursday morning, telling Rubio to keep Mexico out of U.S. midterm politics and calling his remarks electorally motivated. Rounding out the week, U.S. Vice President JD Vance labeled the Mexican flag “a symbol of the far left” after a protester interrupted his convention speech in Dallas, telling the man to “get your ass over there” if he loved Mexico so much.

Poor PISA scores spark a debate over screens

New results from the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), given to 7,843 students across 297 Mexican schools, showed that four in 10 15-year-olds — 41.8% — scored below the basic level in science, math and reading, more than double the 19.7% OECD average and Mexico’s worst showing since 2009.

Mexican students averaged 388 points in math, 408 in reading and 414 in science, all well below OECD averages of 463, 461 and 482, and the country has shed seven points in both math and reading since the 2022 test. The decline wasn’t unique to Mexico — the OECD’s education director called it part of a “dramatic” global drop, particularly in reading — and Mexican students still reported unusually high curiosity (80%, versus a 24% global average who called school “a waste of time”). Education International, the global teachers’ federation, pinned the broader slide on shrinking attention spans, heavy AI use and a worldwide teacher shortage. China, Singapore, South Korea, Estonia and Canada topped the rankings.

Education Minister Mario Delgado blamed excessive screen use for the drop in reading comprehension — arguing that “screens make it easy to ‘read’ or consume images” — while defending the New Mexican School curriculum model and promoting traditional games like yo-yos, marbles and spinning tops as a substitute for phone time. He conceded the PISA sample was “statistically representative” even as he questioned whether the test amounts to a comprehensive evaluation of Mexican education. Sheinbaum later told reporters Mexico will roll out new math and reading textbooks next year, including poems and short stories, and push a “return to pencil and paper,” tying the effort to new national guidelines already restricting cellphone use in schools.

Education Ministry, UNESCO team up on AI in schools

Also this week, Mexico’s Education Ministry signed a letter of intent with UNESCO to guide the “responsible” rollout of artificial intelligence in classrooms, with the U.N. body offering technical assistance, teacher training and research support. Officials said the goal is to ensure AI supports, rather than substitutes for, teaching and critical thinking, and the deal also opens the door to new rules on cellphone use in schools.

Mexico prepares for El Grito and Independence Day

With the country’s 216th independence anniversary approaching, more than 18,000 members of Mexico’s armed forces are readying for the Sept. 16 military parade through Mexico City, featuring drones, horses, dogs and a float marking the country’s World Cup hosting duties this past June and July. The holiday kicks off the night before, with Sheinbaum leading the Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony and Tejano band Intocable headlining a concert in the Zócalo.

Festivities and gritos will ring out from cities across the country, including in Sinaloa, whose capital city of Culicán will hold a public celebration of Independence Day for the first time in two years.

Points of 🇲🇽 pride

A 20-year-old engineering student from a Chihuahua farming family, Luis Ángel Robles Morales, won a national innovation award for an irrigation filter that is already helping 500 drought-stricken farmers use water more efficiently.

Forward Julián Quiñones and Club América’s Scarlett Camberos earned historic Ballon d’Or nominations, marking the first time two Mexican players — and a Mexican club — have featured on the shortlist for world soccer’s top individual honor.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Witnessing the explosive sledgehammer ritual in San Juan de la Vega, Guanajuato
World.content:
A door in the street cracked open just enough for a hand to slip through. A kid, maybe 15, curled his fingers toward himself: come here, come here, then pulled back into the dark. I looked around the street. Nobody. I stepped inside.

The house looked like a drug kitchen. Two folding tables stretched across the room, their surfaces dusted white and yellow. On one side, a bucket of potassium chlorate. On the other, sulfur. Three kids stood around the tables, working the powders together with their bare hands. One kid looked up at me and grinned, then went back to scooping powder into small plastic bags.

Josué was the one who had waved me in from the doorway. One of the boys had no hands. Both arms ended at the wrists. I didn’t want to ask. I asked anyway. He told me it happened during the explosions, a few years back. He said it the way someone tells you about a stolen bicycle, part of life.

Don Juan David, Josué’s father, walked into the room. He greeted me with a handshake and a smile, glanced at the tables of explosive powder where their children worked, and walked back out.

A dangerous tradition

Every year, on Shrove Tuesday, the townspeople of San Juan de la Vega pack homemade explosives onto sledgehammers, carry them to the streets and open fields, and slam them against the ground. People lose limbs. This time, something was different. For the first time in the town’s history, authorities had banned the use of explosives during the carnival.

Families wanted to talk. Each family insisted theirs was the true story. The carnival, they all agreed, celebrates San Juan de la Vega, a saint who saved the town from gold robbers centuries ago. The explosives reenact the gunshots from his battles.

Every family also wanted to make sure we knew that the big explosions, the ones the town is famous for, are not the real tradition. The real tradition is small. Modest. A respectful crack of gunpowder in honor of the saint. Kids started making bigger and bigger explosives, destroying city piping. Everything breaks, they said, shaking their own heads. This is not what we are.

A man named Aquino de la Vega was moving silver shipments by mule along the Camino Real when bandits started robbing him. He prayed to San Juan Bautista. The robbers stopped. Aquino vowed he would honor the saint every year, forever, and so would his sons.

Six families still carry that vow. Each one is tied to a barrio. The families fund the music, the food, the processions. They keep the image of the saint in their home for a year.

Adrenaline and danger

The word I heard more than any other was adrenalina. The afternoon before the carnival, I found Josué sitting on a curb outside a corner store, rolling a cigarette. He was quiet.

“I’m always scared before I do it,” he told me. “But once I blow up one, I can’t stop. The adrenaline is too strong. I want to keep going.”

I asked about the dangers, and stories came easily: a man who burned, another who was paralyzed, people who lost fingers, hands, arms, legs. Accidents happen because the explosives are powerful enough to send 25-kilogram sledgehammers flying through the air. A hammer goes up, a hammer comes down, and sometimes there is a head in the way.

“Police always try to take them away,” one man said, sitting in a plastic chair outside his house, two kids playing in the dirt beside him. “But they will never stop the tradition. Nothing will change.”

On the afternoon before the main event, the streets were empty. Doors closed. No music. No voices.

Boom. The first hammer hit the ground as soon as night fell.

The sound moved through me. The ground shook under my feet. My ears whistled, even from 100 meters away. My chest vibrated. Windows cracked. The pipes beneath the street groaned and split.

Then came another. And another.

Parades took the streets. Villagers singing, dancing, playing instruments, carrying the image of San Juanito through the town. Following them in the back, kids dressed as soldiers, some in boots and gas masks, others with no gloves, no protection of any kind. Everyone carried sledgehammers and backpacks stuffed with explosives.

Defying the ban

I found Josué in the crowd. Face covered in soot, eyes wide. He swung a hammer down and the detonation threw him sideways. He got up laughing and loaded another charge.

Around midnight, the first police cars appeared.

The crowd froze. About 10 men climbed out with SWAT gear, assault rifles and bulletproof vests. They walked toward the kids with the backpacks. The boys scattered.

I saw a grandmother crack her front door open. She let the kids shove their backpacks full of explosives through the gap; she closed the door, and she stood in front of it. When the police asked to enter, she stood immobile like a statue until they were gone.

The police confiscated what they could, caught a few guys, and left. Within minutes, the parades reformed. The hammers came back out. The explosions picked up where they had stopped.

At around 3 a.m., we walked back toward town to catch some sleep. I did not sleep. The bed shook after every boom. Even with earplugs, my ears hurt. It went on until 7 a.m.

We walked outside. Over 10 police cars patrolled the town. They had shut everything down. But beyond the edge of town, we could hear it. Boom. Boom.

We followed the sound.

Moving to the tracks

The townspeople had moved to the train tracks. Flat, open land, sand, rocks and gravel, not a piece of shade anywhere. They placed explosives on the rails and waited for trains to roll over them. Between trains, they took turns blowing up hammers on steel bars laid flat against the ground.

There, away from the police, the hammers got bigger.

It was noon. The sun was directly overhead. People packed more and more powder onto the sledgehammers and took turns. Huge hammers flew tens of meters into the air.

I watched a kid swing a hammer down. The explosion threw him back onto the ground. The hammer launched upward, spinning, and came down on his head. The ring of steel on skull. He tried to stand. Blood ran from his scalp, down his face, into his eyes. His friend pulled off his own shirt, wrapped it tight around the kid’s head, and hauled him onto the back of a motorcycle. They disappeared down the road.

Nobody stopped. The next person stepped up.

The next morning, the market opened in the square as always. People walked slowly, said good morning to each other. A dog slept in a doorway. The church bell rang at 8.

Here was Josué, down the road. He waved.

I went to say goodbye to Don Juan David. He pulled me into a hug that lasted a long time. He held on. We had barely talked. When he finally let go, his eyes were wet. He thanked me. He begged me to come back next year.

“Sí, San Juanito permite,” he said. If San Juanito allows it.

Mattia Astori and Daniele Colucci make Sacratos, a documentary project on extreme rituals with photos, interviews, articles and videos. They’ve worked in Mexico, India, Bolivia, Thailand and Italy.

World.title: SP Open São Paulo Brings WTA Tennis Back to Brazil: Free Entry Ends Today, Ground Passes from US$6
World.content:
BRAZIL · TENNIS

Key Facts — What happened Brazil’s highest-level women’s tennis tournament is under way at Parque Villa-Lobos in São Paulo.

— How big Thirty-two players are in the singles draw, and the 2025 edition drew about 30,000 fans.

— What it means Top-level women’s tennis is back in Brazil’s biggest city for a second straight September.

— The catch Free qualifying entry ends today, and from Monday every session needs a paid ticket.

— Who it affects Anyone in the city can attend, but ticket limits are counted per Brazilian taxpayer number.

— What comes next The main draw starts Monday, and the singles final is played on Sunday 20 September.

The SP Open São Paulo is halfway through its opening weekend in Brazil, and the free part of it ends today. From Monday, watching the main draw at Parque Villa-Lobos costs money.

Parque Villa-Lobos in Alto de Pinheiros, the western São Paulo park that hosts the WTA 250 tournament until 20 September. (Photo: “Parque Villa-Lobos 2018 014” by Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net)., via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

The SP Open São Paulo has been running since Saturday at Parque Villa-Lobos, a public park in Brazil’s largest city. Entry to the qualifying rounds has been free, and that window closes tonight.

What is happening at Parque Villa-Lobos

The tournament is the SP Open and it sits at the WTA 250 level. WTA stands for Women’s Tennis Association, the tour that runs professional women’s tennis.

The 250 in the name refers to the ranking points the champion takes home. It is the tour’s entry-level tier, a step below the big televised events.

This is only the second edition. The first one ran in 2025 and drew about 30,000 people across nine days.

Play runs from 12 to 20 September on outdoor hard courts. The singles draw holds 32 players, with 16 doubles teams alongside them.

The free weekend ends today

Qualifying began on Saturday and finishes today, Sunday 13 September. Entry to those matches is free, with a reservation through the ticketing company Eventim.

Qualifying is the small knockout that decides the last few main-draw places. The tennis is real, the crowds are thin, and the courts are close.

From Monday that free window is gone. Every session from 14 September onwards needs a paid ticket.

Ground passes are sold only for 14 to 20 September. The cheapest of them fall on Friday to Sunday, not on weekdays.

What a ground pass buys you

A ground pass is general admission to the site. It lets you walk the outside courts and watch from standing room.

It does not include a seat inside the main arena. Listings show a large screen on the grounds that carries the centre-court match.

The tournament FAQ prices ground passes at R$30 (about US$6) from Friday to Sunday. Monday to Thursday they cost R$50 (about US$10).

One pass covers the whole day, even on days with two sessions. Currency conversions use the 13 September 2026 rate of 5.11 reais to the US dollar.

Who is playing, and who is not

Leylah Fernandez of Canada is the top seed this year. Paula Badosa of Spain, a former world number two, is also in the draw.

Luisa Stefani is the Brazilian name to watch. She won the doubles title here in 2025 with Hungary’s Tímea Babos.

Beatriz Haddad Maia, a former world top-10 player, is not competing. She announced in August that she is stepping away from the tour for the rest of 2026.

She said the decision was about her own head, not her results. The WTA reported that she plans to return in 2027 using a protected ranking.

Brazilian tennis has had a loud year on the men’s side too. Our report on João Fonseca and the money flowing into the sport covers that shift.

How to reach the park

Parque Villa-Lobos sits in Alto de Pinheiros, in the western half of the city. It is a free public park, with running paths, playgrounds and a lot of shade.

The easiest way in is by train. Villa Lobos-Jaguaré station, on Line 9-Esmeralda of the São Paulo commuter rail network, sits beside the park.

There is no official parking for the tournament. Organisers point fans towards public transport and ride-hailing apps instead.

Give yourself extra time on weekday evenings. Marginal Pinheiros, the motorway along the river, backs up badly at rush hour.

Buying a ticket as a visitor

Tickets are sold through Eventim Brasil, the same platform used for concerts. You buy online and show the ticket on your phone at the gate.

Listings cap purchases at four tickets per session. The site also applies a wider ceiling of 22 tickets per CPF.

CPF is Brazil’s individual taxpayer number, and most buyers enter it at checkout. Foreign visitors do not need one.

The tournament FAQ carries an international sales section. Without a CPF, you pick your country at sign-up and enter your passport number.

What to expect once you are inside

The order of play is released only the night before. You cannot buy a ticket for a named player in advance.

That is normal for knockout tennis, and it cuts both ways. A R$30 (about US$6) weekend pass can land you a big name on a small court.

The site has food stalls, sponsor stands and seating in the open air. It is a park in a hot city, so bring water, sunscreen and a hat.

The singles final is on Sunday 20 September. If you can only come once, the closing weekend is the safer pick.

The city’s sporting calendar does not stop here. Our São Paulo Grand Prix guide covers the next big ticket at Interlagos.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the SP Open in São Paulo, Brazil?

It runs from 12 to 20 September 2026 at Parque Villa-Lobos, with the singles final on Sunday 20 September.

Is the SP Open free to attend?

Only the qualifying rounds on 12 and 13 September were free, and a reservation was needed. Every main-draw session from Monday needs a paid ticket.

How much is a ground pass at the SP Open?

Ground passes cost R$30 (about US$6) from Friday to Sunday, and R$50 (about US$10) from Monday to Thursday.

Is Beatriz Haddad Maia playing in São Paulo?

No. She announced in August 2026 that she is away from the tour for the rest of the season. The WTA says she plans to return in 2027.

World.title: Healthcare in South Africa 2026: What Foreigners Pay and What the Rules Hide
World.content:
SOUTH AFRICA · EXPAT GUIDE

Key Facts — The split 84 percent of people rely on the state system. Medical schemes covered 14.6 percent in 2024.

— The entry price Hospital cover starts near 1,275 rand a month, about US$79, for one person.

— The top price Comprehensive cover runs to about 12,509 rand a month, some US$775, for one person.

— The waiting period Three months with no cover at all for a first-time member, minimum benefits included.

— The penalty Up to 75 percent added for life. Insurance held abroad does not count as prior cover.

— The catch That penalty follows you to every other scheme. Switching insurer does not remove it.

A sixty-year-old arriving with thirty-five years of impeccable cover abroad is treated as though they had none. The surcharge that follows is permanent and follows them between insurers.

Cape Town. Private and public hospitals sit side by side, serving populations with very different means. (Photo: “Ciudad del Cabo desde Cabeza de León, Sudáfrica, 2018-07-22, DD 34” by Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Healthcare in South Africa runs on two systems that barely touch. The state serves 84 percent of the population and medical schemes covered 14.6 percent in 2024.

The money tells the story better than the percentages. Public health spending is 310.4 billion rand, about US$19.2 billion, in the current year.

Medical schemes paid out 259.3 billion rand, some US$16.1 billion, in benefits in 2024. That is for one seventh of the people.

There were 9,168,534 beneficiaries across 71 registered schemes at the end of 2024. Sixteen of those schemes are open to the public and 55 are restricted to particular employers.

Can a Foreigner Join a Scheme

Yes. Nothing in the governing act restricts membership by nationality or residence, and schemes may not discriminate on arbitrary grounds.

Only two visa categories require medical cover as a condition. Study visas and exchange visas both demand proof of cover with a registered local scheme.

Work, critical skills, intra-company transfer and business visas carry no such requirement. What every temporary residence application does require is a medical and radiological report, which is a health check rather than insurance.

The retired person’s visa is contradictory. The regulations list only a police clearance and the income threshold.

The home affairs website, however, lists proof of medical cover among the documents. The two sources do not agree.

Assume you will be asked for it. The income threshold for that visa is 37,000 rand a month, about US$2,292.

What It Costs

One large open scheme publishes its full 2026 table, which makes it a useful reference. Its cheapest option is 1,275 rand a month for one person, about US$79.

A mid-range hospital plan runs 2,747 rand, some US$170. Its top comprehensive option is 12,509 rand, roughly US$775.

For a couple those become 2,550 rand, about US$158, and 24,305 rand, some US$1,506, at the two ends.

The largest scheme publishes starting prices from 1,278 rand, near US$79, to 12,338 rand, about US$764.

Contributions rose steeply for 2026. The industry weighted average increase was 8.10 percent against inflation revised to 3.4 percent.

Open schemes raised prices 6.84 percent and restricted schemes 9.44 percent. Hospitals, specialists and general practitioners all pushed costs up by around 8.5 percent.

Medical schemes paid out some US$16.1 billion of benefits in 2024, against public health spending of about US$19.2 billion for six times as many people. (Photo: “Somerset Hospital 2” by HelenOnline, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

The Waiting Period Nobody Warns You About

This is the most important paragraph in the guide. Anyone who has not belonged to a registered local scheme in the previous ninety days is a first-time joiner.

Such a member can be given a general waiting period of three months and a condition-specific waiting period of twelve. That is standard and expected.

What is not expected is the scope. An exception preserves the prescribed minimum benefits during a waiting period.

That exception covers people moving between local schemes. It does not cover first-time joiners.

So a new arrival can pay full contributions for three months and have no minimum benefit cover at all. One large insurer states this plainly in its own underwriting document.

There are exceptions. A child born during membership faces no waiting period, and neither does someone transferring because their job or their employer’s scheme changed.

The Late-Joiner Penalty

Anyone aged 35 or over who lacks continuous cover since April 2001 is a late joiner. The penalty is calculated from age at application minus 35, minus years of prior cover.

The bands run from 5 percent of the contribution for one to four years, through 25 and 50 percent. The top band is 75 percent, for 25 years or more.

Here is the part that matters to anyone arriving from abroad. Prior cover is defined as a closed list of South African arrangements, and foreign insurance is not on it.

A sixty-year-old with thirty-five years of cover in Britain or the United States therefore counts as having none. The arithmetic puts them straight into the top band at 75 percent.

Take the mid-range hospital plan above. A couple at sixty would pay roughly 8,360 rand a month, some US$518, instead of 4,777 rand or about US$296.

The penalty is permanent and it moves with you. Changing scheme does not cancel it.

It applies only to the member and adult dependant portion of the contribution. On plans with a savings component the base is smaller than the headline figure.

The National Health Insurance Question

The insurance act was signed in 2023 and not a single section of it has come into force. That is the accurate position in September 2026.

In February 2026 the president agreed to delay bringing any section into operation until the Constitutional Court rules. Two challenges were heard in May 2026 and judgment is reserved.

Both concern the public participation process behind the bill rather than the policy itself. Nothing about your medical scheme changes until judgment is delivered and the president acts.

A separate judgment on 18 May 2026 is often confused with these. It struck down sections 36 to 40 of the National Health Act of 2003, the certificate of need scheme, as irrational.

Those provisions would have required state permission to open, move or keep running any health facility. Their removal protects the availability of private care.

The Public System

The realistic assessment is that quality varies enormously by province and by facility. Some teaching hospitals are excellent and much of the district network is not.

Two thirds of the health budget goes on staff pay. The treasury has added 32.3 billion rand over three years, about US$2 billion.

Of that, 21.3 billion rand is for pay and for absorbing unemployed doctors. In dollars that is roughly US$1.3 billion.

That last phrase is the treasury’s own. South Africa managed to have qualified doctors without jobs while posts went unfunded.

The withdrawal of United States aid has been absorbed rather than catastrophic. Antiretroviral drugs, laboratory tests and staff were already domestically funded, and the damage falls on donor-funded programme support and research.

410 million rand, some US$25 million, has been moved to the Medical Research Council to offset withdrawn American research grants. Emergency funding was authorised under public finance legislation.

Practical Advice

Join a scheme before you turn 35 if your life allows it, because the penalty clock starts there. If you are older, join in your first ninety days rather than waiting.

Get the underwriting terms in writing before you pay anything. Ask specifically about the general waiting period, condition-specific exclusions and the late-joiner calculation.

If you have prior local cover, gather the proof. An affidavit is accepted where documents cannot be obtained, and a scheme must recalculate if evidence appears later.

The emergency number that appears on the health department’s own pages is 112. Private ambulance services operate alongside the state service in the cities.

More: Africa news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can foreigners join a medical scheme in South Africa?

Yes. The law does not restrict membership by nationality, though individual scheme rules and underwriting still apply.

Is medical cover compulsory for a visa?

Only for study and exchange visas. Other categories require a medical and radiological report, which is a health check rather than insurance.

What does cover cost?

From about US$79 a month for one person on an entry-level hospital plan to about US$775 on a top comprehensive plan.

Does my insurance from home count?

No. Prior cover is defined as a closed list of local arrangements, so foreign policies give no protection against the late-joiner penalty.

Is the National Health Insurance in force?

No. The act was signed in 2023 but no section has commenced, and the president has undertaken to wait for a Constitutional Court judgment.

Sources: Council for Medical Schemes Industry Report 2024 and Circular 21 of 2026, Medical Schemes Act 131 of 1998, Immigration Regulations 2014, National Treasury Budget Review 2026, Constitutional Court CCT240/24, The Presidency.

World.title: Healthcare in the Dominican Republic 2026: What Foreigners Can Actually Get
World.content:
DOMINICAN REPUBLIC · EXPAT GUIDE

Key Facts — The public route Only through a Dominican employer. There is no voluntary enrolment for the self-employed or retired.

— The alternative A regulated private plan, sold by private insurers and by the state insurer alike.

— The age rule An insurer may refuse you because of your age. It may not cancel you for growing older.

— The basic cover High-cost treatment is capped at 1,000,000 pesos a year, about US$16,973.

— The ambulance The 911 service covers medical emergencies. A quarter of responses take over twenty minutes.

— The catch New members reach the full high-cost cap only after twelve months of contributions.

Almost every guide tells foreigners they can enrol in Dominican social security. Without a local employer they cannot, and the workaround has an age trap built into it.

Santo Domingo. The capital region holds the densest network of hospitals and clinics in the country. (Photo: “Santo Domingo Dominican Republic Architecture” by https://www.flickr.com/photos/miguel_discart_vrac_3, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)

Healthcare in the Dominican Republic rests on a law of 2001 that created three financing regimes. Two of them work and the third has never been rolled out.

The contributory regime covers salaried workers and their families. The subsidised regime pays for healthcare for people without stable income.

The third was designed for independent professionals and the self-employed. Twenty-five years on, national statistics still report only two regimes.

That gap is exactly where a foreign retiree falls. It is the single most misunderstood point in every English-language guide to the subject.

Can You Join the Public System

The law says legal residents may affiliate, not just nationals. The practice is narrower than the law.

The social security treasury accepts three documents from a foreign worker. They are a work visa, a migration card, or a regularisation card.

A residency card alone is not on that list. Nor is the national identity document.

More importantly, the employer files the application, not the worker. A foreigner holding only a passport is registered for tax purposes but does not contribute and has no access to health cover.

There is no voluntary individual enrolment channel. If you are retired or self-employed, the public healthcare system is closed to you.

What You Buy Instead

The answer is a regulated private healthcare plan, called a voluntary plan. These are sold only to people who do not contribute to social security.

The state insurer sells one too, and markets it openly to foreigners holding a passport. Do not mistake that for joining the public system, because it is a private product from a public company.

A medical examination is required from applicants aged 55 and over. That is the first sign of where the real barrier sits.

No Dominican insurer publishes its premiums. Every price is individually underwritten, filed with the regulator, and quoted only by telephone.

Two small insurers do publish reference prices. Their voluntary plans run from about 1,698 to 4,274 pesos a month per person, or roughly US$29 to US$73.

Treat those as a floor rather than a benchmark. They are not the plans a comfortable foreign resident would end up buying.

The eastern region around Punta Cana has the thinnest public hospital network of the ten health regions. (Photo: “Santo Domingo Dominican Republic Neighborhoods” by https://www.flickr.com/photos/miguel_discart_vrac_3/, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)

The Age Rule That Decides Everything

In the compulsory scheme, age is irrelevant by statute. Healthcare providers and insurers may not exclude anyone by age, and a pensioner is covered whatever their health.

Voluntary plans are different. An insurer may apply its own underwriting policy to a new applicant, and that includes refusing on age.

What it may not do is end the contract later because you have grown older. Cancellation for reasons of age is expressly prohibited.

So the rule is asymmetric, and the practical advice follows from it. Get in before the cut-off, because there is no way back in afterwards.

No insurer publishes its maximum entry age. Ask in writing before you rely on anything you read, including this.

There is one clear sign that age loading is normal. The state insurer launched a plan in August 2026 and advertised a flat premium with no age surcharge.

Nobody advertises that unless competitors do the opposite. It covers up to 4,000,000 pesos a year for high-cost care, about US$67,890.

What the Basic Plan Covers

The basic plan was updated on 1 November 2025 and those figures still apply. Consultations are covered to 750 pesos an event, about US$12.73.

A hospital room is covered fully to 1,725 pesos a day, some US$29. Above that it is covered at 90 percent to 2,415 pesos, or US$41.

High-cost treatment is covered at 80 percent, capped at 1,000,000 pesos per event a year, roughly US$16,973. Cancer drugs have their own cap of 2,090,000 pesos, about US$35,473.

A kidney transplant is capped at 3,500,000 pesos, some US$59,404. Outpatient medicines are covered at 70 percent up to 12,000 pesos a year, about US$204.

A normal delivery is covered in full with no ceiling and no co-payment. Co-payments elsewhere are capped at one minimum wage per event, 23,223 pesos or US$394.

Now the part guides omit. High-cost cover is graduated by months contributed and only reaches the full ceiling after twelve continuous months.

A new member diagnosed in the second month has a fraction of that ceiling. Eighteen months are needed if contributions have been intermittent.

Hospitals and Quality

The honest summary is that good private healthcare exists here and the national average is not it. Insured patients do markedly better than the country as a whole.

The private insurers’ association reports maternal deaths of 41 per 100,000 births among its members against 90 nationally. Infant deaths are 8 per 1,000 against 22.

The public network has 1,911 licensed establishments but only 192 hospitals, of which 32 are high-complexity. The eastern region around Punta Cana has the thinnest network of the ten.

The best-documented international accreditation in the country belongs to the Metropolitan Hospital of Santiago, which holds Canadian accreditation. Other large names include the Plaza de la Salud hospital and CEDIMAT in the capital.

Ambulances, Pharmacies and Elective Surgery

The national 911 service does cover medical emergencies with ambulances. It handled 247,627 prehospital cases between January and May 2026.

Response times are the caveat. Under a third of dispatches reached the scene within ten minutes, and a quarter took more than twenty.

If you settle away from a city, identify your nearest capable private hospital in advance. Do not rely on the ambulance for a cardiac event.

Prescription enforcement at pharmacies is loose. The health ministry acknowledges the country shares the regional problem of antibiotics sold without a prescription.

Elective cosmetic surgery deserves a blunt warning. The health ministry ordered 501 healthcare and aesthetic establishments closed between 2024 and April 2026.

Two patients died in cosmetic clinics within three weeks in spring 2026. One of those clinics was operating despite a standing closure order and without a valid licence.

The failure is not in the country’s best hospitals. It is a long tail of unlicensed aesthetic clinics, so verify a facility’s health licence with the ministry before any elective procedure.

What Changed and What to Buy

The per-member payment to insurers rose 12.14 percent on 1 November 2025 to 1,887.54 pesos a month, about US$32. Doctors’ fees across 1,370 procedures rose 20 percent.

From April 2026 the system pays insurers a risk-adjusted amount rather than a flat one, with age among the variables. A wider reform of the social security law remains a proposal, not law.

In September 2026 the regulator banned insurers from interfering with members’ free choice of insurer. Foreigners are obvious targets for mis-selling, so read anything you are asked to sign.

If you want healthcare abroad, the regulated product is a special prepaid medicine plan. It must cover at least the high-cost ceiling and cannot work by reimbursement alone.

More: Caribbean news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a foreign retiree join Dominican public healthcare?

No. Enrolment runs through a local employer, and there is no voluntary route for the retired or self-employed.

What does a private plan cost?

No insurer publishes rates. Two small companies show reference prices of about US$29 to US$73 a month per person, and larger insurers quote individually.

Is there an age limit?

Insurers may refuse a new applicant on age but may not cancel an existing member for growing older. Medical exams start at 55 with the state insurer.

What is covered under the basic plan?

Consultations to about US$12.73 an event, surgery at 90 percent, and high-cost treatment at 80 percent up to about US$16,973 a year.

Does 911 send an ambulance?

Yes, nationwide and free. A quarter of dispatches take more than twenty minutes to reach the scene.

Sources: Ley 87-01, SISALRIL, Consejo Nacional de Seguridad Social Resolucion 624-02, Tesoreria de la Seguridad Social, SENASA, ADARS, Servicio Nacional de Salud, Ministerio de Salud Publica, Banco Central.

World.title: What Is Actually Confirmed About Milei’s United Nations Trip
World.content:
ARGENTINA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — What is confirmed Milei travels to the United Nations General Assembly, with a leaders’ reception referenced for 22 September.

— Also confirmed He is billed as headline speaker at a New York forum on 23 September.

— What is not confirmed A meeting with Trump on the Falklands claim. One outlet reports the foreign ministry is working on protocol.

— The sourcing Infobae, 13 September, citing unnamed people in Washington. Every other report is a reprint of it.

— The correction The New York forum is part of the same trip, not a second journey.

— The background Milei suspended a planned United Kingdom visit amid tensions over the islands.

Protocol staff exploring a bilateral is not a scheduled meeting, and a scheduled meeting is not an agenda. Three different things are being reported as one.

What Is Actually Confirmed About Milei’s United Nations Trip

President Javier Milei travels to the United Nations General Assembly this month, and a report that a meeting with President Trump on the Falklands claim has not been ruled out has been widely recirculated from a single source.

What Is Established

Milei is travelling to the General Assembly in New York. A leaders’ reception on 22 September is referenced in the reporting. His speech date was not confirmed in the sources The Rio Times could locate, and we do not state one.

He is confirmed as headline speaker at a New York forum on 23 September on democratic values, economic freedom and strategic security, organised by the Fundación Federalismo y Libertad and the International Republican Institute, with support from Citibank.

The Correction on the Second Trip

Coverage describing a separate journey to the United States for an economics and security forum is describing the 23 September event, which falls inside General Assembly week.

It is the same trip. Separate Washington and Miami visits have been mentioned in other reporting for later in the year, and those are distinct from this one.

The Falklands meeting report comes from a single outlet.

The Falklands Meeting

The claim that a meeting with Trump on the Malvinas claim has not been ruled out comes from a single Infobae report of 13 September, sourced to unnamed people in Washington.

Infobae’s own wording is narrower than the recirculation. It says the foreign ministry is working with protocol, which describes staff exploring the possibility of a bilateral rather than a scheduled meeting, and says nothing about an agreed agenda.

There is no confirmation from the Casa Rosada, the foreign ministry or the White House. Every other outlet carrying the story is reprinting Infobae, which means the apparent breadth of sourcing is a single source repeated.

Why the Question Is Live at All

Argentina’s claim to the islands is written into its constitution, and the current government has pressed it harder than its predecessors in several concrete ways.

Milei suspended a planned visit to the United Kingdom amid the tensions. His government has tightened sanctions on oil companies operating in waters near the islands and resumed construction of a naval base in Tierra del Fuego, funded from January.

Trump has previously hinted that Washington might revisit its historic position of neutrality, and the Argentine government has been reported as weighing whether to accept a Trump mediation. That combination is why a bilateral would be read as significant.

Argentina’s claim to the islands is written into its constitution.

How The Rio Times Is Treating It

We report the confirmed travel, the confirmed forum, and the single-sourced report about a possible meeting, described as what it is.

A meeting between the two presidents at the General Assembly would be unremarkable on its own. A meeting at which the Falklands question was formally discussed would not be, and nothing yet establishes the second.

The distinction is not academic for readers in Buenos Aires or in Stanley. United States policy on the islands has been neutrality on sovereignty since 1982, and any departure from it would be a material change in a dispute that has been static for four decades.

A claim of that weight should rest on more than unnamed sources in one report, and until it does The Rio Times will report the travel and not the meeting.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Milei going to the United Nations?

Yes. He travels to the General Assembly, with a leaders’ reception referenced for 22 September.

Is a Trump meeting confirmed?

No. One outlet reports the foreign ministry is working on protocol for a possible bilateral. There is no confirmation from either government.

Is there a second US trip?

No. The 23 September New York forum falls within General Assembly week.

Why would a Falklands discussion matter?

Trump has hinted Washington might revisit its neutrality, and Argentina has been reported as weighing a Trump mediation.

What has Argentina done on the claim recently?

Suspended a planned UK visit, tightened sanctions on oil firms near the islands and funded a naval base in Tierra del Fuego.

Sources: Infobae, Canal 26.

World.title: The Director of Argentina’s House in Paris Resigns
World.content:
ARGENTINA · CULTURE

Key Facts — The resignation Santiago Muzio resigned as director of the Casa Argentina in the Cité Internationale Universitaire de Paris on 13 September 2026.

— The accusations Removal of a memorial plaque to the disappeared, expulsions of residents, refusal to sign the Cité’s charter of values, and opaque building works.

— The petition More than 1,096 academics, writers and artists signed.

— Also involved Two Paris municipal officials requested an investigation. Other national houses distanced themselves.

— The government angle One outlet reports the Argentine government pushed him out. Others describe local pressure.

— The successor Alfredo Mario Soto, a law professor and former university vice-rector.

A plaque to the disappeared, removed from an Argentine building in Paris, produced a thousand signatures and a resignation. The pressure was mostly French.

The Director of Argentina’s House in Paris Resigns

Santiago Muzio has resigned as director of the Casa Argentina at the Cité Internationale Universitaire de Paris, after months of accusations from residents, academics and French officials over his management of the residence.

What He Is Accused Of

The accusations centre on the removal of a memorial plaque commemorating the disappeared of Argentina’s military dictatorship, and on the expulsion of students, researchers and artists from the residence.

He is also accused of refusing to sign the Cité’s Charte des Valeurs, the charter of values that governs the international campus, and of opaque and allegedly irregular building works, with a lack of transparency over how funds were used.

Where the Pressure Came From

A petition signed by more than 1,096 academics, writers and artists called for his removal. Student and resident organisations pressed the same case.

Two Paris municipal officials requested an investigation, and other national houses on the campus, including those of Japan, Canada, Germany and Denmark, distanced themselves from the Argentine residence. French press coverage ran for months.

That is the documented weight of the pressure, and it was overwhelmingly French and academic rather than governmental.

The Buenos Aires Angle

Página/12 reports that the Argentine government pushed Muzio out, concerned that the scandal would damage President Milei around a forthcoming visit to France and a Paris Week event scheduled for 30 October.

That is one outlet’s sourcing and The Rio Times attributes it rather than stating it. Other coverage frames the pressure as coming from local authorities and the academic community.

The distinction matters for what the resignation signifies. A government removing an appointee ahead of a presidential visit is a different event from an appointee giving way to sustained French pressure, and only one of the two has been independently established.

The Cité Internationale hosts national residences funded by each country.

What the Casa Argentina Is

The Cité Internationale Universitaire de Paris is a campus of national residences built from the 1920s onwards, each funded and administered by the country it represents, housing students and researchers from that country and others.

The Argentine house is one of the older pavilions and functions as a residence and a cultural presence at once, which is why the removal of a memorial plaque became a question about the Argentine state rather than about a building’s decoration.

The Charte des Valeurs binds the houses to the campus’s stated principles, and a house that refuses to sign it is in an unusual position with its neighbours.

One outlet links the resignation to a forthcoming presidential visit to France.

What Happens Next

The successor is Alfredo Mario Soto, a law professor and former vice-rector at a university in Rosario.

The investigation requested by the Paris municipal officials has not been reported as concluded, and the question of the building works and the use of funds is separate from the resignation.

Whether the memorial plaque is restored is the question the petitioners will measure the new director by, and it is the one with the least ambiguity attached to it.

The Cité itself has its own remedies. A house that will not sign the charter of values can be pressed by the campus administration, and the neighbouring national houses have already shown they are willing to say so publicly.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who resigned?

Santiago Muzio, director of the Casa Argentina at the Cité Internationale Universitaire de Paris, on 13 September 2026.

What was he accused of?

Removing a memorial plaque to the disappeared, expelling residents, refusing to sign the campus charter of values, and opaque building works.

How many people signed the petition?

More than 1,096 academics, writers and artists.

Did the Argentine government remove him?

One outlet reports so. Other coverage describes the pressure as local and academic. It is not independently established.

Who replaces him?

Alfredo Mario Soto, a law professor and former university vice-rector.

Sources: Página/12, Perfil, Filo News.

World.title: Argentina’s 2027 Budget Arrives Without Published Assumptions
World.content:
ARGENTINA · BUDGET

Key Facts — The deadline The 2027 budget goes to the Chamber of Deputies by 15 September 2026, as the financial administration law requires.

— The briefing Milei was reported as briefing legislators on Monday 14 September.

— What is not published The government’s July advance document contained no inflation or exchange-rate projections.

— What that means Any macro figures circulating are third-party forecasts, not official assumptions.

— The arithmetic 129 votes are needed for a quorum in the lower house.

— The obstacle Blocs aligned with several provincial governors have already broken with the government on other votes.

A budget arrives with no published inflation or exchange-rate assumption. That is unusual, and it is the first thing the governors will ask about.

Argentina’s 2027 Budget Arrives Without Published Assumptions

Argentina’s government must submit its 2027 budget to the Chamber of Deputies by 15 September, and it arrives without the inflation and exchange-rate projections that a budget is normally built around.

The Deadline and the Process

The financial administration law sets 15 September as the date by which the executive must send the following year’s budget to the lower house. Milei was reported as briefing legislators on Monday 14 September.

From there the bill goes to the budget committee, then to the floor of the Chamber of Deputies, then to the Senate. Argentina has operated for extended periods without an approved budget, with the previous year’s rolled over, which is the fallback if the process fails.

What Is Missing

The government’s July advance, the pluriannual budget document sent on 2 July 2026, was explicitly issued without inflation or exchange-rate projections. It contained qualitative claims instead: falling inflation, real-wage recovery, growth led by investment and private consumption, falling unemployment and poverty, and a maintained fiscal surplus.

That omission is the story until the full bill is published. A budget without a price assumption cannot be checked, because every spending line is a nominal figure whose real value depends on the number that was left out.

The central bank’s market survey points to about 20.5% inflation.

The Numbers Circulating Are Not the Government’s

The International Monetary Fund projects around 4% growth and 15.7% average inflation. LatinFocus has 3% and 21.7%, with a year-end exchange rate around 1,968 pesos to the dollar. CEPAL has 3.4%. The central bank’s own market expectations survey points to roughly 20.5% inflation and a rate slightly above 2,000.

Primary surplus estimates from private forecasters run between 1.3% and 1.8% of output. None of these is an official assumption, and The Rio Times does not present them as one.

The spread between the IMF’s 15.7% and LatinFocus’s 21.7% is wide enough to change what the budget means, which is why the official number matters.

The government needs 129 votes for a quorum and does not hold them alone.

The Governors

The government needs 129 votes for a quorum in the Chamber of Deputies and does not command them on its own. Blocs aligned with the governors of Misiones, Salta and Tucumán have already broken with it on debt and disability funding this year.

Provincial negotiation in Argentina runs through the same instruments every year: transfers under the revenue-sharing regime, discretionary funds, and public works allocated by province. A governor whose bloc withholds votes is negotiating over those lines rather than over macroeconomic policy.

The 2027 budget is the first to be negotiated after the central bank charter reform and the fiscal bills now before the Senate, which gives the governors a second front to trade against.

What to Watch in the Text

The inflation and exchange-rate assumptions are the first thing to check, because everything else follows from them.

After that, the level of capital spending and the treatment of provincial transfers are the two lines that determine whether the bill can pass. A budget that holds the surplus by compressing both is easier to defend in Washington than in Congress.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

When must the budget be submitted?

By 15 September 2026, under the financial administration law.

What assumptions has the government published?

None on inflation or the exchange rate. The July advance document contained only qualitative claims.

What are forecasters expecting?

The IMF projects about 4% growth and 15.7% inflation; LatinFocus 3% and 21.7%; the central bank’s market survey about 20.5%.

How many votes are needed?

129 for a quorum in the Chamber of Deputies.

Who are the obstacles?

Blocs aligned with provincial governors, several of which have already broken with the government this year.

Sources: El Cronista, Infobae, El Destape, Cipolletti Digital.

World.title: A Copper Case for Cajamarca, Made by a Company That Owns Copper
World.content:
PERU · MINING

Key Facts — The argument Regulus Resources says Cajamarca’s gold mines are within a few years of exhaustion and copper should follow.

— Whose argument John Black, chief executive of Regulus Resources. An interested party.

— His words A mine has a life, and some are a few years, or at most ten, from finishing.

— The project AntaKori, a copper-gold skarn and porphyry system in Hualgayoc province, above 4,000 metres.

— The resource Indicated 250 million tonnes at 0.48% copper. The estimate dates from 2019.

— The stage Exploration and resource definition. No published feasibility study or permitting timetable.

A copper explorer telling a mining conference that the region’s gold is running out is making a case, not reporting a finding. The case is still worth examining.

A Copper Case for Cajamarca, Made by a Company That Owns Copper

Regulus Resources has argued at a Peruvian mining conference that Cajamarca’s established gold mines are approaching the end of their lives and that copper is the region’s next option, an assessment that comes from the company holding the copper project.

Who Is Making the Claim

John Black, chief executive of Regulus Resources, made the argument in comments reported on 13 September 2026. He described Yanacocha as South America’s largest gold mine and said the region’s mines are within a few years, or at most ten, of finishing.

That is an assertion by an interested party rather than an independent finding. Regulus holds the copper project it is proposing as the alternative, and the argument is a pitch.

No specific closure timeline for Yanacocha appears in the reporting, and none for Coimolache, Tantahuatay, Shahuindo or La Zanja. The Rio Times does not supply a date that its sources do not contain.

What AntaKori Is

AntaKori sits in Hualgayoc province in Cajamarca, above 4,000 metres and above agricultural land. It is a skarn and porphyry copper-gold system, the geological setting that produces most of the world’s large copper deposits.

The most recent published resource estimate dates from 2019: indicated 250 million tonnes at 0.48% copper, 0.29 grams a tonne gold and 7.5 grams a tonne silver, with a further 267 million tonnes inferred at 0.41% copper.

A seven-year-old estimate is a limitation worth stating. Regulus has reported expanding the mineralised footprint since, but the published numbers have not been restated.

Copper reached a record price in September 2026.

What Stage It Is At

AntaKori is at exploration and resource definition. No preliminary economic assessment or feasibility study milestone, permitting status or development timetable appears in the accessible reporting.

Regulus presented the project at EXPOMINA 2026 on 11 September as a multigenerational copper asset, and has held progress meetings with Peru’s energy and mines ministry.

The project involves collaboration with Compañía Minera Coimolache and Buenaventura, including an integrated resource estimate across the adjoining ground. Ownership percentages are not confirmed in accessible sourcing and The Rio Times does not state them.

Why the Underlying Argument Holds Anyway

Interested or not, the geological point is sound. Cajamarca’s producing mines are mature, and copper deposits do sit beneath and alongside the gold systems in the same belt, because both are products of the same intrusive events.

Copper at a record price in September 2026 makes the economics of a Cajamarca copper project look better than they did, and the region has the road and power infrastructure that a mining district accumulates over decades.

Social licence is the binding constraint on Cajamarca mining.

The Part No Resource Estimate Answers

Cajamarca is where the Conga project was halted in 2011 after sustained protests over water, and social licence is the binding constraint on mining in the region rather than geology or price.

A project sited above 4,000 metres and above agricultural zones is in precisely the position that produced those conflicts. A multigenerational asset in Cajamarca is a claim about the rock, and the rock has never been the difficult part.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is being claimed?

That Cajamarca’s gold mines are within a few years, or at most ten, of exhaustion, and that copper is the region’s next option.

Who is claiming it?

John Black, chief executive of Regulus Resources, which holds the AntaKori copper project.

What is AntaKori?

A copper-gold skarn and porphyry system in Hualgayoc province, Cajamarca, above 4,000 metres.

How large is the resource?

Indicated 250 million tonnes at 0.48% copper, plus 267 million tonnes inferred at 0.41%, on a 2019 estimate.

What stage is it at?

Exploration and resource definition. No feasibility study or permitting timetable has been published.

Sources: Gestión, Minart, Proactivo.

World.title: Mexico’s AI Cloning Law May Not Cover the Case Testing It
World.content:
MEXICO · TECHNOLOGY

Key Facts — The accusation The YouTuber Luisito Comunica says government-linked accounts used AI to clone his likeness.

— The content Videos praising President Sheinbaum’s annual report, using the faces of well-known Mexicans.

— Where An account called Conversación Pública carrying Mexican government logos. It has since disappeared from platforms.

— Who published it Not established. No federal department has been identified.

— The response None. The government has not commented.

— The legal gap Mexico’s 2026 AI-cloning reform protects artists and performers. Protection for ordinary people’s image and voice was removed before passage.

The interesting part is not whether it happened. It is that Mexico wrote a law against exactly this in May and then took most of it out.

Mexico’s AI Cloning Law May Not Cover the Case Testing It

Luis Arturo Villar Sudek, the YouTuber known as Luisito Comunica, has accused the Mexican government of generating artificial-intelligence videos using his likeness to praise President Claudia Sheinbaum’s annual report, in a case that lands squarely in a gap left by this year’s copyright reform.

What He Said

Writing on Instagram Stories on 13 September 2026, he described what he had seen as videos made by the Mexican government with artificial intelligence, using the faces of famous people, speaking well of the president’s report.

He added that it is very poor form for the Mexican government to use the faces of Mexicans without authorisation.

What Is Not Established

The clips appeared on an account called Conversación Pública, which carried Mexican government logos and has since disappeared from the platforms.

No federal department has been identified as the publisher, and none has confirmed or denied responsibility. A logo on an account is not proof of who operates it, and The Rio Times does not name a ministry.

The government has not responded. That is different from denying, and it should not be reported as a denial.

The videos praised the president’s annual report.

The Law Mexico Passed This Year

Mexico reformed its federal copyright law and its labour law in 2026 to create protection against artificial-intelligence cloning of voice and image. The Chamber of Deputies approved it on 7 April and it was published in the official gazette on 14 May 2026.

Penalties reach 40,000 days of minimum wage. But the protection was written for artistas intérpretes: performers, voice actors and dubbing professionals, the industries that lobbied for it.

Protection for ordinary people’s own image and voice was stripped from Article 87 late in the legislative process, after lobbying by industry associations.

Why That Matters Here

Eduardo De La Parra, who teaches intellectual property at UNAM, described the effect bluntly: consent is irrelevant to the law, and even where people object, the use of their image and voice data can be carried out freely.

Whether a YouTuber falls within the performer category is genuinely unsettled. Someone who appears on camera, scripts and presents content could be argued into it; someone the law drafters had in mind when they wrote artista intérprete probably was not.

That is the story. A country that legislated against artificial-intelligence likeness cloning four months ago may not have legislated against the case now testing it.

The 2026 reform protects performers rather than the general public.

A Sourcing Note

The substantive reporting comes from Infobae México, with other coverage syndicating it. The Rio Times reports it as a single-source account of the accusation.

An unrelated fake circulated in July 2026 claiming Sheinbaum had barred Luisito Comunica from Mexico. It was debunked at the time and has nothing to do with this.

What Would Resolve It

Identifying who operated the account is the first question, and it is answerable: government communications contracts are public, and an account carrying official logos was either authorised or it was impersonating the state.

The second question is whether anyone tests the law. A case brought by a well-resourced public figure would establish where the boundary of the performer category sits, which is the part of this that matters to everyone who is not famous.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the accusation?

That government-linked accounts used AI to clone the likenesses of well-known Mexicans, including Luisito Comunica, to praise the president’s annual report.

Who published the videos?

An account called Conversación Pública carrying government logos, since removed. No department has been identified.

Has the government responded?

No. It has not commented, which is not the same as a denial.

Does Mexican law cover this?

Possibly not. The 2026 reform protects artists and performers; protection for ordinary people’s image and voice was removed from Article 87 before passage.

When did that law take effect?

It was published in the official gazette on 14 May 2026.

Sources: Infobae México, Expansión, Diario Oficial de la Federación, Proceso.

World.title: Belize businessman says country is not ready for medical emergencies after nephew forced to seek care in Melchor
World.content:
Belize businessman says country is not ready for medical emergencies after nephew forced to seek care in Melchor

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Belize businessman is calling for improvements to the country’s emergency medical services after saying his nephew had to travel across the border to Melchor de Mencos, Guatemala, to receive urgent medical attention.

Fernando A. Boteo shared his concerns on social media, declaring that “Belize is not ready for an emergency.”

According to Boteo, he contacted doctors and emergency services while trying to secure immediate medical assistance for his nephew, but none of the services he contacted were available to provide the help needed at the time.

He said his nephew eventually had to travel to Melchor to obtain medical attention.

Boteo stressed that his criticism was not intended simply to assign blame, but to call attention to what he believes are serious shortcomings in emergency preparedness.

He called for better emergency services, greater availability and a healthcare system capable of responding when lives are potentially at risk.

“We should never have to leave our country to find emergency medical care when someone needs help right now,” Boteo wrote.

The circumstances surrounding his nephew’s medical emergency and the specific services contacted were not detailed in the post.

World.title: Diesel hits $15.96 per gallon as concerns grow over cost to Belize businesses
World.content:
Diesel hits $15.96 per gallon as concerns grow over cost to Belize businesses

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Concerns are growing over the cost of doing business in Belize following another increase in the price of diesel.

A social media post circulating this weekend highlighted that diesel has risen to $15.96 per gallon, describing the increase as another blow to the country’s business sector.

The higher price of diesel has implications beyond motorists filling their tanks.

Businesses that depend heavily on transportation, generators, construction equipment and delivery vehicles can face higher operating expenses when fuel prices rise. Those costs can eventually affect the prices consumers pay for goods and services.

The transportation sector is particularly exposed since buses, trucks, taxis, tour operators and other commercial vehicles depend on fuel to operate.

Businesses involved in agriculture and construction can also face additional pressure because diesel powers much of the heavy equipment used in those industries.

The latest increase comes amid growing public discussion over fuel and energy costs in Belize.

Opposition Leader Tracy Taegar Panton also criticized the latest diesel increase this weekend, arguing that businesses and working families are being placed under increasing financial pressure.

The price of diesel has therefore become another focal point in the wider debate over Belize’s cost of living and the cost of doing business.

World.content:
Woman says electricity bill soared from $340 to $1,040, sparking questions online

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A social media post questioning a sharp increase in a household electricity bill is generating discussion among Belizeans.

The woman behind the post says she normally paid approximately $340 per month, but a recent amount due reached $1,040.55.

Factors such as higher consumption, unpaid balances, adjustments or other billing issues could potentially affect the total, but the exact reason is not known.

There has been no independent confirmation that the bill was incorrectly calculated.

The complaint comes at a time when the cost of electricity and household expenses remain major concerns for many Belizean families.

Customers who notice unusual increases on their electricity bills are encouraged to review their consumption history and seek an explanation directly from BEL.
