World.title: Sweden exit poll: Left on course for election win in blow to far right
World.content:
Two separate exit polls for Sweden’s SVT public broadcaster and TV4 showed Andersson’s left bloc on track to take 51% of the vote. (Sweden’s electoral system is based on proportional representation.) Kristersson’s alliance on the right was projected to win 47%.

Exit polls have not always been accurate in the past, but the picture should become clearer later on Sunday night when broadcasters are expected to announce updated forecasts after a critical mass of districts declare results. Whoever ends up winning, party leaders will take weeks to finalize a new coalition agreement.

“Swedish elections are always close,” Andersson told POLITICO earlier on Sunday as she toured the suburbs of Stockholm in her dark red campaign bus. “When I’ve been around Sweden, a lot of people I’ve spoken to said they see things that the government has done that they like but there are also lots of things that they don’t like. And many people say to me that it’s enough now.”

With the prospect of the far right entering government for the first time, the vote marks a watershed moment for Sweden that will be watched closely elsewhere in Europe, where other populist nationalist parties are gaining ground.

Even Andersson accepts that a victory for her left bloc would not consign the Sweden Democrats to history, especially if the final result is a narrow one.

“The hate that they have spread through this election, and if they would become ministers and use their platforms as ministers to spread hate? Well, we’ll see if the Swedish people are very tempted on that,” she said.

World.title: Suspected Russian spy behind drone attack in Leipzig
World.content:
Some 1.8 kilograms of the explosive Semtex was to be used across all three drones — about 600 grams per drone — according to the high-ranking German security official. The Antonov aircraft, which was the target of the attack, was fueled with approximately 25,000 liters of jet fuel.

Two of the senior security officials, both directly involved in the investigation, said that if the charge had detonated, it would have triggered a massive explosion and destroyed parts of the airport. Previously unseen surveillance camera footage obtained by Welt shows the drone lying right next to the Antonov aircraft. According to authorities, the explosive was concealed inside a food can. The explosion did not occur because a detonator broke off.

One day after the attempted attack, police officers found an antenna structure secured with tape in a tree near the airport. It is believed to have been used to control the drones, according to the confidential documents. On the structure, forensic technicians found remnants of a glove with traces of DNA previously recorded in Finland and Lithuania. The Belarusian suspect has a criminal record in those countries, according to one of the senior security officials (in Finland, for example, he was charged with theft, among other offenses).

The Polish authorities also believe the suspect was involved in a fire at a home improvement store in the city of Łódź in the summer of 2024, according to a senior security official. (The Łódź public prosecutor’s office has likewise classified the incident as sabotage.) German investigators view the fact that he was also involved in the Leipzig attack as further evidence of Russian involvement.

According to the high-ranking German security official, the explosives used in Leipzig were transported to Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia. Investigators believe they were transported in hidden compartments in trucks and subsequently cached underground. Police found several possible hiding places near Leipzig airport after analyzing data from a rental car used by the suspects.

The confidential police documents also refer to a concrete slab with two handles that was discovered near a pedestrian bridge south of the airport, in the city of Schkeuditz. Authorities believe it had provided access to a hidden storage site. Shortly thereafter, police found another suspected hideout north of the bridge; both storage sites were empty. Investigators also located a hideout in the city of Merseburg, part of the Halle-Leipzig area. According to the police documents, the Russian suspect may have temporarily stored the explosives there.

World.title: Trump calls on Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries
World.content:
Trump said officials from his administration had asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop drone and missile attacks on any Russian sites that produce diesel.

“Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said during a pause on his tour of his Doonbeg golf course on Ireland’s west coast. “Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel fuel.”

The U.S. leader maintained that the conflict Washington initiated with Iran more than six months ago is not to blame for the shortfall. “This isn’t done by the Middle East,” Trump said. “This is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine. So we spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”

Ukraine’s increasingly deep-range strikes on Russian energy infrastructure are seen as a key part of its strategy to make Russia’s 4-year full-scale invasion of the country prohibitively costly for Moscow.

But a senior European official familiar with U.S.-brokered mediation talks between Moscow and Kyiv told POLITICO that the Trump administration was searching for scapegoats ahead of crucial Nov. 3 midterm elections in the United States. The official was granted anonymity to comment on sensitive aspects of the three-way discussions.

“This administration is blaming Ukraine because they do not know what to do with their war [in Iran],” the official said. “Russian exports of diesel and oil have never been significant for U.S. consumption. The very idea is absurd. Moreover, we have all heard President Trump say that America itself can supply as much oil as anyone wants.”

World.title: France climbs down in social media row with U.S. after ambassador’s appointment blocked
World.content:
AFP reported that the U.S. State Department responded positively to the apology. “We take note of France’s statement and appreciate it; we look forward to collaborating with them to promote our common values ​​and interests,” a State Department official told AFP on condition of anonymity.

The appointment of French diplomat Aurélien Lechevallier as ambassador to the U.S. was blocked by Washington as a result of the spat, France24 reports.

The dispute began in July when the French mission to the U.N. in Geneva posted on X that “The U.S. used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore.” This comment came after the U.S. voted against renewing the term of the UN Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk.

Two days later after the French mission’s social media post, the U.S. walked out of a U.N. security council meeting when France’s representative began to speak.

The apology from France and acceptance from the U.S. paves the way for Lechevallier to be confirmed for the Washington role. Currently chief of staff to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, Lechevallier is set to replace Laurent Bili as France’s U.S. envoy.

It’s not the first time the two countries have had a diplomatic spat. Last year, France summoned U.S. Ambassador Charles Kushner after he published an open letter accusing President Emmanuel Macron’s government of not doing enough to combat rising antisemitism in his country.

World.title: Russian drone hits passenger train headed from Kyiv to Warsaw
World.content:
Ukraine's Foreign Affairs Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s forces are “knocking directly on the doors of the EU and NATO.” | Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha responded to the attack by stating that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s forces are “knocking directly on the doors of the EU and NATO.”

BRUSSELS — Russian drones attacked a crossing point on the Polish-Ukrainian border on Sunday morning, hitting a passenger train two kilometers from the frontier in Volyn Oblast.

Ukraine’s state rail operator confirmed that a strike hit the locomotive of a passenger train bound for Warsaw. The train crew were warned of the threat in advance by Ukrainian authorities and no one was injured, the operator added.

Separately, social media videos showed a large fire at a gas station near the Yahodyn–Dorohusk crossing point between Ukraine and Poland. According to local media, there are no reports yet of casualties from the gas station fire.

World.title: How to watch Sweden’s election like a pro
World.content:
That means there are only two realistic candidates to be prime minister: the incumbent, conservative Moderate party leader Ulf Kristersson; and Magdalena Andersson, the former PM who leads Sweden’s biggest party, the center-left Social Democrats.

Swedish Prime Minister and Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson speaks to the media upon arrival to a televised election debate hosted by TV4 in Stockholm, Sweden, on September 10, 2026, three days ahead of the country’s general election. | Jonathan Nackstrand/ AFP via Getty Images

Kristersson has run the right-wing coalition for the past four years thanks to influential support from the second biggest party, the far-right Sweden Democrats. They backed him in votes in parliament and drove policy in a hardline direction, including crackdowns on crime and especially immigration. But the Sweden Democrats did not join the coalition cabinet. That could now change.

Can the far right enter the government?

Kristersson divided opinion in 2022 when he broke a decades-long taboo against working with the far right and did his deal with the Sweden Democrats, who had won 20% of the vote. The SD was founded in the 1980s and some members in those days had roots in neo-Nazi movements. The party has taken steps to clean up its act in recent years, though not to everyone’s satisfaction.

Now Kristersson says he will give the SD ministerial seats in government if his side wins on Sunday, as part of an agreement with the far-right leader, Jimmie Åkesson. That would be another huge step for Sweden and one that the opposition has seized on.

“Of course this would be a different country with a government with half of the ministers from the Sweden Democrats,” opposition leader Andersson told AP recently. “It would not be good for Sweden if they would get the keys to the ministry of defense or the ministry of foreign affairs.”

Kristersson insists he would still be in charge overall. He points to his work with Åkesson over the past four years which he says has revived the economy and cut rates of violent crime and immigration, both of which had been major public concerns. “I can guarantee you that it will only be very skilled and experienced and people with good judgment that would be part of my government,” he told POLITICO.

World.title: Will Lagarde bite the apple? ECB president leaves everyone guessing in Normandy
World.content:
On stage, she even encouraged reporters who made the trip to Normandy to cover her potential political comeback to pack up early, promising that they would be disappointed.

But there are signs suggesting that the ECB chief, who entered into politics during the presidency of France's apple-loving Jacques Chirac, is increasingly willing to weigh in on the campaign.

While she promised to stay at least until the end of the year, Lagarde previously refused to rule out leaving before the end of her term, which ends in October 2027.

Earlier this week, she announced that she would publish her first autobiography, Lady First, in January. She also waded into the French presidential debate by rejecting French far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s proposal to wipe out government debt.

Her presence at the apple festival in the 15th-century Manoir de la Fortière — an unconventional locale for a central banker's speech — might be yet another signal. Opening the event, Morin said that he tried to invite her for years but never managed to make it work. Until this year.

Christine Lagarde is seen at the Fête de la Pomme in France on Sept. 12, 2026. | Giorgio Leali/POLITICO

“Everyone is happy to have you here and I realized to what extent you have an exceptional reputation,” said Morin, who worked with Lagarde when they both served as ministers under conservative president Nicolas Sarkozy, including during the 2008 financial crisis.

World.title: EU-Parlament öffnet sich für härtere China-Politik
World.content:
Brüssel und Peking führen derzeit Verhandlungen darüber, wie das Handelsdefizit der EU gegenüber China in Höhe von 1 Milliarde Euro pro Tag ausgeglichen werden kann. Ein Anstieg der chinesischen Exporte hat die einheimischen Hersteller unter Druck gesetzt und Schrecken geschürt, dass der Kontinent angesichts vielbeachteter Werksschließungen in der Automobil- und Chemieindustrie eine Deindustrialisierung durchläuft.

EU-Handelskommissar Maroš Šefčovič wird im Oktober im Rahmen der Gespräche nach Peking reisen. Er erklärte, die Union sei bereit zu handeln, falls bis zu diesem Zeitpunkt keine Fortschritte erzielt würden.

Die Kommission erwägt Maßnahmen, um Chinas industrieller Dominanz entgegenzuwirken, darunter neue Vorschriften, die Unternehmen dazu anregen sollen, ihre kritischen Lieferketten zu diversifizieren, sowie Schutzmaßnahmen, die die Einfuhr wichtiger Güter wie Hybrid-Elektrofahrzeuge begrenzen würden.

In einer gemeinsamen Erklärung vom Donnerstag sprach sich der Ausschuss für auswärtige Angelegenheiten des Europäischen Parlaments für eine Eindämmung der chinesischen Exporte und der übermäßigen Abhängigkeit Europas von Rohstoffen bis hin zu Halbleitern aus und forderte die EU auf, Maßnahmen zu ergreifen, um die „Instrumentalisierung der wirtschaftlichen Abhängigkeit der EU“ einzudämmen.

„Business as usual“ gibt es nicht mehr

Canfin erklärte, unter den EU-Abgeordneten setze sich zunehmend die Erkenntnis durch, dass „Business as usual“ in den Beziehungen der Union zu Peking keine Option mehr sei. Als Beleg für den Wandel in der Haltung gegenüber China verwies er auf die wachsende Unterstützung im Parlament für eine offensivere Industriepolitik.

Die Abgeordneten arbeiten derzeit an ihrer Position zum vorgeschlagenen „Industrial Accelerator Act“, mit dem im Rahmen der umweltorientierten öffentlichen Beschaffung eine europäische Präferenz in strategischen Industriezweigen verankert werden soll. Die federführenden Abgeordneten dieses wegweisenden Gesetzentwurfs streben einen eng verbundenen „Made in Europe“-Club sowie eine strengere Prüfung ausländischer Direktinvestitionen an.

World.title: Sweden’s left-wing opposition leads election, far right loses ground: exit polls
World.content:
Sweden’s centre-left opposition bloc, which backs Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson for prime minister, was projected to win 51.3% of the vote in Sunday’s parliamentary election, according to an exit poll by broadcaster SVT.

 

A separate election-day poll conducted by broadcaster TV4 also put the centre-left opposition ahead.

The Sweden Democrats came third in the SVT/Valu poll, behind Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s Moderates.

A victory for the right-wing bloc would bring the far-right Sweden Democrats into government for the first time.

Swedish exit polls are often indicative but have not always proved accurate. In 2022, an exit poll projected Andersson’s bloc would prevail, but a right-wing coalition led by Ulf Kristersson ultimately won.

Kristersson is seeking another term after leading a minority government made up of his centre-right Moderate Party, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals. The coalition relies on the backing of the Sweden Democrats, which have become increasingly influential in Swedish politics.

Kristersson has said he could go a step further after the election and form a governing coalition that formally includes the Sweden Democrats. Such an outcome would mark a historic breakthrough for the far right, giving the party direct access to government for the first time and underlining its growing role in Swedish politics.

The exit-poll result could complicate the right’s efforts to retain power, particularly if the Sweden Democrats demand a formal role in government.

Around eight million people are eligible to vote in the Nordic country of roughly 10.6 million. More than half have already cast their ballots in advance, reflecting Sweden’s traditionally high voter turnout.

Official results are expected within a week, while preliminary results from the Swedish Election Authority are due within hours.

World.title: Peter Magyar announces upcoming changes to child adoption regulations for singles and same-sex couples
World.content:
The Hungarian government has published a 220-page, comprehensive child-protection report which concluded that the child adoption system is on the verge of collapse.

 

The document will serve as the basis for rewriting adoption rules, a move that has triggered fierce political reactions among opposition parties.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that the government will change the regulations governing adoption by single persons and same-sex couples, arguing that the current system is unsustainable.

He stated that deciding who may adopt a child should not be a political decision but one taken by professionals, like psychologists and child-protection experts. Politicians, Magyar said, need to take a step back from this issue.

He stressed that the "system cannot function properly in its current state," and that the overpowering consideration must always be that children can grow up in a loving family, not the parents' sexual orientation or marital status.

The Hungarian premier said the government is already working on amendments to the existing legislation, which was introduced earlier by Fidesz under longtime Prime Minister and Magyar's predecessor, Viktor Orbán.

The system Magyar wants to overhaul, in its current state, favours married couples and severely restricts the options available to single people and same-sex couples.

The announcement has generated strong criticism in local media, with opposition outlets slamming the move, accusing Magyar of "giving in to the LGBTQ lobby", while independent media reported it as a pledge to restore professional standards.

Policy break from Orbán-era

The move marks a sharp ideological and policy break with the legacy of the Orbán governments in power between 2010 and 2026, and is one of the most significant steps taken yet on human rights and child protection in Hungary since the change of government in April 2026.

In December 2020, the Orbán government tightened the Hungarian Fundamental Law and the adoption act, which tightly defined a mother as a biological female and the father a biological male, effectively restricting adoption to married couples as the default.

Because same-sex couples in Hungary cannot marry, and can only enter into registered partnerships, they had previously been able to adopt by having one partner submit the application as a single person.

A 2020 law ended this loophole, as it forced single applicants to adopt only with a valid personal ministerial permit, initially granted by former President Katalin Novák and later by the minister responsible for family policy.

The amended legislation effectively blocked members of the LGBTQ community almost entirely from the possibility of having children.

After the Tisza Party won the elections in April this year by a landslide, thereby ending Fidesz's 16 years in power, international and domestic human rights organisations expected immediate steps to restore LGBTQ rights.

Pressure increased further when, just before the vote, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Hungary's earlier "child-protection/homophobic" law seriously breaches EU law.

According to the government's narrative, the current system is unsustainable because, while large numbers of children live in state-care, suitable prospective parents, whether single or in same-sex relationships, are blocked in the system due to strict political filters and bureaucratic hurdles.

The new measure effectively restores the pre-2020, profession-based assessment system and sends a strong signal that the new government intends to approach social issues, previously used as symbolic political battlegrounds, in a pragmatic, expert-led way.

World.title: Canada eyes ‘associate member’ status with EU amid US tensions, WSJ reports
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is exploring closer ties with the European Union, including becoming an “associate member” of the bloc, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.

 

The status does not currently exist, but the EU could be open to creating special membership arrangements, the newspaper said, citing unnamed EU and Canadian officials. The European Commission did not respond to a request for comment.

The report comes ahead of a speech by Carney to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday, where he is expected to set out his vision for Canada-EU ties in a challenging geopolitical environment.

Ottawa is locked in a historic trade war with the United States, with steep tariffs in place and no signs of de-escalation.

The EU and Canada want to bolster trade ties of goods, services and workers, particularly in areas including energy, artificial intelligence, defence and critical minerals, according to the report.

The two are also said to be discussing major joint projects, including undersea cables, data centres, cloud infrastructure and satellite networks. Canada also wants to expand energy exports to Europe, the WSJ said.

Still, securing any form of “associate member” status could prove difficult. The EU has strict rules on membership and a lengthy process for making changes to its existing arrangements.

Yet the impact of Trump's presidency, marked by tariffs and threats on both sides of the Atlantic, could encourage a more flexible approach.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz earlier this year outlined his own vision for an “associate member” status, originally intended for Ukraine but potentially applicable to Canada. The model would deepen ties with the EU without requiring full membership.

Macron and Carney in joint visit

French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will visit the French territory of Saint-Pierre-and-Miquelon next week, about 20 km off Canada’s Atlantic coast, in a show of support for their close ties amid tensions with US President Donald Trump, Paris said on Sunday.

Trump posted an image on his Truth Social account on Monday showing a map of North America with the US flag over several French overseas territories, including Saint-Pierre-and-Miquelon, as well as Guadeloupe and Martinique. The map also included Iceland, Greenland, Mexico, Canada, much of Central America and the Caribbean.

The visit will highlight the shared values of France and Canada, including “freedom, democracy, the rule of law and respect for the sovereignty of nations”, the Elysee Palace said.

“In a world marked by the return of power politics, geopolitical tensions and new forms of dependency, France and Canada share a common ambition” to strengthen their ability to act independently, it added.

The visit will be the first by a Canadian prime minister to the archipelago, the French presidency said. The last French president to visit was Francois Hollande in 2014.

World.title: Le Pen kicks off presidential election campaign amid party tensions
World.content:
Back in her political stronghold in northern France, Marine Le Pen is delivering her first major campaign speech this Sunday. The far-right candidate for 2027 will be in Hénin-Beaumont as part of her presidential election, after MPs from her party met in Le Touquet (Pas-de-Calais) on Saturday.

 

Le Pen is currently leading in the polls, with 34% of voters declaring they intend to vote for her in the first round — across different tested scenarios — according to a survey carried out on 8 and 9 September by OpinionWay for Les Échos.

Despite this, recent weeks have been marked by a series of mishaps, amid alleged tensions between Le Pen and the president of the National Rally (RN) party, Jordan Bardella, as well as controversial remarks over aid to Ukraine and the release of a video in which a police officer — and former volunteered of the RN’s security team — makes racist, sexist and conspiracy-theory-based remarks.

Meanwhile, Le Pen has still not reacted to the signing of an immigration pact between Bardella and Nigel Farage, the leader of the UK's hard-right, anti-immigration Reform UK party, which provides for migrants intercepted in British waters to be sent back to France — should the two parties be elected.

What role will Bardella play?

In recent weeks, rumours around alleged tensions between Le Pen and Bardella — who is vying to be France's next prime minister — have been swirling.

According to French newspaper Libération, the president of the National Rally is said to have declared "it’s her or me" on 31 August, after Le Pen reportedly announced she intended to give her niece — Marion Maréchal — a greater role in the campaign.

During the 2022 presidential campaign, Maréchal backed Éric Zemmour, the leader of the rival far-right party Reconquête over her aunt.

Bardella subsequently denied any tensions, telling the French broadcaster BFM-TV: "Everything is going very, very well, I assure you. I support her 2,000%." He added that he had an "unbreakable political and personal affinity" with Le Pen while also denying that he wanted to "impose" his line on the party.

The two leading figures of the National Rally have presented different economic visions, especially concerning pensions. According to Bardella, the current French pension system "is not economically sustainable." He also seems hesitant to have his "boss" turn her proposed ban on the wearing of the veil in public spaces into a central campaign issue.

On 31 August, he insisted that the aim was not "to impose a dress code," stressing that a referendum on the issue would be held. The president of the Patriots for Europe group in the European Parliament also appears more pro-market than Le Pen, who has traditionally been more supportive of protectionist measures.

Support for Ukraine

Beyond this, the RN is also facing disagreements over international issues.

Speaking to BFM-TV on 4 September, Louis Aliot, the party’s vice-president and mayor of Perpignan, was asked about aid to Ukraine

"We turn off the tap. The health system, the education system, the whole economy, everything has been cut to the bone, and yet we still find money to fund more weapons (...) I’m willing to accept that, but who pays for all this? You also have to know how to stop a war," he said.

His comments quickly sparked a debate.

Taking to X, Édouard Philippe, the centre-right Horizons party’s candidate for 2027, seized the opportunity to accuse the RN of "its support for Putin’s regime," arguing that "turning off the tap for Ukraine means serving Russia."

"Weakening Ukraine, as Marine Le Pen wants, means threatening the security of Europe and France. I will do everything to stop her," he added.

Le Pen hit back within the hour, reminding the former prime minister that he was in office when the Russian president was "received with great pomp at the Palace of Versailles and then at the Fort of Brégançon," and that he himself had welcomed Dmitry Medvedev, then Russian prime minister, to his home city of Le Havre in June 2019.

National Rally grapples with police scandal

On 8 September, French regional daily Midi Libre released a video from November 2025 showing several municipal police officers in Carcassonne making racist, sexist and conspiracy-related comments during a nighttime patrol.

The patrol leader, responsible for nearly 90% of the remarks made that evening, is a former paratrooper, but he had also volunteered for the RN's internal security service.

He notably escorted Bardella on several trips, including during the promotional tour for his book, as well as at the launch of the RN's municipal election campaign.

The officer in question was expelled from the National Rally on Wednesday. Bardella, for his part, has described his comments as "despicable."

The Carcassonne public prosecutor’s office also announced on Wednesday the suspension of the four municipal police officers who appear in the video.

World.title: Trump accuses Ukraine of pushing up energy prices while on two-day visit to Ireland
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has called on Ukraine to stop attacking diesel refineries as part of its military’s counteroffensive operations against Russia, accusing the attacks of contributing to diesel shortages around the world.

 

“Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump told reporters. "Let him go after targets, but not diesel, because he's causing a shortage of diesel."

Trump was speaking in Ireland where he’s on a 48-hour trip primarily to attend the Irish Open Golf Tournament held at his private golf links hotel in Doonbeg, County Clare.

He appeared to blame Ukraine’s war efforts in targeting Russia as the main reason for spiralling energy prices, despite experts pointing to his and Israel's war on Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, from which 20% of the world's oil typically flows, as the main culprit.

Trump said Ukraine has "plenty of other targets" to strike, noting that Kyiv’s strategy in going after Moscow’s oil and gas reserves in response to Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 is "hurting the world."

Meanwhile, Dublin is breathing a sigh of relief after a successful round of diplomatic engagements with Trump which culminated in his calls for a united Ireland.

Trump met with Irish Prime Minister Taoiseach MicheálMartin as part of his round trip where he is due to present the winner of the tournament with the trophy on Sunday evening before returning to Washington.

Trump raised the issue of the Republic of Ireland and the UK's Northern Ireland ‘merging’ to become one country in the future on numerous occasions including in a 45-minute speech at the US Ambassador's residence in the Phoenix Park, Dublin.

He said it was "natural to put north and south together.”

"I've always loved the people of Ireland. It just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland," he said.

"It seems to me that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together," he said to reporters after his meeting with Micheál Martin on Saturday.

Trump also reportedly initiated the topic of a united Ireland with Irish President Catherine Connolly, a left-wing politician who has on numerous occasions criticised her US counterpart in the past, and even lambasted him as a "bully".

President Connolly presented Trump with a book of poems from Belfast-born poet Michael Longley. Regarded as one of "the finest poets Ireland has produced", Longley's work spans love, war, nature, and art.

"His sonnet ‘Ceasefire’, drawing on Homer, has become one of the defining Irish poems about what it is to forgive," her press team said in a statement after the meeting.

Irish government sources say the issue of uniting Northern Ireland and Ireland – which would mean Northern Ireland to break away from the United Kingdom – is an issue Trump frequently raises whenever he’s in the company of diplomats or government officials.

Trump declared on Saturday that a unified Ireland "would be fantastic" and is "going to happen eventually.”

Newly-appointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently said a referendum on a united Ireland is currently "off the table".

"I'm here, as I said earlier, to listen, and I will take a collaborative approach, but some issues will be off the table, and that is one issue that will be off the table.”

Burnham detailed that until there is overwhelming evidence of a desire for a referendum, one would simply not be pre-emptively triggered. Sources close to Burnham have reiterated on Saturday that the UK premier's opinion has not changed following Trump's declarations.

Under the 1998 Good Friday Agreement peace settlement which ended over 30 years of armed conflict in Northern Ireland, a united Ireland can come about if it's the preference for the majority of the population.

A referendum on a so-called “border poll” must be triggered by the British government. The UK government did not respond to request for comments at time of writing.

Sources also revealed to Euronews that the timing of Trump's calls comes amid tensions between the US and UK over the war in Iran.

Washington has repeatedly slammed European NATO allies for not joining in the war in Iran. He was particularly scathing about former UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer who initially refused the US access to basing rights at military bases on British territories.

Starmer soon relented and allow US forces to use UK air bases for “defensive purposes.” But Trump frequently expresses his indignation over the matter, stating, "your country was not there to help me.”

More recently, the Trump administration has questioned British sovereignty over the Falkland islands after Argentine President Javier Milei again claimed the territory slightly off his country's shores.

Many believe Trump, a close friend of Milei's, may be retaliating against the UK by not leaping to their support.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | September 13th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: MOTELX ends 20th edition with awards for Nordic cinema
World.content:
In a landmark year marking its twentieth edition, MOTELX once again gave Lisbon audiences a fright with the best and most diverse horror cinema from different latitudes and styles, bidding farewell on Saturday night to an already loyal public with the crowning of an imaginative short about Portugal's Estado Novo and two Nordic films.

 

The MOTELX Award – Best Portuguese Horror Short 2026, the largest cash prize for national short films, worth €5,000, was presented to "A Hora do Chico!", by João Severo and Rafael Sá Carneiro. The jury, made up of Fernando Vasquez (programmer), José Santiago (journalist and programmer) and Sandra Henriques (journalist and author), highlighted the "ambition and maturity" of the film, "a disturbing journey through a past that few miss, which merges, in the best possible way, with an alternative reality".

There was also a Special Mention for "Consumido", by [carrozo], for its "humour and visual care, combined with narrative economy that turns the roles of predator and prey on their head".

As for the Meliès d'Argent awards, which select a feature and a short of European production to go on to compete for the Meliès d'Or in Sitges, the jury opted for "Mancave", by Norwegian director Fredrik S. Hana, in the short film competition, and "No Rest for the Wicked", by Dane Kasper Kalle, for features. The film is set in the Faroe Islands in the 19th century and showcases breathtaking landscapes.

The film "weaves desire, religion, repression, beauty, love and death together with rare elegance", as underlined by the jury composed of Isilda Sanches (journalist and music broadcaster), Leone Niel (director) and Teresa Nicolau (cultural director and columnist).

The juries also handed awards to "Hóspede", by Miguel Monteiro Rico (MOTELX Award – Best Portuguese Horror Screenplay), "Lexi" (Spain), directed by Portuguese filmmaker Bruno Simões, in the "Lobo Mau" section, aimed at younger audiences and families, and "Gunman", written and directed by Argentine filmmaker Cris Tapia Marchiori, winner of the Audience Award.

Julie Corman with João Monteiro, MOTELX director, at Saturday's Ricardo Figueira / Euronews

The festival paid tribute to Portuguese-Swedish filmmaker Solveig Nordlund with the Noémia Delgado Award for outstanding women in horror cinema and to Julie Corman, widow of American director and producer Roger Corman, to mark the centenary of his birth. Julie Corman returned to MOTELX for a masterclass largely devoted to her husband's long career, having previously accompanied Roger Corman when he was a special guest at the 2017 edition.

World.title: Austria's new headscarf ban for under-14s sparks debate over religious freedom
World.content:
Since the start of the 2026/27 school year on 1 September, female pupils in Austria under the age of 14 have been prohibited from wearing any headscarf at school that "covers the head in line with Islamic traditions."

 

Teachers' representatives say the new rule has generally been implemented calmly and respectfully. At the same time, some schools have reported conflicts and, in some cases, aggressive reactions.

The new law was already controversial before it came into force, with critics questioning whether it was compatible with freedom of religion and the principle of equality.

In 2020, Austria's Constitutional Court (VfGH) overturned an earlier headscarf ban. That law had prohibited primary school pupils from wearing religious or ideologically motivated clothing that covered the head and applied to children until the end of the school year in which they turned 10.

However, the VfGH found that the rule violated the principle of equality and freedom of religion. In the court's view, the law in practice was primarily aimed at the "Islamic" headscarf.

An international issue: women protest in Lahore on 13 February 2022 against a headscarf ban for Muslim schoolgirls in neighbouring India. AP Photo

The new law differs in its higher age limit.

The government says the main goal is to protect children's development and their freedom to develop as individuals, arguing that girls should be protected from potential family or social pressure to wear a headscarf.

The VfGH has not yet ruled on whether this revised justification, and the new design of the ban, address the constitutional concerns raised previously.

Teachers required to enforce ban

For the time being, schools and teachers are responsible for putting the ban into practice.

If a teacher notices that a pupil is wearing such a headscarf despite the ban, they are required to ask the pupil to remove it as a first step. If the pupil refuses, further discussions will take place. If necessary, the education authority may be brought in. Only at later stages can administrative penalty proceedings be initiated.

Students who repeatedly violate the ban can expect to face a multi-stage process, and parents or guardians could be fined between €150 and €800 if the headscarf continues to be worn despite being asked to remove it.

Representatives of the teachers' union have criticised the obligation on teachers to report breaches and warned that it risks putting them in a monitoring role that goes beyond their educational work.

Reports of threats and refusal to attend school

Possible threats and refusal to attend school have also become part of the debate surrounding the new law.

Austria's government had, even before the law was passed, pointed to cases in which girls or women were put under pressure both to wear and to remove a headscarf.

Integration Minister Claudia Plakolm referred, among other things, to instances of threats within families.

There are currently no statistics that would show how often such situations arise in Austrian schools.

Reports of pupils who do not attend lessons at all or do so only irregularly because of the headscarf ban also still need to be properly assessed. There are indications of isolated cases of refusal and conflict.

Women hold up a banner reading: AP Photo

Supporters of the new rules argue that girls at this age are particularly dependent on their families and could therefore be exposed to considerable social or religious pressure.

Critics have countered these concerns by questioning whether a state ban really strengthens the self-determination of the pupils concerned. A girl who wishes to wear a headscarf "of her own conviction" can no longer follow through with that decision at school because of the ban.

People protest in Rome on 1 October 2022 over the death of Mahsa Amin (22), who died in police custody in Iran. She had allegedly worn her head covering too loosely. AP Photo

There are also concerns from education experts. Psychologist Christiane Spiel warned on ORF of potential loyalty conflicts for children if parents insist on wearing a headscarf while the school demands that it be removed.

New constitutional challenge is pending

Before the law came into force, several parents had already tried to challenge it directly before the VfGH.

The court rejected these applications on formal grounds, as those concerned had not yet been directly affected by the law at that point.

A new application for the law to be struck down has now been filed.

The key issue, once again, is likely to be the relationship between freedom of religion and the principle of equality.

Among other things, the court will have to examine whether protecting children from religious or family pressure justifies an "interference with freedom of religion" and whether a general headscarf ban is necessary and proportionate to achieve this.

World.title: Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is signalling a move to expand nuclear power cooperation with Russia, just as his country’s first Russian-built nuclear station prepares to go live later this year. The deepening partnership is likely to unsettle Turkey’s western allies.

Advertising

On the sidelines of a recent gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan told his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that Russia and Turkey “will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant”.

The Akkuyu nuclear power plant, built by Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due to go online later this year.

Erdogan’s announcement comes amid strained ties with Russia, as the Turkish leader has deepened relations with United States President Donald Trump.

Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, head of the Ankara office of US think tank the German Marshall Fund, describes Erdogan’s move as a “gesture” to Putin.

“Although Turkey is competing with Russia geopolitically, and although Turkey is firmly anchored in NATO and is improving its relationship with the United States, it does not intend to sever all ties with Russia,” Unluhisarcikli explained.

“Indeed, Turkey sees the Turkey-Russia relationship as a long-term strategic one. And this is, by the way, consistent with Turkey's balancing act.”

Trump tests Turkey's energy dependence on Russia with lure of US power

Nuclear lifeline

For Ankara, nuclear energy promises to help it break free from its heavy reliance on imported power. Once operational, the Akkuyu plant in southern Turkey will supply as much as 10 percent of the country’s electricity.

Rosatom owns the Akkuyu power plant and will recoup the estimated €21.5 billion construction costs by selling electricity to Turkey, generating annual income of around €2-3 billion.

Such income could be a vital tool for Moscow to mitigate tightening sanctions by both the European Union and the United States.

“The Akkuyu nuclear power plant allows Russia to build itself various state-to-state payment channels to store liquidity in Turkish banks without necessarily interfering with any sanctions regulations,” according to George Voloshin of Acams, a global organisation dedicated to anti-financial crime, training and education.

Voloshin believes that, given the project's 60- to 80-year lifespan, Turkey’s commitment to Russian nuclear power will shape bilateral ties for the long term, with consequences.

“It will be a source of scrutiny from western partners of Turkey. At the same time, nuclear energy has been so far shielded from any sanctions, so for Russia it is clearly a kind of lifeline,” he said.

The Akkuyu plant, currently under construction, will be Turkey's first nuclear power station. © AFP/Dogan News Agency/Ibrahim Mese

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ankara has maintained that it is not bound by EU or US sanctions on Moscow. Yet behind the scenes, it has quietly followed many restrictions and secured crucial waivers, especially for Russian gas.

By leveraging its pivotal location near Syria and Iran, Ankara has walked a diplomatic tightrope between its western partners and Moscow.

However, deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia threatens to complicate the already difficult balancing act.

“It would reinforce the already existing distrust between Turkey and Europe and Turkey and the United States,” warned Unluhisarcikli.

“But at the same time, Turkey is in talks with other countries, the United States and South Korea. These are the main two competitors for Russia.”

Mutual dependency

Turkey’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels has stirred unease at home, and the idea of doubling down with Russian nuclear energy only heightens the sense of anxiety. “It is a dilemma,” Unluhisarcikli conceded.

Yet with Russia willing to shoulder the hefty construction costs, cash-strapped Ankara has a strong incentive to continue the partnership.

Russia expert Zaur Gasimov of Istanbul’s Turkish-German University points out that more than a decade of joint investment makes it tough for Turkey to turn to alternative suppliers.

"It's quite a profound project,” said Gasimov, “Russia conducts the training of Turkish specialists in the field of nuclear energy, which started 15 years ago. We now have three or four waves of Turkish engineers who stayed for longer periods in Russia; they learn the Russian language for two years, and you have an infrastructure of specialists.”

However, Gasimov stresses that, given the scale of investment by both sides, it has created an important mutual dependency. “Its importance makes the two sides, somehow, at the end, interested in preserving a certain level of the relationship,” he said.

This shared reliance might help keep Turkish-Russian rivalries in check, from North Africa to the Middle East, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

Yet any step toward deeper nuclear cooperation is bound to invite sharper scrutiny and rising suspicion from Ankara’s western allies.

World.title: Turkey: 162 arrested in LGBTQ+ raids
World.content:
Turkish authorities have arrested at least 162 people in a weekend crackdown on the country's LGBTQ+ community. Ankara says police raids on gay bars and other venues are aimed at protecting family values.

Turkish police have arrested at least 162 people and searched the offices of six LGBTQ+ associations in weekend raids designed to support the country's campaign to protect family values.

The Ankara-based LGBTQ+ rights group Kaos GL claimed that beyond arrests, the government had also cut access to dozens of websites and social media accounts belonging to associate groups and rights advocates.

Government says its fulfilling duty to 'protect families and children'

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said investigations — prompted by accusations of prostitution and obscenity — were coordinated by prosecutors in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Aydin and Mersin and involved judicial proceedings against 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces.

"As per the duty to protect families and children given to the state by the constitution, no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated!" Gurlek added in a social media post.

Authorities say they seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a gun in weekend police operations targeting gay bars and night clubs as well as a hammam that was said to be a place of prostitution.

The Istanbul prosecutor's office added that it had found evidence indicating that children and minors were being inappropriately swayed on issues tied to sexual orientation and gender identity.

Rights groups say the government is unfairly targeting the LGBTQ+ community, with Kaos GL saying that it had been accused of making "posts containing obscenities" accessible to children.

Being gay in Turkey To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Erdogan scapegoats LGBTQ+ 'perverts' for falling birthrates, avoiding actual contributing factors

The weekend police operation was dubbed "My Family is Safe" by the government and was part of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's "Decade of Family and Population" scheme, which is designed to reverse plummeting birthrates in the aging country.

Authorities say it was intended to make sure that society does not see LGBTQ+ activity as "normal" and that raids were carried out to "protect children, the institution of the family, and our shared moral values."

Although same-sex relations are not illegal in the country, homophobia is rife, with President Erdogan blaming LGBTQ "perverts" for Turkey's rapidly declining birthrates.

That would seem a rhetorical diversion from the actual complexity of reasons for the decline, which Erdogan — who has ruled as the country's authoritarian president since 2014 as well as serving as its influential prime minister for 10 years before that — has called "a disaster."

Though Turkey's statistical agency, TurkStat, tracked a sharp decline in the total fertility rate between 2013 and 2023 (from 2.11 to 1.51 ), the shift brings birthrates in the country closer to those in other developed nations.

Observers say the real reasons for the drop are more likely of a structural and institutional nature rather than one chalked up to lifestyle.

Turkey's chronically worsening financial crisis, inflation, skyrocketing housing prices, family unfriendly workplace environments, limited access to affordable childcare, and higher educational and employment rates for women are all considered reasons for Turks to postpone having children, as well as for having fewer when they finally do.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

World.title: Ukraine, Poland say Russia hit Warsaw-bound passenger train
World.content:
The strike hit a locomotive of a passenger train headed to Warsaw with reports that senior Western figures were at the station shortly before the attack.

Russia launched two drone strikes on western Ukraine, close to its border with NATO member Poland, Ukrainian and Polish authorities said on Sunday.

One of the drones hit a locomotive of a passenger train at the Yahodyn railway station in the Volyn region, some 2 kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border crossing.

"The monitoring team gave the train crew advanced warning, and thanks to that, no one was injured," Ukrainian railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in online post.

Separately, Poland's PKP Intercity confirmed that they have taken control of the affected train following the attack in the Ukrainian territory.

"The train is carrying 206 people. There are no Polish citizens among the passengers," the operator said online. "After completing customs clearance, it will continue its journey towards Warsaw."

Putin rejects Zelenskyy's G20 talks offer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Senior Western figures said to be at station before train strike

Ukrzaliznytsia later said that senior Western figures, including former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and former CIA Director David Petraeus, were at the station shortly before the Warsaw-bound train was struck.

"Shortly before the locomotive was hit at the Ukrainian-Polish border, a diplomatic train was at Yagodyn station," Ukrzaliznytsia said in a statement.

"There were, among others, security advisers from several EU member states and former European leaders on board, including former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson. In another train that was at Yagodyn station at the very moment of the attack was former CIA Director David Petraeus."

Johnson didn't specifically mention that he had been near the vicinity of the attack, but called for more action to be taken against Russian President Vladimir Putin, once reports of the attack emerged.

"I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning," Johnson said.

"When are we going to give them the air defenses they need? Why won't we unfreeze Putin's cash and give it to Ukraine? There is more than €140 billion [$163 billion] in a Belgian bank account — and about £10 billion [€11.7 billion or 13.5 billion] in London," Johnson said, adding that Britain could lead the way in this regard.

"This wasn’t our train, but the one just minutes after us by the border crossing. It was evacuated as the drone approached and no one ​was hurt," Carl Bildt, Sweden's former prime minister, said on X.

Poland says attacks on its territory cannot be ruled out

Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski urged for increased support for Ukraine, calling the incident an "escalation."

"This is an escalation, this is another great challenge for Ukraine and for the hypothetical future victims of Russian aggression and this means that we should double our efforts to support victims of aggression," Sikorski told a press briefing.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk chaired an emergency meeting on Sunday to address Russian drone attacks near the border and warned the country must be prepared for the possibility that drones could target Polish territory.

"The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side," Tusk said, adding Poland "cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory."

Zelenskyy: Locomotive 'deliberately burned'

On Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the locomotive was "deliberately burned" and a gas station damaged in Volyn.

"It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand," he said.

Moscow did not immediately comment on the reports.

Falling debris set a gas station on fire near the border checkpoint in Volyn Image: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS

Ukrainian officials also reported another drone strike on Yahodyn overnight, some half a mile (800 meters) from the Polish border.

The border with Poland serves as essential transit point for military and humanitarian aid.

'Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors' — Ukrainian foreign minister

Commenting on the Yahodyn incident, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric" attacks were more than "just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders."

"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he said in an English-language post on X.

He urged Ukraine's Western allies to make Russia "feel the consequences of its terror. Not just half-decisions, but uncompromising, powerful steps. Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. Full sanctions on the military-industrial complex.

"Putin needs to understand that his barbarism will be met with decisive action that increases the cost of war for him to an unacceptable level," he added.

World.title: Russians on the Goethe-Institut: 'Hostage to politics'
World.content:
Canceled language exams, disrupted plans to study in Germany and the disappearance of an important cultural link: DW users shared how the closure of Germany's Goethe-Institut in Russia has affected their lives.

Germany's Goethe-Institut is set toclose all Russian branches by Sunday, amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany.

The Russian Foreign Ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in early August.

In early September, German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions, which included closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House, and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens.

"All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Goethe-Institut Secretary General Gitte Zschoch said in a statement on Tuesday. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany."

The library of the Goethe-Institut's Moscow branch won't be accessible after September 13 Image: Timur Gusarov/TASS/picture alliance

DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities have labeled DW an "undesirable organization," making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense.

'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams

Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates.

Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard.

"I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said.

DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany.

"My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said.

Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online.

Goethe-Institut closures hit teachers hard

The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years.

"This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote.

"I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW.

"It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote.

Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services have remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025.

'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions'

Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany.

"We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians."

Fact check: Fake campaign about alleged division of Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Some DW readers from Russia specifically drew attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions.

"Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries.

Part of the audience considered Moscow's decision expected.

"The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote.

Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship

Some Russians, however, believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia.

"German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants.

A 2011 bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so.

Gesche Joost, president of the Goethe-Institut, called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations."

According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

World.title: Croatia: 'Monster' fire triggers evacuation on Brac island
World.content:
A rapidly spreading wildfire threatened homes and tourist accommodations on the Croatian island of Brac, with firefighters battling the blaze overnight.

Nearly 700 people were evacuated amid a wildfire on the Adriatic island of Brac, Croatian media outlets reported on Sunday, following a tense night which saw hundreds of firefighters defending homes and tourist accommodations from the approaching blaze.

The situation was especially dramatic near the small town of Milna on the island's western coast.

"Last night was a disaster. It was simply impossible," Milna Mayor Frane Lozic told Net.hr news outlet. "I would have not believed that [the fire] can wipe out everything in its path so quickly."

Over 220 firefighters and 69 vehicles fought the blaze overnight Image: Ivo Cagalj/Pixsell/IMAGO

The fire was first reported on Thursday, but firefighting efforts were complicated by inaccessible terrain.

Even so, Lozic said that the authorities believed they had the situation in hand by Saturday.

"We thought we got it reined in yesterday, that it is all over, and then it happened: Sea wind starts blowing at 9 p.m. and out of nowhere, there is a monster," he said.

No deaths reported in blaze

Tourist ships joined the rescue efforts overnight, with many tourists spending the night at the beach, waiting to be evacuated.

No deaths were reported due to the blaze. However, one 76-year-old Croatian woman was hospitalized in critical condition, according to Index.hr news portal. The woman is believed to have fallen off a ship during the evacuation process. A 27-year-old man required medical aid for smoke inhalation and was then released.

Authorities estimated some 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) were affected by the fire, according to a report by the AFP news agency.

Officials confirmed some buildings were damaged, but said it was too early for a full damage assessment.

Firefighting planes active on the scene

As of Sunday morning, Croatian authorities said there were no more "open fires" but added teams were still in the field to prevent reignition. Four specialized firefighting planes are also operating in the area.

The blaze on the island of Brac was visible from Croatia's second city, Split Image: Zvonimir Barisin/Pixsell/IMAGO

Two government ministers and the head of Croatia's national firefighting service are set to attend a high-level meeting on Brac this afternoon with local officials and leaders of the local firefighting teams, after which they are expected to provide more information about the blaze.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: Vanuatu ferry capsize leaves one dead, 30 missing
World.content:
Rescue efforts have been slow after a South Pacific inter-island ferry sank in bad weather on Friday. An investigation has already begun into negligence on the part of the operator.

At least one person has died and another 30 remain missing after an inter-island ferry in Vanuatu sank in poor weather on Friday.

The South Pacific archipelagic island nation with a population of just under 350,000 is located about 1,750 kilometers (1,090 miles) east of Australia.

The vessel went down in very heavy seas somewhere between the islands of Santo and Ambae, according to authorities.

The MV Matui, operated by the Tui Shipping Agency, set sail Friday from Santo with more than 40 passengers and crew but never arrived in Ambae.

Prime Minister Jotham Napat's office on Sunday morning said that one body had been recovered, 15 passengers had been "accounted for alive" and "over 30 people are missing at sea."

Napat's office took charge of the search and rescue effort on Sunday afternoon after the prime minister expressed frustration over being unable to reach senior officials.

In a statement, Napat's office said, "Search and rescue operations are continuing," adding that the search "in open waters is being eased off whilst efforts ‌move ​toward a search along the southeast coast, where currents may have carried survivors."

"To the survivors, we pray for your strength and recovery. To ⁠the ​families of those missing and those we ​have lost, please know that the nation stands with you in this time of grief," ​the statement continued.

Napat's office also announced that an investigation into the incident had already been launched amid suspicion of negligence on the part of operator Tui.

"This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded," it said, "and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel."

Local frustration at lack of urgency from authorities

Reports of how the rescue effort began are hazy, with Vanuatu parliamentary representative Matai Seremaiah — who took part in the search — telling New Zealand public broadcaster RNZ that a crew member had swam ashore and "alerted us that the ship had capsized."

French news agency AFP cited a hotel owner on Santo who told reporters an employee of his had pulled a survivor in a life vest to shore on Saturday afternoon and authorities were immediately alerted.

It is unclear if these accounts refer to the same survivor.

"He looked like he had been in the bathtub for 25 hours — he was wrinkled up and white. He was cold," said hotel owner Ashley Beveridge.

"There was no rescue started until this guy got washed up on our beach — lucky he got washed up in an inhabited area," he added.

Beveridge told AFP that locals had expressed great frustration at the lack of urgency shown by authorities, with private citizens mobilizing cargo ships and a plane on Saturday afternoon to search for survivors on their own.

The Maritime Rescue Coordination Center (MRCC) in Noumea, New Caledonia, has said it is now assisting in the search effort.

A French Armed Forces aircraft from New Caledonia was also deployed on Sunday morning.

The MRCC said that 12 people had been located Sunday morning.

Local media reported that survivors were being treated at Northern Provincial hospital on Santo Island.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: Indonesia rescuers search for 130 people after ferry sinks
World.content:
The ship was carrying over 240 people in the Java Sea when it ran into bad weather. Officials say six people have died and 130 are still missing.

An Indonesian passenger ship carrying 243 people sank in the Java Sea on Sunday after it was hit by bad weather, local authorities said.

Officials said six people had died, while 107 were brought to safety and some 130 passengers were still missing.

"We have carried out efforts to search for victims to the fullest extent. There were passengers who ... had already been successfully evacuated by the units at the scene," I Putu Sudayana, head of the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office, told reporters.

The Virgo Transport 8 was traveling from Indonesia's second-largest city of Surabaya to Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan province on Borneo island.

It departed on Saturday at 10:13 a.m. local time (0330 UTC), but the ship's operator lost contact with the vessel early Sunday amid bad weather. It was scheduled to arrive in Banjarmasin at about 2 p.m. local time on (0700 UTC) Sunday.

Over 100 people have been rescued during ongoing search and rescue operations Image: Infuz/AFP

Search operation underway

Search and rescue teams launched an operation after the operator alerted authorities. Ships and a helicopter were deployed to the vessel's last known location.

"The ship's operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather," Sudayana said in an earlier video briefing.

The ship's last known position was in the Java Sea, roughly 148 kilometers (92 miles) from a pier in Banjarmasin, according to the Associated Press.

Sudayana added that authorities were mobilizing all available personnel and equipment given the large number of people aboard. The agency was coordinating with maritime authorities while closely monitoring weather conditions in the area, he said.

Indonesia, a nation of roughly 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries for transportation, with sea travel often cheaper and more accessible than flying. But safety enforcement across the country's maritime sector has been inconsistent, contributing to a comparatively high rate of accidents.
