World.title: Polish far-right leader Braun vandalises Ukrainian monument with hammer
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland dedicated to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two partisan formation that fought against the Soviet Union but was also responsible for massacring Poles. Braun declared that the monument, which was also recently vandalised by other unknown perpetrators, should be removed as it “insults the memory of victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles” and “glorifies Nazism”. The incident comes amid recent tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, and in particular the fact that the UPA continues to be honoured in Ukraine. Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️ Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ — Grzegorz Braun (@GrzegorzBraun_) September 10, 2026 The monument in question is located in the village of Liski, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and marks the burial site of 41 UPA soldiers killed while fighting against the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, in 1946, in the aftermath of World War Two. The area previously had a large ethnic-Ukrainian population. The memorial was vandalised last month, when it was sprayed with black paint and its arch was damaged. On Monday this week, further damage was discovered to the inscription on the monument. Police announced that they had launched an investigation into vandalism, property damage and ethnic hatred, but had not yet identified the perpetrators, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). On Wednesday evening, Braun published a video showing himself and another man using a hammer to repeatedly strike the front of the monument, causing visible damage to the stone, which contains the names of the killed UPA soldiers. They also appear to attempt to remove a separate plaque. During the video, Braun, who is a member of the European Parliament and finished fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, claimed that local residents are “afraid they would be set on fire” if they attempted to remove the memorial themselves. It is not clear when the video was recorded. Shortly after Braun published it, local police in Hrubieszów county, where the monument is located, issued a statement saying that officers were investigating damage to the monument. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka shared their statement and declared that “the perpetrators will not go unpunished”. Sprawcy zniszczenia pomnika w Białymstoku nie pozostaną bezkarni. Policjanci zabezpieczają dowody i przesłuchują świadków. https://t.co/7HCApuhPZ1 — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) September 10, 2026 Braun, who regularly carries out stunts intended to demonstrate his anti-Ukrainian, antisemitic and anti-LGBT views, and is already facing multiple legal cases over such incidents. He is currently on trial for attacking a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament using a fire extinguisher. Last month, he was charged with the crime of denying Nazi crimes for claiming that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake”. He was also charged with theft over incidents in which he tore down Ukrainian and European Union flags, and with vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition. If convicted, some of the crimes Braun is charged with carry potential years-long prison sentences. Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, which recently called for a “normalisation of relations with Russia”, enjoys support of around 8-9%, according to polling averages. That could make it a key player in deciding who can form a government after next year’s parliamentary elections. Figures from Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun's party celebrated Russia Day at the Russian embassy and presented a letter hailing Russia's development, blaming "globalists" for the Ukraine war and calling for normalisation of Polish-Russian relations https://t.co/SU3gEdVod0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2026 At the time of writing, there had been no response from Ukrainian authorities to Braun’s latest stunt. However, when the same monument was vandalised last month, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw issued a statement expressing its “deep indignation”. “Regardless of the difficult and tragic chapters of our shared history, burial and memorial sites should remain outside the realm of political disputes and be treated with respect,” they wrote. The embassy also expressed “particular concern that this incident occurs against the backdrop of a rising number of hostile acts toward Ukrainians in Poland, including reports of aggression and attacks on Ukrainian citizens” “Any attempts to shift historical disputes into the realm of vandalism, intimidation or hostility toward modern Ukraine and Ukrainians are dangerous and must be met with an appropriate legal response,” they added. Poland and Ukraine have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. His Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, responded by stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. Tensions have since cooled, and Ukraine has made moves to defuse the crisis. However, significant differences remain, in particular over memory of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the killing of around 100,000 Polish civilians. Poland regards the episode as a genocide. Ukraine strongly rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Recent months have also seen a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland, including a series of cases of verbal or physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported anti-Ukrainian hate crimes were up 30% in the first half of this year. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine responded to the dismantling of a UPA monument in Poland by introducing a ban on exhumations of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres on its territory. It is believed that tens of thousands still remain buried in unmarked mass graves. However, last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Kyiv allowed such exhumations to resume, and since then the remains of dozens of victims have been found, researched and reburied. Earlier this month, Poland also granted Ukraine permission to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. World.title: Polish train drivers announce go-slow protest after deadly crash at rail crossing
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Following a crash between a train and a truck at a rail crossing that left one passenger dead and both drivers with serious injuries, Poland’s main train drivers’ union has announced a go-slow protest that will take place on Friday. They note that they have long been warning about a lack of sufficient safety measures at rail crossings, and say that a “red line has now been crossed”. In the wake of Wednesday’s tragedy, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has pledged that the government will introduce “very tough” new punishments for those who violate regulations at crossings. Poczułam takie jakby silne hamowanie, takie bardzo silne i nagle takie bujanie i do człowieka dociera, że zaraz się wykoleimy – mówiła pasażerka pociągu Intercity "Koziołek", jadącego z Lublina do Szczecina, który wykoleił się w miejscowości Sokolniki Suche w Mazowieckiem.… pic.twitter.com/enyjD2Wo6K — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 9, 2026 On Wednesday morning, a train travelling between the cities of Lublin and Szczecin partially derailed in the village of Sokolniki Suche in central Poland after colliding with a heavy goods vehicle that, initial findings suggest, had entered the tracks at a rail crossing despite warning lights flashing. The crossing had no barriers. The train was carrying at least 114 people, including three crew. One passenger in the first carriage, a 39-year-old woman, died in hospital from her injuries, prosecutors announced later on Wednesday. Four others, including the drivers of both the train and the truck, remain hospitalised in serious condition. Prosecutors say that, from the evidence collected so far, they will launch an investigation into the crime of unintentionally causing a rail disaster, which carries a prison sentence of six months to eight years. However, they have not yet been able to interview either driver due to their health conditions. On Thursday, the head of the Polish train drivers’ union, Leszek Miętek, announced that a protest would begin at midnight and last through the whole of Friday. “We are appealing to train drivers to travel at a safe speed of 20 km/h (12.4 mph) across every level crossing in Poland,” he said, adding that he had “received reports from across the country” that “there’s full support for this type of action”. Miętek noted that the Polish labour code allows employees to refrain from work if they believe it poses a threat to their life or health. While drivers would not go that far, they want to demonstrate in a bid to prompt “action from those responsible for safety.” He warned that train delays should be expected on Friday. However, “a red line has [now] been crossed”, he added, quoted by news website Interia. Miętek noted that, for over 18 months, the union has been running a campaign, titled “I Want To Live”, focused on safety. Just two days before the accident, it had issued a special appeal to drivers over “growing safety concerns on Polish railways”. “We have been doing everything we can in parliament and at the infrastructure ministry to make sure this problem is noticed,” added Miętek, who also welcomed the fact that, following Wednesday’s accident, Tusk has pledged to take action. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Katastrofa kolejowa w Sokolnikach miała miejsce na przejeździe kolejowym, dlatego natychmiast rozpoczniemy prace nad zaostrzeniem przepisów dla tych, którzy wjeżdżają na przejazdy kolejowe, mimo zapór i czerwonych światel. pic.twitter.com/BgaZQLEPbR — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 9, 2026 In those remarks, the prime minister lamented that the accident in Sokolniki Suche was “yet another case of such a catastrophe happening at a rail crossing”. “We must immediately begin urgent work on tightening regulations,” he continued. However, critics noted that the ministry had already announced such plans in July 2025, and had failed to implement them since then. – Chcemy wprowadzić przepis, na podstawie którego każdy kierowca, który wjedzie na przejazd drogowo-kolejowy kiedy jest zapalone czerwone światło, straci prawo jazdy, zostanie mu ono zatrzymane na trzy miesiące. However, 24% of Poland’s accidents took place at rail crossings, compared to 16% in Germany. In total, Poland had by far the highest number of deaths caused by accidents at rail crossings (45), ahead of Germany (26), France (20) and Hungary (18). When taking into account the size of countries’ rail networks, Poland had 4.3 rail deaths (from all causes, not just accidents at crossings) per thousand kilometres of track, which was the fifth-highest figure in the EU, behind Portugal (6.2), Hungary (5.8), Slovakia (5.7) and Lithuania (4.6). World.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia. The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded. In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed. Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid. Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”. That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government. In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.” The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred. “We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.” With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”. Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked. “A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”. In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission. “NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added. Błaszczak to stan umysłu. Mało im było niszczenia SAFE, to dziś były szef MON podważył sens istnienia NATO wskazując, że Wojsko Polskie nie powinno bronić Litwy, Łotwy czy Estonii. Przyjaźń tego skompromitowanego środowiska z Orbanem to nie był przypadek… — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) September 1, 2026 On Wednesday, Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, visited Latvia, including the base in Ādaži where a Polish military contingent has been based since 2017 as part of a multinational NATO brigade. “Poland and Latvia face similar threats in the security domain,” said Sikorski. “We must speak with one voice and take our security seriously. Only such actions can guarantee effective protection against the threat from Russia.” “We do not want an escalation of the conflict, but Putin must know that we are not going to sit idly by and wait for his next step,” he continued. “We understand that the defence of our allies also contributes to Polish security. We stand ready to share the burden of defending the eastern flank.” 📍 Ādaži 🇱🇻 Continuing visit to Latvia, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs @sikorskiradek visited the base of the Polish Military Contingent. World.title: Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: Poland secures further $4bn financing from US to buy American military equipment
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”. The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”. .@UnderSecT took part in the signing of a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee—an important step in U.S.-Polish security cooperation. Poland’s significant investments in its defense capabilities and the U.S. defense industrial base reflect our shared… pic.twitter.com/Dz3huAp8pj — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) September 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery. The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”. In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself. Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”. “Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”. This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”. 💬 Obecna umowa została zawarta na korzystniejszych warunkach niż dwie poprzednie umowy z gwarancjami pożyczkowymi dzięki subsydiowaniu części kosztów finansowania w ramach grantu przyznanego w tym celu przez Rząd USA. To kolejny wyraz bardzo bliskiej, transatlantyckiej… pic.twitter.com/Ipd4cYDeFo — Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego 🇵🇱 (@BGK_pl) September 9, 2026 The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year. President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending. They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement. However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”. Amerykański sprzęt wojskowy ponownie wzmocni Wojsko Polskie i bezpieczeństwo Polaków! Właśnie zabezpieczyliśmy środki w wysokości 4 mld dolarów, czyli prawie 15 mld zł na jego zakup. Łącznie w ramach amerykańskiego programu Foreign Military Financing pozyskaliśmy już blisko 20… pic.twitter.com/hhzXcE1hoC — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) September 9, 2026 While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington. In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation, including DiNanno, was in Poland this week to discuss potential locations for the base. World.title: EU Moves to Curb Airbnb-Style Rentals to Boost Long-Term Housing
World.content:
The EU has introduced a framework to support long-term rentals in tourist-heavy cities. Airbnb warns it creates regulatory uncertainty without improving long-term housing outcomes.

The EU has announced an affordable housing plan aimed at encouraging long-term rentals and making housing more accessible for Europeans.

Unveiled on Wednesday, the plan aims to create clarity and predictability in how rules are applied by local authorities, particularly in neighbourhoods popular with tourists where short-term rentals have displaced residents.



“Lack of affordable housing is a matter of concern for so many of our European citizens,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press statement. “Essential workers and students cannot afford to live where they serve and study. But most importantly, it is about fairness. Today, we are delivering for all Europeans.”

“The new rules are designed to help competent authorities identify ‘areas under housing stress’ using a common methodology,” a Commission press release explains.

Housing in Europe is getting worse

The latest data on access to accommodation across Europe are worrying, and have pushed the Commission to intervene.

Recent Eurobarometer data shows that 50 per cent of European city dwellers think that housing is an urgent problem they experience. House prices have skyrocketed faster than local incomes across most European capitals, rising 64.9% between 2015 and 2025 and rents 21.8%, according to EU data.

Even people who cannot afford to buy are facing rising rents, which consume 40% of household income, and middle-class families are also increasingly facing a reality where they can’t afford to buy or rent, but also aren’t eligible for social housing.

Many residents in cities like Lisbon, Barcelona and Prague complain that short-term rental platforms like Airbnb have removed homes from the market and pushed prices up, often forcing them to move.

Short-term rentals represent only 1.2% of the EU’s total housing stock, but they can account for up to 20% in some tourism hotspots. With too few homes being built where demand is strongest, Brussels estimates it needs more than 2 million new homes every year to fix the problem.

Airbnb, the largest worldwide platform for short-term rentals, has criticised the plan as not sufficiently clear.

“Airbnb shares the Commission’s ambition to make housing more affordable. But as drafted, the Affordable Housing Act will not add a single home to the long term rental market, while adding regulatory uncertainty for hosts across European cities,” the company wrote in a press statement after the Commission’s announcement.

The plan must now be negotiated by the EU co-legislators before being approved.

World.title: Prague’s Industrial Palace to Reopen to the Public for Guided Tours
World.content:
After a major renovation costing more than CZK 3 billion, Prague’s Industrial Palace at the Výstaviště exhibition grounds will open its doors to the public in two weeks.

From September 25 to October 11, visitors will be able to explore the history and architecture of the landmark and see how it has been transformed during the renovation on guided tours organised by Výstaviště Praha and Prague City Tourism.



According to Výstaviště Praha, the palace will not remain open to the public on a regular basis after the tours. Instead, it will serve as a venue for exhibitions, trade fairs and other scheduled events.

The renovation of the Industrial Palace, including the reconstruction of its fire-damaged left wing, began in February 2022, more than 13 years after the wing was destroyed by a fire in October 2008.

The approximately one-hour guided tour costs CZK 91. Organisers say the symbolic price refers to 1891, the year the Industrial Palace first opened. Tickets are available through the Prague City Tourism website. Places are limited, and some tour dates have already sold out.

The first major event scheduled at the renovated palace will be the Designblok festival in early October.

Built in Just Ten Months

The Industrial Palace was built for the 1891 Jubilee Provincial Exhibition based on designs by architect Bedřich Münzberger. It is considered an important example of both artistic and technical heritage. The building was the first in the Czech lands to feature an architectural design based on a prefabricated iron structure.

Contemporary records show that 450 workers completed the building in just ten months, despite flooding and severe frosts affecting the exhibition grounds during construction.

From the beginning, the palace served as a venue for exhibitions and cultural events, although it was originally intended as a temporary structure.

Between 1952 and 1954, the communist government decided to repurpose the building, ordering its main hall to be converted into a social and dance hall. The building was also renamed the Congress Palace and became part of the Julius Fučík Cultural and Recreation Park, which operated at the site at the time.

One Wing of the Palace Was Destroyed by Fire

On October 16, 2008, a fire destroyed the left wing of the Industrial Palace after items left on an electric hot plate caught fire. The person responsible was never identified.

The renovation did not begin until early 2022. Under the original plans, the work was supposed to be completed last year.

However, once the foundations, floors and suspended ceilings of the right wing were uncovered, it became clear that the condition of the historic building was worse than expected, leading to additional work and delays.

World.title: New York Inspired New Residential Project in Prague’s Smíchov
World.content:
A new seven-story residential building planned for Prague’s Smíchov district has moved closer to construction after securing a zoning decision.

The project, known as Smíchovská Žehlička, is being developed by BPD Partners and Top Estates and is expected to be completed in 2029.

The building will contain 66 apartments as well as eight commercial units for shops, services and restaurants. It will also include shared coworking and community spaces. The total gross floor area is expected to be close to 8,000 square meters.

The project is planned for a wedge-shaped site between Kováků and Na Zatlance streets, directly below Mrázovka Park. The unusual shape of the plot and the significant difference in elevation between the two streets have made the site particularly difficult to develop.

The project has been in preparation for more than a decade. BPD Partners, the investment group owned by Czech businessmen Vasil Bobel, Petr Pudil and Jan Dobrovský, began working with architect Patrik Hoffman on the scheme in 2010.

Inspired by New York’s Flatiron Building

The shape of Smíchovská Žehlička is largely determined by the site’s narrow, wedge-shaped plot and surrounding streets. The design also takes inspiration from New York’s Flatiron Building, whose distinctive triangular form became a response to an equally unusual urban site.

The Prague project aims to use the constraints of its location in a similar way. Rather than attempting to conceal the site’s difficult geometry, the design makes it a defining feature of the building.

The residential units and commercial premises will all be offered for sale. The development will also provide shared areas intended for coworking and community activities.

If permitting and construction follow the current schedule, Smíchovská Žehlička could be completed by the end of 2029.

World.title: Award-Winning Holocaust Documentary to Premiere in Prague
World.content:
Award-winning Holocaust documentary UnBroken will have its Czech premiere at Prague’s Edison Filmhub on Friday, September 25.

The screening will take place alongside the opening of the new “Rescuers of Children” exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum.

Director, producer and writer Beth Lane will attend the Prague screening.



The documentary tells the story of Lane’s mother, Ginger Lane, and her six siblings, who survived the Holocaust after being hidden for two years by German farmers Paula and Arthur Schmidt.

The seven Jewish children were sheltered on the couple’s farm in Brandenburg, about 60 kilometers east of Berlin. They survived the war and emigrated together to the United States in 1946.

They are believed to be the only known family of seven Jewish siblings to have survived the Holocaust and later emigrated together as a family. Ginger Lane, now 86, is one of two surviving members of the family.

Paula and Arthur Schmidt were later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations, an honor given to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews during the Holocaust.

Their story is also featured in “Rescuers of Children,” the new exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum. The exhibition examines the experiences of children and other vulnerable people during the Holocaust and presents stories of individuals who risked their lives to help those facing persecution.

The Prague screening follows the documentary’s German premiere in Dachau on July 17, where UnBroken received the inaugural Lichtbrücke Prize for Human Rights in Film.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by UnBroken (@unbrokenthefilm)

The film premiered in 2023 at the Heartland International Film Festival, where it won Best Documentary Feature Premiere. It has since been screened in more than 50 cities, including at the United Nations in New York and Vienna, the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York and the Pilecki Institute in Warsaw.

UnBroken was released on Netflix in the United States in April 2025 and has since surpassed 1.5 million streams there.

The Czech premiere will take place at Edison Filmhub in Prague on September 25, 2026.

World.title: GALLERY: One of Europe’s Largest Aquariums Set to Open in Czechia in 2028
World.content:
A new public aquarium costing around CZK 700 million is planned for the Brno Exhibition Centre, with construction expected to begin in 2027 and the first visitors arriving in the second half of 2028.

The project, called Green Planet: National Aquarium, will occupy Pavilion C at the Brno Exhibition Centre. It is expected to contain around 100 aquariums and water tanks holding more than four million liters of water.



The facility will be home to about 400,000 animals representing roughly 500 species, including rare species. Developers say the project will rank among the largest aquarium complexes in Europe.

Brno Mayor Markéta Vaňková said the aquarium could attract around 500,000 visitors during its first year of operation, including people from across the South Moravian Region and neighboring countries.

The main attraction will be a 2.5 million-liter ocean tank featuring a 55-meter underwater tunnel.

Visitors will be able to walk through the tunnel while observing marine life around and above them. The aquarium will also feature hundreds of other aquatic species across its various tanks.

The developers say the number of animals will put the complex among Europe’s largest aquariums. They estimate that it will contain around 36 times as many animals as the Barcelona Aquarium.

The project is also designed around reducing water consumption.

According to the plans, recirculation systems will clean and treat water before returning it to the tanks. The developers say efficient water management will be one of the project’s priorities.

Czech and international specialists are involved in preparing the aquarium, which is expected to include both educational and visitor-focused elements.

World.title: Prague to Host Central Europe’s First Climate Week
World.content:
Prague will host the first international climate week in Central Europe from September 14 to 20, with more than 50 conferences, seminars, workshops and other events planned across the city.

Climate Week Prague will bring together representatives from climate research, finance, government, business and other sectors to discuss how cities and economies can respond to climate change.

The official opening will take place at the Prague Planetarium on Monday, September 14, at 2:30 p.m.



Speakers will include former European Commissioner for Climate Action Connie Hedegaard, Deputy Director-General for Climate Policy at the European Commission and a former Czech environment minister Jan Dusík, and Prague Mayor Bohuslav Svoboda of the ODS party, who is supporting the event.

The program will cover a broad range of issues, including how cities can adapt to rising temperatures, water management, energy, construction, agriculture and transport.

Finance will be a major part of the agenda. The CEE Sustainable Finance Summit, running from September 14 to 16, will examine the impact of geopolitics and artificial intelligence on Europe’s economic competitiveness.

Climate Week Prague has been organized by a coalition of independent organizations led by the International Sustainable Finance Centre. The group also includes research institutions, the Climate Facts think tank, banks, investors and trade unions representing workers in the construction and energy sectors.

The organizers say the increasing effects of climate change, including more frequent heat waves, were among the main reasons for launching the event.

Data cited by Fakta o klimatu illustrates the change in Prague’s summer temperatures.

Between 1961 and 1990, the city recorded seven tropical nights, when temperatures remained at or above 20 degrees Celsius throughout the night. Over the following 35 years, that number increased to 165, according to data from the Czech Academy of Sciences’ Institute for Global Change Research.

Average summer minimum temperatures in Prague also increased during the period, rising from 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, according to Fakta o klimatu.

The local figures come as international assessments warn of further warming. Reuters reported earlier in September, citing the United Nations Environment Programme, that global temperatures are expected to exceed the key 1.5-degree-Celsius threshold above pre-industrial levels within the next few years.

Further warming is expected to contribute to more extreme weather and increase pressure on ecosystems, glaciers and low-lying coastal cities.

World.title: Prague’s Petřín Funicular to Return to Service on September 22
World.content:
Prague’s Petřín funicular will resume passenger service on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, following a two-year reconstruction of the railway and its infrastructure, the Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has announced.

Service will begin at 7 a.m., with the new fourth-generation cars departing from both Újezd and Petřín stations.

Trains will then run according to the regular timetable, with departures every 10 minutes until 10:15 p.m.



The reopening comes almost exactly two years after the previous funicular was taken out of service. The third-generation cars made their final journey on September 13, 2024, after prolonged heavy rainfall destabilized and eroded sections of the hillside.

New cars increase capacity

The two new cars were designed by Czech designer Anna Marešová and built by Swiss manufacturer CWA Constructions SA. The vehicles cost a combined CZK 137.7 million and were delivered to Prague in April.

Each car can carry up to 120 passengers, compared with a capacity of 100 on the previous vehicles. The design also introduces glass roofs, giving passengers a clearer view of Petřín Hill during the journey.

Air conditioning, however, will not be installed. Because of technical limitations, the cars will instead use forced-air ventilation. The decision has already drawn criticism from some Prague residents, who have questioned how comfortable the cars will be during hot summer days, particularly given their large glass roofs.

The two-year reconstruction involved more than replacing the vehicles. Workers strengthened the foundations beneath the track, installed new rails and upgraded the funicular’s traction system.

How much will the new funicular cost?

A single journey will cost CZK 100 when purchased on site. Passengers using the PID Lítačka mobile application will pay CZK 90.

Passengers with valid long-term Prague public transport passes covering one month to one year will continue to ride without paying an additional fare.

The same applies to holders of 24-hour and 72-hour passes, children under 15 and passengers aged over 65.

World.title: Prague Botanical Garden to Host Grape Harvest Festival
World.content:
The Prague Botanical Garden will host its traditional grape harvest festival at St. Clare’s Vineyard on September 12 and 13, bringing two days of wine, fresh burčák, live music and activities for visitors.

The festival, known as Vinobraní na Vinici sv. Kláry, will feature wines from producers across the Czech Republic, Moravia and other countries.

Visitors will also have the chance to taste white and red burčák made from grapes harvested this year at St. Clare’s Vineyard.



The first grapes for the festival have already been picked by hand. Workers harvested 2,700 kilograms of table grapes and the Modrý Portugal variety. The grapes are now being used to produce this year’s burčák, a young wine that is still undergoing fermentation and is traditionally associated with the Czech grape harvest season.

Alongside wines from the St. Clare’s winery, the festival will present a selection of wines from other producers from the Czech Republic, Moravia and abroad.

Two days of live music

Music will be a major part of the weekend program. Saturday’s main stage lineup includes Jordan Haj and Emma Smetana, YES BROTHERS and 20 MINUTES.

On Sunday, visitors can see the Děda Mládek Illegal Band, BRASS AVENUE, MOVEBREAKERS and OFF BEAT ORCHESTRA. A second music stage will also operate near the St. Clare’s wine shop.

The festival program includes more than music and wine. Visitors can join guided tours of the vineyard, take part in workshops and creative activities, or attend the Vínohrátky educational program. The guided tours are included in the admission price.

The event will run from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both September 12 and 13. Activities will take place at St. Clare’s Vineyard and in the Ornamental Garden of the Prague Botanical Garden.

Tickets bought at the venue cost CZK 280 for adults and CZK 180 for children and young people aged 3 to 17.

Online tickets purchased by September 11 are CZK 250 for adults and CZK 150 for children and young people. Children under three can enter free of charge.

World.title: Could the Danube help save Lake Velence? A plan is back on the table
World.content:
One of Hungary’s best-known lakes has fallen to an alarmingly low level after another dry summer. With Lake Velence struggling for water, local officials and experts are once again looking towards a much bigger neighbour for help: the Danube.

A new round of talks was held in Gárdony over how to replenish Lake Velence, with one of the main ideas being to bring water from the Danube to the lake through a new supply system.

The discussion comes as the situation at the lake has become increasingly urgent. On Wednesday, the water-level gauge at Agárd showed just 10 centimetres, compared with the previous record low of 53 centimetres measured in 2022, Infostart reported, citing local sources. The figure refers to the gauge reading rather than the actual depth of the lake.

Lake Velence. Photo: Facebook/Élhető Velence Egyesület

Lake Velence, roughly 50 kilometres southwest of Budapest, covers about 26 square kilometres and is one of Hungary’s most popular lakes for swimming, cycling and weekend trips. Its shallow waters, however, also make it particularly sensitive to prolonged drought and evaporation.

How could Danube water reach Lake Velence?

The idea is still at an early stage, but several possible routes are now being examined. Experts discussed whether water could be brought from the Danube from the area around Ercsi, Adony or Dunaújváros, while the route and cost of a possible new pipeline would also have to be assessed.

Other options are on the table as well. These include currently unused wells operated by regional water utility DRV around Gárdony, as well as wells near Szabadegyháza. But for now, no final solution has been selected. Those involved in the talks stressed that any project would have to be assessed not only from an engineering point of view, but also in terms of water quality, ecology and cost.

Photo: Facebook Gesztenye Biciklikölcsönző

Satellite data could now be used to examine the terrain between the Danube and Lake Velence, while preliminary estimates are expected to determine how expensive the different options might be.

If you missed it: The end draws near for Lake Velence

Simply dredging the lake may not solve the problem

The talks also covered another frequently suggested solution, dredging Lake Velence. However, experts cautioned that removing sediment is not necessarily a straightforward answer. There are concerns that dredging could damage parts of the lake’s naturally water-retaining mud layer and potentially increase water loss through seepage.

The condition of the lake’s extensive reed beds is another problem. Rotting reeds can have ecological consequences, meaning experts believe reed management and water replenishment should be considered together rather than as separate issues.

The proposal to use Danube water is therefore far from an approved construction project, but discussions are moving forward. According to Feol.hu, further calculations are expected on water consumption, evaporation and possible investment costs, with a broader meeting planned for later in September involving government representatives, water-management bodies and municipalities around the lake.

For now, rain may offer some temporary relief. But with Lake Velence repeatedly reaching exceptionally low levels, local decision-makers are increasingly looking for a longer-term answer — and the Danube may yet become part of it.

World.title: PM Péter Magyar: ‘Love is a fundamental right’ in Hungary
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has issued one of his clearest statements yet on personal freedom and relationships, declaring that people should be free to love whomever they choose. His comments come just a day after he announced plans to reverse an Orbán-era restriction on adoption by same-sex couples.

In a social media post on Sunday, Magyar wrote that “Love, including romantic love, is a fundamental right.”, adding that in a humane Hungary, everyone should be free to love whomever and however they wish, provided they do not harm others or break the law.

“In a humane Hungary, everyone should be free to love whomever they choose, and however they choose, as long as they do not harm others or break the law,” Magyar wrote.

He ended the short message with a reference to 1 Corinthians 13:13, the biblical passage about faith, hope and love, which describes love as the greatest of the three. The statement is brief, but it comes at a politically significant moment.

Magyar signals change on LGBTQ rights?

Just one day earlier, Magyar said his government would move to scrap an Orbán-era restriction that effectively prevented same-sex couples from adopting.

Under legislation introduced during Viktor Orbán’s government in 2020, unmarried people could adopt only with special ministerial approval. Because same-sex marriage is not recognised in Hungary, the rule effectively made adoption considerably more difficult for gay and lesbian couples.

Magyar said decisions on adoption should instead be made by professionals rather than politicians. Reuters described the announcement as a significant shift from the policies of the previous government, which had introduced a series of restrictions affecting LGBTQ people.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples remain legal in Hungary, while same-sex marriage is still not recognised. Magyar’s Sunday statement therefore did not announce another specific legislative change, but it reinforced the broader direction signalled by the government’s adoption plans.

More on this topic: Péter Magyar’s remarks point to a radical U-turn on same-sex couples’ right to adopt

Not the first time Péter Magyar has used this message

The prime minister has made similar remarks before. At his international press conference on 13 April, one day after his election victory, Magyar said that people in Hungary were free to assemble and to live with and love whomever they chose, as long as they did not harm others or violate the law.

The same theme also appeared repeatedly during the election campaign, particularly during debates surrounding Budapest Pride and restrictions introduced under the previous government.

Sunday’s post puts the message in unusually direct terms: love itself, Magyar argued, should be treated as a fundamental right.

Check out some more articles concerning the adoption of same-sex couples in our LGTBQ in Hungary archive.

Featured image: Péter Magyar / Facebook

World.title: 40 Hungarians evacuated as wildfire still rages on Croatia’s Brač island
World.content:
A group of 40 Hungarians was evacuated from Milna on the Croatian island of Brač as a major wildfire continued to threaten coastal areas. Hundreds of people were moved to safety overnight, while a 76-year-old woman was reported to be in critical condition. Hungarian authorities say they have no information about any Hungarian citizens being injured.

The wildfire, which broke out near Ložišća on 10 September, has already burned through more than 3,500 hectares of pine forest, scrubland and grassland on Brač, one of Croatia’s most popular Adriatic islands.

According to MTI, the situation became particularly serious around Milna overnight from Saturday to Sunday, as the flames spread towards Osibova Bay and Baterija. Firefighters worked through the night to protect residential buildings and other properties.

Croatian fire authorities said 227 people were moved to safety in Supetar, Postira and Bol during the night. Local media put the total number of evacuees at close to 700, although that higher figure had not been officially confirmed by the fire service by Sunday morning.

Ivana Marković, mayor of Supetar, told MTI that 45 foreign tourists had been accommodated in the town’s sports hall and that most of them were Hungarian. None had been injured.

Hungarian group evacuated from Milna

Hungary’s Foreign Ministry separately confirmed to Telex that a group of around 40 Hungarian citizens had been evacuated from Milna shortly before midnight on Saturday.

“The Consular Service received one phone call in connection with the fire, from a group of 40 Hungarians who were evacuated from Milna around midnight on Saturday. According to their account, they are safe and are receiving appropriate care at the reception centre. They did not request consular assistance for their return home,” the Foreign Ministry told Telex.

The ministry added that it had no information about any Hungarian citizens being injured in connection with the wildfire.

According to the ministry, people staying at the reception centre were later told that they could return to Milna after the road to the town was reopened, although restrictions remained in place towards the more distant port of Duboka.

If you missed it: Tragedy at Transylvania’s famous gas bath leaves one man dead, another hospitalised

One woman in critical condition

The fire has nevertheless caused injuries and property damage. A 76-year-old woman is in critical condition after she nearly drowned while fleeing the area. Croatian media reported that she fell into the water from a boat during the evacuation. A 27-year-old man was also treated for smoke inhalation and later released from hospital.

Several buildings and vehicles were damaged, including properties in the Gava holiday resort, although firefighters managed to save numerous homes and other structures threatened by the flames.

Although conditions around Milna improved on Sunday, the wildfire remained active around the bays of Duboka and Osibova. Croatia’s firefighting service said 235 firefighters and 68 vehicles were working at the scene, with aerial units also supporting the operation.

The situation on Brač remained volatile. At around 2:30 p.m. on Sunday, a separate wildfire broke out above Bol, prompting authorities to deploy local firefighters and two Canadair aircraft. Fire crews continued working to contain both blazes.

World.title: Temu, Shein and AliExpress lose ground in Hungary after new EU customs charge
World.content:
Hungarian shoppers are becoming more cautious about ordering from Temu, Shein and AliExpress after new EU customs rules made low-value purchases from outside the bloc more expensive. PwC Hungary says shopping habits are already shifting, while some European marketplaces are beginning to benefit.

The new rules entered into force on 1 July and ended the previous customs-duty exemption for low-value consignments worth up to EUR 150 arriving from outside the European Union. A temporary EUR 3 customs duty now applies per item based on tariff classification, meaning a parcel containing different types of products can attract the duty more than once.

Speaking to InfoRádió, Szabolcs Timár, senior e-commerce consultant at PwC Hungary, said consumers are now paying much closer attention to the final price of an order, rather than simply looking at the advertised cost of individual items.

PwC says this has encouraged more shoppers to compare offers from Hungarian and EU-based retailers before ordering from Asian marketplaces.

Temu’s rapid rise in Hungary faces a setback

The change is particularly significant because Chinese marketplaces have become a major force in Hungarian online retail.

According to PwC, Hungarian consumers placed more than 13 million orders on Temu in 2025, worth around HUF 195 billion. Hungary’s total online product market was worth roughly HUF 2.1 trillion, meaning Temu alone accounted for close to one-tenth of the market.

“So when we ask whether it was necessary to restrict Chinese platforms and level the playing field, the answer is definitely yes,” Timár said.

The platform grew even faster ahead of the customs change. In the first quarter of 2026, Temu recorded almost 5 million Hungarian orders, up 92 percent year-on-year, and reached 1.8 million consumers. The shift had already begun before the new customs duty entered into force, where PwC has observed a noticeable decline in orders from outside the EU.

Between the first and second quarters of 2026, the number of parcels arriving from outside the EU fell by around 750,000, while orders from within the bloc increased by more than 1.25 million.

Timár said Temu, Shein and AliExpress are among the clearest losers so far, although he does not expect Hungarian consumers to abandon them altogether.

Earlier: Temu takes over, Hungarian online shoppers now spend more abroad than at home!

European retailers could benefit

Some of the spending moving away from Chinese platforms is expected to shift towards Hungarian and other European retailers. PwC says the strongest regional beneficiary so far appears to be Polish marketplace Allegro, while Romania’s eMAG and Czech-based Alza are also well positioned. Hungarian platforms themselves have not gained as much ground.

Chinese marketplaces are also likely to adapt, with expanding their warehouse networks inside the European Union.

Goods imported in bulk into an EU warehouse can then be delivered to consumers from within the bloc. The customs cost still exists, but instead of appearing as an extra charge at checkout, it can be incorporated into the product price.

Timár said this distinction matters because shoppers are often more sensitive to an unexpected fee added at the final stage of a purchase than to a slightly higher listed price.

Cheap prices are no longer enough

Low prices remain one of the main attractions of Temu, Shein and AliExpress, but PwC says their success also comes from huge product ranges, simple payment systems, fast delivery and customer-friendly services.

For Hungarian shoppers, the change is unlikely to mean the end of ordering from Chinese marketplaces. Instead, PwC expects consumers to become more selective and pay closer attention to the true final cost of their purchases. For Temu, Shein and AliExpress, the next challenge will be to adapt quickly enough to keep the remaining shoppers from moving elsewhere.

World.title: Monaco’s Prince Albert II hails Budapest as an ultimate city of sport — and jokes about facing PM Péter Magyar
World.content:
Prince Albert II of Monaco has praised Budapest and the new World Athletics Ultimate Championship after attending the event in the Hungarian capital, describing the opening night as a successful experiment in making athletics faster and more engaging.

Prince Albert spoke to Hungarian newspaper Blikk during the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest. He attended the event not only as Monaco’s head of state, but also as president of the Monegasque Athletics Federation and honorary president of the International Athletics Foundation.

The prince gave a positive assessment of the championship’s opening night, highlighting its fast pace, atmosphere and efforts to experiment with a different way of presenting athletics. He said the format offered memorable moments and very little downtime, although he added that the full three-day event would need to conclude before its success could be properly judged.

Prince Albert praises Budapest

Albert was particularly complimentary about the Hungarian capital and its sporting audience.

“It is fantastic that the Ultimate Championship is being hosted by Budapest, one of the finest cities for sport.”

He also congratulated the organisers and Hungary, saying the enthusiasm of Hungarian spectators for sport was clearly visible. The praise comes as Budapest hosts the first edition of the World Athletics Ultimate Championship, a new season-ending competition designed to offer a more compact and fast-moving athletics format.

An exciting moment from the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest. Photo: Atlétikai Világdöntő Budapest 2026 / Facebook

Albert has been involved in international athletics for decades and told Blikk that the sport has changed significantly over that period. In his view, athletics has become more dynamic and audiences are now much more involved than they were several decades ago.

He argued that the sport should continue searching for ways to become easier to follow and more attractive outside its biggest summer events.

Could athletics ever rival football?

The prince was also asked whether higher prize money could eventually bring athletics stars closer to the financial and social status enjoyed by leading footballers and tennis players.

Albert said he did not expect that gap to disappear soon. Football, he noted, benefits from a long and continuous season, giving its stars far greater and more regular media exposure.

He nevertheless welcomed the growing sums being offered to athletes and described the prize package at the Budapest competition as one of the strongest he had seen in athletics.

If you missed it: Stress-free autumn travel: motorists face strict parking rules at Budapest Airport

And what about Péter Magyar?

The interview ended on a lighter note when Albert was asked which athletics discipline he would choose if he ever competed against Prime Minister Péter Magyar. The prince laughed and said no such contest had been discussed. He noted that Magyar enjoys football and said he was pleased to have met and spoken with the Hungarian prime minister in Budapest.

He nevertheless left the door open to the imaginary showdown:

“Perhaps one day such a competition could take place.”

Highlights from the Budapest championship

The inaugural championship has already delivered several memorable moments. Hungary’s Bence Halász claimed silver in the men’s hammer throw with 80.30 metres, giving the home crowd a major success, while some of athletics’ biggest international stars also produced standout performances across the weekend.

The event has drawn further attention for its record USD 10 million prize fund, with individual champions earning USD 150,000.

World.title: Tragedy at Transylvania’s famous gas bath leaves one man dead, another hospitalised
World.content:
A man has died and another was taken to hospital after the pair lost consciousness during treatment in a mofetta in Szeklerland, central Romania. The accident occurred at Büdösfürdő, an unusual mountain resort known for its naturally occurring volcanic gas baths.

Emergency services were called to Büdösfürdő, or Sântimbru-Băi in Romanian, on Saturday after two men were found unconscious inside a mofetta, Romanian news agency Mediafax reported, citing Harghita County emergency services.

According to authorities, both men were around 40–45 years old. Rescue teams attempted to resuscitate them, but one of the men could not be saved. The other was transported to hospital.

Firefighters had to enter the gas-filled area wearing self-contained breathing equipment to remove the victims. Emergency crews described the environment as heavily saturated with carbon dioxide and dangerous to breathe.

Police have launched an investigation into the circumstances of the incident, while an autopsy is expected to determine the exact cause of death.

What is a mofetta and why can it be dangerous?

Unlike a conventional spa bath, a mofetta contains no water. Visitors instead sit or stand in a sunken chamber where naturally occurring volcanic gases seep out of the ground and collect close to the floor.

Büdösfürdő lies high in the Harghita Mountains, an area shaped by ancient volcanic activity and still known for its mineral springs and natural gas emissions. More than ten such gas outlets have been identified around Sântimbru-Băi, several of which have traditionally been used for therapeutic purposes.

Mofetta at Büdösfürdő in Transylvania. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

According to the official Visit Harghita tourism portal, gas samples from the area can contain anywhere between 14 and 99 percent carbon dioxide, together with hydrogen sulfide and radon. The treatments are traditionally associated with cardiovascular, musculoskeletal and certain nervous-system conditions.

Even the Hungarian name of the resort hints at its unusual geology: Büdösfürdő roughly means “smelly bath,” a reference to the sulphurous gases that rise naturally from the ground.

If you missed it: Foul stench and heavy police presence at Pécs Pride – pictures

A traditional treatment that can also be dangerous

The same physical properties that make mofettas unusual can also make them hazardous. Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, so it can accumulate close to the ground in pits and enclosed depressions.

At high concentrations, it can displace oxygen and lead to dizziness, unconsciousness and potentially fatal asphyxiation.

Carbon dioxide itself is colourless and odourless. The natural gas mixture at Büdösfürdő, however, can also contain hydrogen sulfide, which is responsible for a characteristic sulphurous smell. That is why visitors must keep their head above the concentrated gas layer and follow safety instructions while undergoing treatment.

This is not the first fatal incident at Büdösfürdő

A similar tragedy occurred at the same resort in 2016. A 39-year-old woman was found dead inside a mofetta at Sântimbru-Băi in July that year. Emergency services recovered her body from the facility, and initial investigations at the time indicated that her death was likely the result of an accident.

The latest incident has once again highlighted the unusual dual nature of Transylvania’s mofettas: the naturally occurring gases have been used as part of local therapeutic traditions for decades, but exposure to high concentrations can pose a serious danger.

Authorities have not yet established what caused the two men to lose consciousness, and the official cause of death remains under investigation.

World.title: From Legolas to Liszka — Hungary rewrites its baby-name rules again
World.content:
Hungary is preparing to reverse a controversial overhaul of its tightly regulated baby-name system. A previous decision to remove 145 given names from the official list has been overturned, while ten new names are already set to be added.

Hungary’s Ministry for Social Relations and Culture is preparing major changes to the system for approving new given names, following talks with the ELTE Research Centre for Linguistics in early September, 24.hu reported.

The new government has effectively invalidated decisions made by the former Given Name Approval Committee, which was established under the previous Fidesz government and chaired by former Fidesz politician Lajos Kósa.

The most striking consequence is that 145 names previously earmarked for removal will remain on Hungary’s official list of permitted given names. At the same time, ten new baby-names have already been approved for inclusion.

Ten new names are on the way

Among the newly accepted names are Liszka, Benna, Floriána, Doron, Zeliha and Gittel.

According to Judit Raátz of the Research Centre for Linguistics, four of six names previously recommended by linguists were accepted during the review, while another six were approved at the September meeting. This means the official list is already certain to expand by ten names.

And the list may not stop there. Applications submitted after 12 May are expected to be evaluated in the coming weeks, after which officials and linguists will meet again and could approve further names. The updated list will still have to be formally published before the changes fully take effect.

The names that sparked Kósa’s crackdown

Hungary has long had stricter rules on baby-names than many other countries, as parents must go through an approval procedure. The controversy began in 2025, when Lajos Kósa pushed for tighter political control over Hungary’s official list of given names.

Explaining the proposal in parliament, Kósa singled out several names that were already legally available to Hungarian parents. He pointed to Kandida and Orália among female baby-names, as well as Késav, Orda, Gida and Legolasz among male baby-names, arguing that the country’s stock of given names forms part of Hungary’s national identity.

As we reported at the time, the reform transferred the final authority over Hungary’s official given-name list from linguistic experts to the minister responsible for culture.

If you missed it: Hungary tightens baby-names: new ministerial list in force

Under the old system, linguistic experts assessed applications and applicants were generally informed of a decision within 30 days. After the reform, however, the final list had to be formally issued by the minister — a change that critics said dramatically slowed the process.

281 applications, and only one initially made it through

The problems became particularly visible in January. The Kósa-led committee reviewed 281 applications for new given names submitted since the previous August. The Research Centre for Linguistics recommended seven of them, but the committee approved just one: Vinka, a female name also associated with the periwinkle flower.

The committee also examined 198 existing names that were not being used by any Hungarian citizen and proposed removing 145 of them from the official register. Neither decision ultimately became official.

For some parents, however, the delay had very real consequences: according to 24.hu, children were born while their parents were still waiting for decisions on the names they had requested.

Former culture and innovation minister Balázs Hankó never published the changes in the Hungarian Gazette, meaning the planned deletion of the 145 names — and the addition of Vinka — never formally entered into force.

Back to the linguists

The new ministry and the Research Centre for Linguistics now want to redesign the procedure and return a much larger role to linguistic experts. The September review overturned the previous committee’s decision to remove the 145 names, meaning none of them will now be deleted.

The longer-term aim is to restore a faster system in which applications can once again be dealt with largely on professional linguistic grounds rather than requiring repeated political approval.

Doing so will require amendments to both regulations and legislation. Hungary’s currently published legal name list is still based on the 2025 ministerial decree, and the present application procedure continues to direct parents through the ministry.

For Hungarian parents looking for something a little less conventional, however, the direction is clear; the list is about to get longer, not shorter.

World.title: Building economic bridges: Hungary and Malaysia deepen ties in green energy and high-tech – VIDEO
World.content:
Malaysia is seeking closer economic cooperation with Hungary in green energy, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals and advanced manufacturing, as representatives of the two countries met in Budapest for the first Malaysia–Hungary Business and Investment Forum. The Malaysian state of Sarawak is meanwhile targeting almost EUR 70 billion in total investment by 2030.

Around 60 Hungarian business leaders, chamber representatives and government officials attended the inaugural Malaysia–Hungary Business and Investment Forum 2026 in Budapest, according to the Embassy of Malaysia in Hungary.

The meeting focused on potential cooperation in several rapidly growing industries, including green energy, semiconductor manufacturing, pharmaceuticals and advanced manufacturing.

The Malaysian Embassy described the forum as a milestone in strengthening economic links between the two regions. In a Facebook post following the event, it wrote:

“Together, we build strong economic bridges between Southeast Asia and Central Europe.”

Malaysia and Hungary could open doors to two regions

Speaking at the forum, Norafizan Mustaffa, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim of the Malaysian Embassy in Budapest, highlighted the geographical and economic advantages of closer cooperation between the two countries.

“Malaysia serves as a strategic entry point to the ASEAN market, while Hungary’s position in Central Europe makes it an ideal partner for Malaysian businesses looking to expand into Europe,” he said.

The two countries could therefore serve as gateways for companies seeking to enter the Southeast Asian and Central European markets.

Malaysia is already a significant player in the global electronics and semiconductor industriess. Around 7% of global semiconductor trade passes through the country, while it accounts for an estimated 13% of global semiconductor assembly, testing and packaging. Hungary could be a good partner, has also developed a major manufacturing base in areas including automotive production, electronics and battery manufacturing.

If you missed it: Hungarian passport remains one of the world’s strongest — but why, and can it climb higher?

Sarawak targets almost EUR 70 billion in investment

Sarawak’s economic plans played a central role at the Budapest forum. Datu Lester Matthew, Permanent Secretary of Sarawak’s Ministry of International Trade, Industry and Investment, presented the state’s Post COVID-19 Development Strategy 2030.

Under the strategy, Sarawak aims to attract EUR 69.99 billion in total investment by 2030, with clean energy, carbon capture and storage, semiconductor manufacturing and digital infrastructure among its priority areas.

The state is seeking to position itself as a sustainable, high-income investment destination while expanding sectors linked to the green and digital transitions.

For Hungarian companies operating in engineering, energy technologies and advanced manufacturing, these developments could create new business opportunities in Malaysia.

Hungarian and Malaysian companies held direct talks

The Budapest forum also included business-to-business matchmaking sessions aimed at establishing direct links between Hungarian and Malaysian companies.

Representatives of the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, the Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation and the Hungarian Export Promotion Agency also briefed participants on trade and investment opportunities.

Hungary’s Ambassador to Malaysia, Sándor Sipos, attended the event as well. The forum could mark another step towards closer economic ties between Hungary and Malaysia, particularly in sectors where both countries are seeking new investment and international partners.
