The draft says that the system for making decisions on citizenship matters will also change. In particular, the interagency commission that reviews applications for the granting or termination of citizenship will be abolished.

The Interior Ministry considers that the commission’s work provides little practical benefit. It has almost never reviewed negative decisions or changed the administrative body’s preliminary position.

A specialised commission will be established in its place. Its task will be to verify applicants’ ethnicity, including their Armenian ancestry.

Until now, the authorities have based the verification of ethnicity solely on the availability of certain documents.

However, the Interior Ministry has concluded that applicants’ documents do not always provide a reliable basis for confirming Armenian ancestry. There have been cases in which people submitted forged or altered documents to take advantage of the simplified citizenship procedure available to ethnic Armenians.

According to the ministry, more than 70 such cases were identified between 2023 and 2026. The number of such incidents has also tended to increase each year.

“There were five such cases in 2023, 21 in 2024, 26 in 2025, and 19 in the first half of 2026 alone,” the Interior Ministry reports.

New requirements for obtaining Armenian citizenship

World.title: EPRC: Wildberries expansion poses significant risks for Georgia
World.content:
According to the Economic Policy Research Center (EPRC), the expansion of the Russian online platform Wildberries in Georgia poses significant risks for the country.

The centre makes this assessment in a new report examining the threats that Wildberries-related activities could pose to Georgian brands represented on the platform, consumers, Georgian banks and Georgia’s economic and financial system as a whole.

Wildberries is an online marketplace often described as “Russia’s Amazon”.

According to EPRC, at least eight Wildberries warehouses were put out of operation by Ukrainian strikes in late August 2026, while more than 20 facilities were damaged. During the same period, part of the company’s financial ecosystem, Wildberries Bank, was placed under international sanctions.

The centre says that, while Wildberries’ warehouse infrastructure in Russia became a target for Ukrainian drones and the company’s banking arm was placed on a sanctions list, Wildberries used Georgia and other neighbouring countries to expand its trading network and logistics capabilities.

EPRC predicts that, as a result, Georgia could become part of a regional infrastructure helping a company linked to the Kremlin and sanctioned Russian businesses reduce losses caused by the war and sanctions.

The report notes that Wildberries’ official infrastructure in Georgia includes warehouses, sorting centres and collection points. According to the company’s instructions, updated on 4 June 2026, Georgian sellers can choose a warehouse or sorting centre and review the conditions for accepting products, logistics rates, sorting times and delivery times to consumers.

According to EPRC, this indicates that the company’s activities in Georgia are no longer limited to collection points. Local infrastructure is also being used to receive, sort and subsequently deliver products. However, open sources do not currently confirm the existence of a large logistics centre in Georgia. A similar situation exists in Azerbaijan.

According to the report, information spread in September 2025 that local businesses had been given the opportunity to sell their products directly through the Wildberries platform.

EPRC also publishes what it believes is an incomplete list of Georgian brands available on the platform. The centre explains that finding a complete list is difficult because Wildberries does not allow users to search for brands by country of origin.

At this stage, the list of Georgian products and brands on the platform is believed to include Borjomi, Nabeghlavi, Natakhtari, Zedazeni, Gurieli, Kula, Badagoni, Chateau Mukhrani, Askaneli, Sarajishvili, MACH & MACH, ANOUKI and Aleksandre Akhalkatsishvili.

EPRC stresses that Wildberries operates as a marketplace. The presence of a particular product on the platform does not automatically mean that the manufacturer or an official brand representative is selling it directly. The product may be listed either by the manufacturer or by an independent reseller.

According to the centre, if an independent retailer sells the product, the brand may restrict those sales by protecting its intellectual property or using contractual mechanisms.

In EPRC’s assessment, Wildberries’ expansion in Georgia is no longer solely a matter of developing online trade. The centre identifies several major risks.

In particular, the report says Wildberries is linked to Russia’s trading and financial system, and its ties to the Kremlin have also been confirmed. The company’s financial arm, Wildberries Bank, has been placed under UK and EU sanctions. According to EPRC, the sanctions are linked to the bank’s role in financially supporting the military and the Russian authorities’ aggressive interests.

The centre also says the Wildberries platform is used to purchase goods needed by the Russian military, including military equipment and dual-use goods. According to EPRC, independent journalistic investigations have also confirmed this.

Against this backdrop, the report’s authors question the effectiveness of controls over the trade and export of such products in Georgia. In their assessment, this increases the risk that sanctioned goods or dual-use items could enter or be re-exported through the country.

EPRC pays particular attention to the development of Wildberries’ logistics capabilities in Georgia. The centre believes that, after a significant part of the company’s warehouse network in Russia was damaged, infrastructure outside Russia has become even more important to Wildberries. Georgia could therefore become part of the company’s regional diversification network.

The report also describes the growing integration of Georgian businesses into the Wildberries system. Products from Georgian brands are already sold on the platform, and Georgian entrepreneurs can join it as direct sellers. EPRC believes this creates both reputational and potential financial risks for companies in the future.

According to the centre, Georgia’s financial sector is also at risk. Wildberries Bank came under UK and EU sanctions in 2026, while 5% of the bank is also owned by the sanctioned Russian bank VTB.

EPRC says that the fact that customers in Georgia pay for purchases on Wildberries using Georgian bank cards means that the local banking sector must comply with the sanctions regime and carry out additional transaction checks. According to the centre, after sanctions were imposed on Wildberries Bank, the National Bank of Georgia shifted responsibility to individual financial institutions, explaining that each bank must assess the risks of violating or circumventing sanctions independently.

In EPRC’s assessment, given these circumstances, the development in Georgia of infrastructure linked to a sanctioned financial institution, a business close to the Kremlin and a platform used to supply the Russian military cannot simply be viewed as foreign investment or the expansion of retail trade.

The centre suggests that if Wildberries continues to expand in Georgia without state oversight or proper customs and financial monitoring, and Georgian companies and banks deepen their cooperation with the platform, the country could become part of an economic and logistics network that helps Russian businesses continue operating amid war and international sanctions.

EPRC believes that such a process could have long-term economic and reputational consequences for Georgia.

EPRC on the risks posed by Wildberries in Georgia

World.title: Georgian Legion commander on former prosecutor general: ‘He is following directives from Russian intelligence services’
World.content:
According to a statement by Mamuka Mamulashvili, commander of the pro-Ukrainian Georgian Legion, former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who recently took command of a unit fighting on Russia’s side, is following directives from Russian intelligence services. Mamulashvili also said Partskhaladze’s value as a military figure was zero.

The Georgian Legion is a volunteer formation established in 2014 after Russia invaded eastern Ukraine. In 2016, the Georgian Legion officially joined Ukraine’s 25th Motorised Infantry Battalion. It is now subordinate to the Main Directorate of Intelligence of Ukraine’s Defence Ministry. The unit includes Georgian volunteers as well as fighters of other nationalities. It currently has around 2,000 members. In 2023, Russia’s Interior Ministry added Georgian Legion commander Mamuka Mamulashvili to its wanted list.

According to Mamulashvili, Otar Partskhaladze will try to draw ethnic Georgians living in Russia into his adventure — the war against Ukraine. However, his chances of success are doubtful, as very few Georgians fighting on Russia’s side are seen on the front line, and most of them have already been killed.

Former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze, who is fighting on Russia’s side, told Russian pro-Kremlin media that members of the Georgian Legion are “war criminals” and will face prosecution under Russian law. Earlier, on 7 September, it became known that Partskhaladze would lead the international “St George” unit, which was created to take part in the war against Ukraine.

Mamuka Mamulashvili: “Partskhaladze will get a response. He will realise that he made a serious mistake by launching a campaign against the Georgian Legion.

No unit, not even Ukrainian ones, has faced the kind of pressure the Georgian Legion has endured. We are one of the oldest units, even compared with Ukrainian volunteer formations. Russia does not like the fact that so many Georgians are fighting on Ukraine’s side. That is why Russia has been fighting us for more than 12 years, both informationally and physically.

Since they failed to destroy the Georgian Legion physically, they have now tried to create a counterweight by forming another Georgian unit that supposedly will fight on Russia’s side. In reality, this is an attempt to discredit Georgia and bring it under the same sanctions that Russia faces. To do this, they are using people with Georgian surnames who live in Russia and who make all sorts of absurd claims that the Georgian Legion should be tried under Russian law.

In 2022, Russia designated the Georgian Legion as a terrorist organisation. This is hardly surprising, as the Georgian Legion has inflicted enormous damage on the Russian Federation. We can see that their disinformation machine has become much more active. Attempts to kill us physically and attacks have also increased. I have personally been attacked seven times and have survived three attempts to poison me.

Partskhaladze is following directives from Russian intelligence services because his own value as a military figure is zero. I doubt that this man knows which end of a weapon fires. Most likely, he was ordered to finance and create another battalion. He will then try to draw people with Georgian surnames who live in Russia into this adventure. I do not know how successful he will be, because over these 12 years I have encountered very few Georgians on the front line — and those I did encounter were already dead.

The battalion will most likely consist of Russians, with a few Georgian-speaking people who will claim that the unit is mainly made up of Georgians.”

Commander of the Georgian Legion on former prosecutor general

World.title: Mzia Amaglobeli: ‘All it takes to avoid asking the regime for pardon is self-respect’
World.content:
“I don’t need advice to avoid apologising to an aggressor or asking the regime for a pardon. A sense of self-respect is enough,” political prisoner Mzia Amaglobeli writes in response to a statement by Shalva Papuashvili, speaker of the parliament of Georgia. At a briefing on 9 September, Papuashvili called prisoners of conscience “prisoners of Brussels’ shamelessness”.

The publication Batumelebi published Amaglobeli’s letter.

Mzia Amaglobeli: “The briefing in parliament was a display of shamelessness and nothing else. The regime has no morals. They do not even want to take responsibility for the unjust verdict that, in the name of Georgia, sent us to prison and branded us dangerous criminals.

They point the finger at Brussels and European diplomats. Shame on them. I don’t need advice to avoid apologising to an aggressor or asking the regime for a pardon. A sense of self-respect is enough.

If two years in prison is not humiliating enough, it will not be difficult for you to come up with something else if you want to keep me behind bars.

Power and state institutions are in your hands.

As for me, I will wait for international justice. I will wait for the day when the European Court of Human Rights examines the legality of the charges against me and the sentence imposed on me for slapping someone.

And you wait too, Mr Papuashvili. The European Court will examine the fairness and legitimacy of the repressive laws you have adopted, as well as their compliance with the Constitution and democratic processes.”

What Shalva Papuashvili said

On 9 September, commenting on the situation of political prisoners and prisoners of conscience, Shalva Papuashvili said they were “prisoners of Brussels’ shamelessness”. Papuashvili also spoke specifically about convicted journalist Mzia Amaglobeli, claiming that the court had given her the lightest possible sentence.

“Under Georgia’s Criminal Procedure Code, a lesser sentence is possible only through a plea agreement. That is what both the law and practice provide. A plea agreement was offered to her. It required only one thing: for Mzia Amaglobeli to acknowledge that what she had done was a crime and that her conduct had been wrong.

Mzia Amaglobeli is a prisoner of the shamelessness of those ambassadors who sat in court, looked her in the eye and effectively told her: ‘Do not plead guilty. Stay in prison.’ It is also the fault of those who awarded her completely unjustified prizes, including the European Parliament, thereby encouraging her not to admit that attacking a police officer is a crime,” Papuashvili said.

Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the well-known publications Batumelebi and Netgazeti, is the first female journalist in Georgia to become a prisoner of conscience.

Authorities arrested her in January 2025 in the city of Batumi during a protest after she slapped the head of the local police, Irakli Dgebuadze. The incident followed a confrontation between protesters and police, which the officers had provoked.

On 6 August 2025, Batumi City Court sentenced Mzia Amaglobeli to two years in prison. The court rejected her lawyer’s request to change her pre-trial measure.

Mzia Amaglobeli responds to the speaker of parliament

World.title: Türkiye’s producer inflation tops consumer prices in August 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Türkiye's producer price growth in August 2026 was estimated to have exceeded consumer price inflation during the month.

The estimate is derived from TURKSTAT's report on real investment returns, cross-referenced with the agency's separately published Consumer Price Index (CPI) data. The calculations suggest that domestic producer prices increased by approximately 2.55-2.6% month-on-month in August, compared with officially reported CPI inflation of 1.84%.

"Gold (ingot) yielded the highest monthly real profit rate," TURKSTAT said in the report, noting that the same financial instruments showed different real return figures depending on whether returns were adjusted using the domestic producer price index (D-PPI) or CPI. For example, gold's monthly real return was 7.17% based on D-PPI and 7.93% based on CPI, while deposit interest generated 0.33% by D-PPI and 1.05% by CPI.

Since each instrument's nominal return in lira terms remains unchanged regardless of the inflation measure applied, Trend's calculations use the difference between the two real-return figures to estimate the implied monthly D-PPI inflation rate. Using gold, deposit interest, the U.S. dollar and the euro as four separate reference points, and TÜİK's officially reported CPI monthly inflation rate of 1.84% for August, the calculations indicate an implied D-PPI increase of approximately 2.55-2.6% during the month.

Trend's calculations indicate that the estimated D-PPI rate was around 0.7-0.8 percentage points above CPI inflation for August.

The calculations also show that, if a similar difference between producer and consumer prices continued over a full year, the implied annual D-PPI rate would be approximately 9-10 percentage points above Türkiye's annual CPI inflation rate of 31.51% recorded in August. However, a single month's comparison does not necessarily represent a longer-term trend.

For reference, TÜİK (TURKSTAT) publishes official Domestic Producer Price Index figures separately from CPI data. The calculation above represents an independent Trend estimate based on TÜİK's investment returns report and should not be considered an official D-PPI figure.

World.title: Azerbaijani gymnasts win silver medal at World Championships (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 13. Azerbaijani gymnasts achieved a successful result at the World Aerobic Gymnastics Championships, held in the Spanish city of Pamplona from September 11 to 13, the Azerbaijan Gymnastics Federation said.

Representing Azerbaijan in the mixed pairs event, Madina Mustafayeva and Vladimir Dolmatov delivered a confident performance in the final and won the silver medal, finishing just 0.1 points behind the winners.

The Azerbaijani pair, who are European champions, scored 19.050 points in the qualification round to advance to the final. Based on the results of their final performance, the Azerbaijani gymnasts took second place on the podium.

More than 350 gymnasts from 38 countries competed in the prestigious event, which brought together the world’s top aerobic gymnasts.

World.title: NRL and NRLW finals dates and times announced for next week
World.content:
Dates and times for the second week of the NRL finals, and the opening week of the NRLW finals series, have been released.

The Sydney Roosters and New Zealand Warriors, losers in week one's qualifying finals, will host the NRL semifinals this weekend, September 18-20.

The Roosters will face the Cronulla Sharks at the Sydney Football Stadium on Saturday night, with kick-off at 7:50pm AEST. The winner of that match will face the Dolphins in a preliminary final the following week.

The other semifinal between the New Zealand Warriors and Newcastle Knights will be on Sunday, kicking off at 4:05pm AEST. The winner of that match will face the Penrith Panthers in a preliminary final.

It was confirmed on Sunday that the Warriors-Knights semifinal will be moved to Eden Park in Auckland, away from the Warriors' usual home ground at Mt Smart Stadium.

In the NRLW, the Wests Tigers and Canberra Raiders face off on Friday night, in each club's maiden finals appearance.

On Saturday, the Brisbane Broncos and Newcastle Knights battle in a knock-out final.

The Sydney Roosters and Gold Coast Titans have the week off after finishing in the top two on the NRLW ladder.

World.title: Patient suffers torn oesophagus after using unapproved peptide
World.content:
A patient who used an unapproved peptide labelled as the weight-loss drug retatrutide has suffered a potentially fatal torn oesophagus.

The medicines regulator, the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), has revealed details of the case to the ABC as part of its latest warning against the use of unapproved peptides.

It said the peptide user experienced uncontrollable vomiting and required hospitalisation.

The TGA said laboratory testing found the product contained no retatrutide, but instead had undeclared semaglutide, the drug used in weight-loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy.

The testing also revealed an exceptionally high dose of the drug.

What's the point of peptides? We want to hear your stories Have you come across injectable peptides yet? They're everywhere on social media right now and we want to know why people are using them, and what their experience has been like.

"The amount of semaglutide detected was approximately eight times higher than the level found in semaglutide products assessed by the TGA," the regulator's safety advisory said.

The results follow testing by the ABC in partnership with the University of Queensland, which found vials of black market retatrutide had much higher doses than declared on their labels.

The results follow testing by the ABC and UQ, which found vials of black market retatrutide had much higher doses than declared on their labels. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Melbourne gastroenterologist Darcy Holt has treated patients who have suffered adverse effects from injecting unapproved counterfeit retatrutide.

He said a torn oesophagus, which is the tube that carries food and liquid to a person's stomach, was a medical emergency.

"Without prompt medical attention a ruptured oesophagus is almost universally fatal," he said.

"A tear of the oesophagus can mean that stomach contents can enter the part of the body where the heart and main blood vessels are, and infection and inflammation in that area are extremely serious.

"Many of the peptides we are talking about do have gastrointestinal effects and require titration of dose to minimise those effects.

"But in overdose, the gastrointestinal effects can be severe. A high dose of the drug can cause extreme nausea and forceful vomiting leading to an oesophageal tear."

Darcy Holt says a ruptured oesophagus is "almost universally fatal". (Supplied)

Dr Holt said patients had also suffered liver toxicity and severe secretory diarrhoea from taking unapproved peptides, which can also be life-threatening.

A new TGA safety advisory says retatrutide was currently undergoing clinical trials in humans and has not been approved by it or any comparable international regulator.

It should not be used outside of a clinical trial setting, the note said.

The TGA's chief medical advisor, Robyn Langham, said "the biggest risks with unapproved peptide products are not knowing what is in the vial, how much of, or even what substance it contains, whether its sterile or whether it contains other contaminants or toxins".

"These risks are particularly concerning for injectable products, where contaminated or non-sterile manufacturing can increase the risk of infection and harmful immune responses including anaphylaxis," she said.

Robyn Langham says unapproved peptide products are very risky. (Four Corners: Keana Naughton)

Dr Holt said he had seen a noticeable increase in patients telling him they were using unapproved retatrutide this year.

"Over the past three to six months the use of peptides like retatrutide has gone from something that basically we would never elicit from a patient's medication list to something that now quite frequently pops up when we're asking someone what drugs they're taking," he said.

World.title: Ballarat girl in child protection system found dead in squat house
World.content:
Mia, whose name has been changed to protect the identity of children, loved to dress up as a child, and would sing along to every song, even if she didn't know the words.

Warning: This story contains descriptions of alleged child sexual abuse.

"I loved her laugh," said her grandmother Michelle, whose name has been changed to protect the identity of children.

Mia's teachers at daycare would always be excited to find out what superhero or princess she would be each day.

Michelle, who looked after her, said she had a normal childhood right up until COVID-19, when she was in grade 6.

"Then everything went south for her," she said.

If you or anyone you know needs help: Police: Triple Zero (000) if it is an emergency

Kids Helpline: 1800 551 800

Headspace:1800 650 890

ReachOut: au.reachout.com

Bravehearts: 1800 272 831

Lifeline: 13 11 14

1800 Respect National Helpline: 1800 737 732

On June 22, 17-year-old Mia and her 26-year-old boyfriend Marcus, whose name has been changed to protect the identity of children, were found dead in a "squat house" in Ballarat that had no running water or power.

The coroner heard the pair died from carbon monoxide poisoning believed to have been from a barbecue or grill in the room.

Their bodies were surrounded by drug paraphernalia.

Mia had been living in residential care since she was 14, a state-run last resort for children who could not live at home.

Two days before her death, Michelle and Mia's mother Ava, whose name has been changed to protect the identity of children, alleged Mia's bed at her residential care facility Berry Street was closed with less than a days' notice.

The ABC understands that before Mia died, she had been approved to live in a "safe house" with a woman known to have an extensive criminal history.

Michelle said Mia was supposed to be living with the woman, but she and Marcus went to a squatting house they occasionally stayed in.

"Why would they shut her bed?" Michelle said.

"She didn't die from drug use, she died from neglect.

" In state care, this has been allowed to happen. She was found dead in a squat house. "

Mia was raised by her grandmother due to Ava's drug dependence and being in an abusive relationship.

But Michelle said Mia's life started to derail when an older man began targeting her when she was 14.

After discovering Mia and her boyfriend Marcus were doing drugs in the house, Michelle asked Marcus to leave.

Mia then followed the next day.

Mia's death is the subject of a coronial inquest.

A Department of Families, Fairness and Housing spokesperson said that as the matter was before the Coroners Court, they were not able to comment, but that "the death of any child is tragic".

Michelle said when Mia moved into residential care at 14, she was targeted by an older man and he would often assault her.

"He would beat her black and blue," Michelle said.

It's believed this man was known to police, but he had never been charged.

Residential care homes, where children are grouped together in share house-like accommodation, house about 450 children across the state.

They include children as young as seven.

The ABC has reported on the "invisible" children of residential care, who are free to roam at night and are often targets of child sexual exploitation.

Last year, a 13-year-old girl became pregnant in residential care.

Residential care staff have also detailed prolific drug use inside the homes.

In an email to staff in December 2024, Berry Street wrote that some staff at facilities in Sebastopol, Ballarat East and Diamond Creek were worried they were drug-affected at work due to second-hand exposure.

Residential care staff have previously detailed prolific drug use inside residential care homes. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

'Safe house'

The ongoing coronial inquest has heard Mia was subject to care by secretary order, meaning the state government retained total legal guardianship, but residential care provider Berry Street remained responsible for her daily care and housing.

Victoria Police is expected to deliver its findings to the court in November.

Do you know more? Contact Coco Veldkamp using cocoveldkamp@proton.me or Eden Hynninen using Hynninen.Eden@abc.net.au

If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

Berry Street did not respond to questions about why Mia's bed in the residential care facility was allegedly closed two days prior to her death or why Mia had been allegedly allowed to stay in the squat house she died in.

It also did not answer questions about Berry Street's awareness of her relationship with her boyfriend Marcus.

"Berry Street acknowledges that the death of any young person is a tragic loss for their family, friends and the broader community," Berry Street said in a statement.

"As this matter is currently the subject of an active investigation before the Coroners Court, it would be inappropriate to comment further."

Methamphetamine was found in Mia's system after she died. (936 ABC Hobart: Fred Hooper)

The coroner's court has heard that while under the care of the state, Mia had gone missing 94 times, had a "complex mental health history", and took drugs like GHB and methylamphetamine.

Michelle said that while Mia and Marcus were staying in her home briefly, Marcus was served a harbouring notice, a written warning issued by Child Protection or Victoria Police to a person suspected of hiding, concealing, or allowing an at-risk young person to stay at their property.

Mia's mother Ava said a week before Mia's 17th birthday, she confided in her about the dark and abusive nature of her relationship to Marcus.

She said the pair were often taking drugs together, including GHB, and Mia had had multiple overdoses.

Ava said Mia told her Marcus had also been physical and threatened her.

In the week before her death, Michelle and Ava said they had begged Mia to come home.

"I would speak to her all night on the phone begging her to come back," Michelle said.

World.title: Tomahawks and wine: How long was Gold Coast mayor's 'dinner' with Trump?
World.content:
Tom Tate, mayor of Australia's glitziest city, the Gold Coast, was in the middle of an expensive ratepayer-backed trip around the world, the icing of which would be dinner with US President Donald Trump.

"He knew who I was, and he came up and called me Mr Mayor," Mr Tate later recalled.

The February dinner, he said in interviews, had taken place at Mar-a-Lago, the president's famed Florida holiday retreat, following the signing of a deal with a Queensland developer for a proposed Trump Tower on the Gold Coast.

Conflicting accounts have emerged of Gold Coast mayor Tom Tate's dinner with Donald Trump. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

They shared tomahawk steaks and "expensive wine". "Mate, I had dinner with him," Mr Tate told Triple M Gold radio about meeting the president.

But the ABC has uncovered conflicting recollections and questions about openness for the headline-making trip.

The White House has told the ABC that the US president and First Lady Melania Trump "did not have dinner with that group," including the mayor.

And an ABC right-to-information request for documents turned up next to no documents about a moment the mayor described as the Gold Coast getting a "guernsey to meet the leader of the free world".

Do you know more? Contact Liam Walsh on encrypted email or Signal. Please note end-to-end encryption is only possible with your own encrypted email system like Protonmail or Signal account.

World trip

The Gold Coast is Australia's sixth-biggest city, a tourism mecca of glamour and surf with a population swelling past 647,000.

Mr Tate, 67, is its controversial four-term mayor, selling the city with a message of being "open for business" and camera-friendly stunts such as wielding a golden sledgehammer.

He had been busy overseas throughout February. In cold Milan, he wore a white, pink and orange windproof jacket and a white Olympic beanie as he held the silver torch as an official Games torchbearer. He posted a picture on Instagram.

Tom Tate was recently in Milan where he took on the role of an official Olympic Games torchbearer. (Supplied)

That day started jam-packed. An itinerary released under right-to-information laws shows Mr Tate, on the Brisbane 2032 Olympic committee, was instructed to wear neutral or white shoes, leave the hotel at 6:45am, not forget his identification, and start his 200 m torch walk at 10:13am.

Other days were similarly hectic. That included multiple meetings with infrastructure officials in Dubai, interspersed with lunch at the high-class Sexy Fish restaurant. Mr Tate also posted on Instagram: the mayor meeting a Dubai official in traditional Arab robes; the mayor in a hard hat on a building site.

A visit to Dubai this year was posted to Instagram. (Supplied)

The council itinerary includes separate briefing packs, outlining who Mr Tate was meeting and details about their background. Even Mr Tate's meeting with the Dubai Future Foundation's boss recommended the mayor wear business attire.

It all contrasted with a dearth of information about what happened when Mr Tate, after Dubai, arrived in Florida and pulled into 20 acres of landscaped gardens that constitute the Mar-a-Lago Club, founded by Mr Trump in 1995.

Mr Tate said he was there to sign an ultimately doomed deal between the Trump Organization, run by Mr Trump's son Eric, and Queensland developer Altus to construct a Trump Tower on the Gold Coast. The plan was a $1.5 billion deal for a 340-metre-tall, six-star luxury complex on the beach at Surfers Paradise.

Altus was led by David Young, a former bankrupt developer who had returned to build housing near Rockhampton and secured a long-sought deal with the Trump Organizsation. Mr Young posted online a photo shaking hands with Eric Trump in Florida that February.

Altus CEO David Young with Trump Organization executive vice president Eric Trump. (Supplied: Altus Property Group)

The dinner

Yet all that is listed in council documents for the mayor's three days at Mar-a-Lago is a four-word entry for a Friday: "Meeting with Trump Organization."

Mr Tate later told the media about the signing and then having dinner with the president. He said his wife marvelled at how beautiful the first lady was "in real life".

US President Donald Trump. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

During a Triple M Gold radio interview (which started by playing the lyrics "Tom Tate, he's our mayor and he is great" to the tune of English pop band Madness's Our House), he twice noted dining with the president.

Triple M: Tom, so you have had, you had dinner with Donald? Mayor: Yeah, yeah, and Eric [Trump] and Lara [Eric's wife]. He added: "We were drinking expensive wine and a couple of tomahawks."

The White House, asked about the dinner and Australians that night, told the ABC: "The President and the First Lady did not have dinner with that group."

Another account of the dinner, told to the ABC, is that the two politicians met briefly when the president came to where his son Eric and the Australians were sitting, but the US leader was seated at another table at Mar-a-Lago that evening.

An aerial view of the Mar-a-Lago estate. (AP Photo: Steve Helber)

Mr Tate had insisted he had flown to Florida following an "invitation" from the Trump Organization.

"I was there as mayor of the city. So that's the gift to the city," he told the ABC in an earlier interview.

No record of an invitation exists, according to a right-to-information search of Gold Coast council records. Mr Tate's office since said: "The invitation was issued verbally."

Mr Tate had also initially listed on his council register of interests that the Trump Organization had paid for his accommodation and meals, along with transfers.

A rendered image of The Trump International Hotel & Tower Gold Coast development. (Supplied: Altus Property Group)

It caused a stir, with questions about the mayor potentially having a conflict of interest with a Gold Coast Trump Tower proposal, which had attracted almost 100,000 petitioners objecting. Local Gold Coast media also hammered council over official overseas travel.

The invoice

But Mr Tate's office has since changed the register declaration to say he had personally paid for the accommodation and transfers.

Gold Coast Trump Tower scrapped The branded tower proposed for Surfers Paradise would have been Australia's tallest building.

"My intention was always to personally fund any hospitality provided to me at Mar-a-Lago," he said in a statement.

"Pending receipt of the invoice, and in an abundance of caution, I disclosed the hospitality on my register of interests to ensure my disclosures remained consistent with my reporting obligations.

"Once the invoice was received, I promptly paid the amount personally and immediately updated my register."

He did declare receiving a red hat, along with the meals.

The mayor has declined to answer many questions, only issuing statements. He will not supply the Mar-a-Lago invoice, even after a right-to-information request from the ABC.

Mr Tate's office said the trip was "private".

The whole council trip was bookended. Mr Tate had work events in Los Angeles in late February. Again, the council itinerary indicates Los Angeles was full of meetings, such as Mr Tate attending Amazon MGM Studios, which worked with Gold Coast-linked contractors.

Mr Tate's office insisted that the Barbados side-trip was economical given his Los Angeles events. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Still, the ABC can reveal, in between Florida and Los Angeles, Mr Tate took a week-long private holiday, flying in and out of Barbados, allowed under council rules.

Flights involving Barbados were paid personally. Council records show the cost to ratepayers of flights from Australia to Italy and Dubai and Florida, and then to Los Angeles and home, was almost $33,000, the ABC can reveal. (He was entitled to a business class flight and paid personally to upgrade to first-class).

Mr Tate's office insisted that the Barbados side-trip was economical given his Los Angeles events.

"Doing so avoided the need for two separate trips to the United States and ensured no additional airfare costs were incurred by the city," it said.

The Gold Coast Trump Tower proposal fell over in less three months.

World.title: Wind farm proponent wants to build 280 turbines on public land
World.content:
On the numbers, the Whaleback Ridge wind farm proposal is enormous.

With a planned capital spend of almost $3.5 billion, Westcoast Renewable Energy (WRE) wants to build 280 wind turbines, each up to 250 metres tall at the blade tip, across a 40,000-hectare tract of public land to the north and west of Zeehan, on Tasmania's west coast.

WRE said once it was operational, after a decade-long construction timeline, the wind farm would be capable of generating 2.8 gigawatts of power, which is more than the state-owned electricity generator Hydro Tasmania's capacity.

The 40,500 hectare project area to the north and west of Zeehan, on which Westcoast Renewable Energy intends to erect 280 wind turbines over the next decade. (ABC News)

The company claims the development would be an economic boom for Zeehan, with up to 350 jobs based in town during construction, and 90 ongoing positions.

In Zeehan, some residents are excited for that prospect, but a wildlife foundation is critical of the use of public land for a wind farm it believes will threaten native wildlife.

West coast wind a 'unique advantage'

The company has previous form in large-scale wind farm developments, having built and sold the Granville Harbour Wind Farm, which is visible from Whaleback Ridge and started generating power in 2020.

But the Granville Harbour Wind Farm, with 30 turbines, is much smaller than what's proposed for Whaleback Ridge. And it was built on private farmland.

The bulk of the Whaleback Ridge proposal, north and west of Zeehan, is to be built on three reserves: the Meredith Range, Parting Creek and Mount Heemskirk regional reserves.

Stephen Casey says the wind on the west coast is a "unique advantage" for Tasmania. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

WRE chief executive Stephen Casey, a former TasPorts and Incat boss and a former BHP mining executive, compared the quality and consistency of wind on the west coast to a rich iron ore seam in Western Australia's Pilbara desert:

" It is a unique advantage for Tasmania and something we can really contribute to the transition to renewable energies across Australia. "

Mr Casey said the company intended to privately finance the entire multi-billion dollar project, and had no plans to seek public funding.

He said that pending state and federal government approvals, the company hoped to start construction on the first phase — 70 turbines capable of generating up to 432 megawatts — in late 2028.

He also said energy-hungry data centres, several of which are currently being planned or built in Tasmania, were being considered as potential users of the project's power.

Whaleback Ridge is currently being assessed under the federal Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, and in 2024 the state government declared the proposal a major project, meaning it will be assessed by a Tasmanian Planning Commission panel at the state level.

The project has been downsized substantially since 2024, when it was aiming to build 500 turbines and create hundreds of permanent jobs and thousands of construction jobs.

Earlier this week, WRE announced former Tasmanian premier Peter Gutwein as its chair.

Questions over use of public land

Bob Brown Foundation campaigner Scott Jordan said the project was "terrible", and he questioned why public land would be allowed to be used for a large-scale private development.

He said it would put at risk native Tasmanian species such as the wedge-tailed eagle and the critically endangered orange-bellied parrot.

Scott Jordan says the Whaleback Ridge wind farm will threaten native Tasmanian wildlife. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

He also dismissed the company's claims that its turbines and associated works would only disrupt 500 hectares of the 40,000-hectare site.

"If we put a tower in the middle of the [MCG], its footprint is going to be fairly small, but you can't play football anymore," he said.

" To pretend the physical impact is the extent of the total impact is a fallacy. "

Mr Jordan said the foundation was not opposed to renewable energy projects, but that they must not come at a cost to the environment.

"If the profit is coming before the environment, then their credibility doesn't stack up," he said.

The company says it has chosen turbine locations to avoid the orange-bellied parrot's migration path. (Supplied: NRE Tas)

Mr Casey said the company had been surveying the site for several years and had chosen specific turbine locations to avoid the orange-bellied parrot's migration route.

"We know the path of the birds, and we're making sure we're building further away from there," he said.

He said the company was committed to building its turbines where they had the least environmental impact, and that it would continue to have conversations with its opponents.

Cautious hope to see Zeehan 'thrive again'

In town, some residents are cautiously optimistic about the economic claims WRE has made.

Luke Munro moved to Zeehan about a year ago to buy land and start a barber shop, which he said people were lining up for even as he was still building the shop's fixtures.

Luke Munro, originally from New South Wales, recently moved to Zeehan and opened a barber shop. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Mr Munro said wind farms were "majestic", but that "nothing is perfect" when it comes to renewable energy production.

"I know a lot of people don't share that same thought, but I think it's a lot better than digging up dinosaurs and burning them," he said.

Andrew Cronin and his wife recently purchased property in Zeehan, and are optimistic about the proposal. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Andrew Cronin is familiar with Zeehan's storied history as a mining town and the one-time economic centre of Tasmania, and has hope for its future.

World.title: Will building three warships be worth Australia's $27 billion?
World.content:
In a massive shed at Adelaide's Osborne shipyards, a ceremonial coin is placed under the keel of the first Hunter-class frigate — continuing an ancient shipbuilding ritual that will hopefully bring the new ship good luck.

After a troubled journey so far, the Hunter frigate warship might well need it.

The first of six new Hunter-class frigates recently hit a major construction milestone — with two separate 'blocks' joined together — and is due for delivery in 2032.

In the years since the Turnbull government began searching for a 'future frigate' to replace the aging Anzac-class frigate, the Hunter has become a pin-up for all that can go wrong in defence procurement.

But its advocates argue that when it does arrive, it will be one of the world's most capable warships of its kind, and in a contested Indo-Pacific, well worth the delays and cost blowouts it suffered early on.

The federal government has found itself making both arguments at once.

In a speech to the national press club in July, Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy pointed to the Hunter frigates as a perfect example of a project launched with the right ambition, but plagued by poor decision-making.

"A project with the right intent and capability at the time, but let down by a system that prioritised gold-plated requirements without considering cost and schedule impacts," he said in the speech.

Budget documents show that close to $27 billion has been allocated to building the first three ships.

That figure includes both the cost of the ship's construction and the cost of building the shipyards at Osborne in South Australia.

The Hunter frigates are under construction in South Australia. (ABC News: Tom Lowrey)

Billions more — though much less than $27 billion — will be needed for the final three ships.

In an interview with the ABC, Mr Conroy said despite his own highlighting of the project's hurdles, the price tag would be justified.

"I believe it is because we are getting the most advanced submarine-hunting warship in the world," he said.

"Ninety-eight per cent of our trade is through maritime sea lanes.

" It is really important that we have the ability to protect our maritime trade, as well as deter others, and the ability to hunt submarines is a critical part of that. "

A troubled start

When the Turnbull government announced in 2018 its intention to build the Hunter-class frigate, based on BAE Systems' Type 26 Global Combat Ship, it described the future warship as "one of the world's most advanced anti-submarine warfare frigates".

Early warning signs suggested the path ahead would be troubled.

Early planning for a future frigate to replace the aging Anzac-class frigates was for an "off-the-shelf" design — that is, an established warship that would require minimal changes and could be built in Adelaide.

An Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) report in 2023 found that of three options shortlisted in early 2016, two other options — one from Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri and one from Spain's Navantia — were considered the "most viable designs".

How Australia's surface naval fleet is being reshaped Don't know your frigates from your AWDs and OPVs? Here's a run down of how Australia's surface naval fleet looks, and how it will change under the federal government's new plan.

The BAE Type 26 was included as a third option, and the ANAO noted that there were no records explaining why it was picked as the third, over another French option.

Defence records also noted that while the clear preference had been for an off-the-shelf option, the Type 26 was not yet a "ship in water".

It was eventually selected, and the 2018 announcement suggested that Australia would build nine ships for $35 billion, with the first to enter service in the late 2020s.

By the time Defence released its 2020 Force Structure Plan, the nine frigates were to cost $45 billion.

And within a few years, questions were swirling about whether the frigates would be built at all, as the Albanese government questioned what sort of surface fleet the navy would need to best complement nuclear-powered submarines.

The Hunter program survived the surface fleet review, but the total number of ships was cut from nine to six.

Contracts have been signed with BAE to build the first three ships, all due to enter service in the 2030s, and another 'batch two' contract will be needed for the final three.

Half submarine hunter, half air warfare destroyer

The initial idea for the frigates to replace the Anzac class was a warship with "a strong emphasis on submarine detection and response operations", according to the 2009 Defence white paper that first signalled the plans.

But the ship now being built does much more than that.

From the outset, Defence planned two major modifications to BAE's Type 26 model — adding the extremely powerful Australian-made CEA phased array radar, and an Aegis combat system.

The CEA radar is already a feature of Australia's Anzac frigates, and is widely regarded as one of the world's best military radar systems.

The Aegis combat management system is an American product used by the US Navy, and aims to add as much interoperability with the United States as possible.

Both additions add enormous cost and complexity to the build, but both were included in the Hunter project from the 2018 announcement of BAE as the successful bidder.

Pat Conroy speaking at National Press Club in July 2026. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Mr Conroy said the former Coalition government "mis-characterised" the project from the outset.

"They presented it as acquiring an off-the-shelf design, an existing platform that the UK was building for themselves," he said.

"But what they actually decided to do was take the hull from a Type 26 frigate and then put in a very different combat system, the Aegis combat system, put in a very advanced radar that we developed, as well as an Australian combat system in addition to Aegis.

"So it was a developmental project, but they didn't tell the Australian public it was developmental, and they weren't honest about the risks and possible delays that developmental projects cause."

But he said those additions would also make it an extremely capable warship.

"[The ships] will be the most advanced anti-submarine warship in the world," he said.

"And they will also be equipped with one of the most advanced radars in the world and the most advanced combat system in the world, which means that they will be very good at both hunting submarines, but also defending both themselves and ships that are escorting against air attack.

"So they'll be a very effective ship. But that doesn't mean that the project ran perfectly from its origin."

Marcus Hellyer, the head of research at Strategic Analysis Australia, is a strong critic of the Hunter frigates and argued it was simply trying to do too much.

He pointed to the ship having 32 vertical missile-launch cells, compared to 96 on many US Navy destroyers, as one example of its limitations.

"We picked an anti-submarine warfare frigate, but then kind of wrapped an air warfare destroyer radar and combat system around it," he said.

"So it's sort of trying to do everything — trying to do anti-submarine warfare, it's trying to do air warfare, it's trying to do surface warfare in terms of maritime strike and land strike.

" And as we know, a system that tries to do everything well ends up not doing anything particularly well. "

Rebuilding in the valley of death

A massive hurdle in the construction of the Hunter frigate has been reconstructing Adelaide's shipbuilding industry, and trying to make it a permanent feature of Australia's industrial landscape.

Adelaide's shipyards entered what became known as the "valley of death" in 2016, as years of work building three Hobart-class air warfare destroyers wound down.

With no major shipbuilding project to move onto, skilled workers in the Osborne shipyards had to turn elsewhere for work, like major road projects in Adelaide or other opportunities interstate.

By 2016, the problem was well-known, and establishing continuous naval shipbuilding became a stated aim of the Hunter project.

But even the ambitious early deadlines attached to the project only saw construction of the ships starting in Adelaide from 2020, and in the end, steel would not be cut on the first ship until 2024.

The hope is that the shipyards will eventually produce a new Hunter frigate every 18 months to two years.

The first three ships are expected to cost $27 billion. (Supplied: BAE Systems Australia)

Andy Coxall from BAE Systems Australia is tasked with steering the frigates' construction, having previously worked in BAE's UK shipyards.

He said the Osborne shipyards suffered enormously from lost momentum as the build of the Hobart destroyers wound down, and workers were left with nowhere to go.

"They were just hitting their straps, and just got through all the difficult bits, then suddenly there's no more work," he said.

"People have got to feed their families. Even if they want to do shipbuilding, they'll say 'I'm off to do road construction'.

"And then once you reset like that, it's very difficult to get them back."

He said the early years of construction were hit with rolling challenges beyond rebuilding the industry, including the COVID-19 pandemic, which prevented specialists from BAE's UK shipyards from moving to Australia.

And he pushed back on some of the criticism of the ship — arguing that while the changes have undoubtedly added complexity, it would be a better warship for it.

"Anyone that's working on [the ship] understands why the Commonwealth is doing it. They're doing it for what we believe are the right reasons," he said.

"And as a consequence I actually think we're getting a much more capable ship than even its reference ship design."

US–Australia talks on AUKUS changes have been underway for 18 months The changes announced over the weekend will see Australia buy three second-hand submarines, rather than two second-hand and one new.

He said they accepted there had to be a level of flexibility to make sure the warship was as capable as possible.

"What we're doing is talking about national defence, and in some cases life and death of Australian servicemen and women," he said.

"So if something occurs in Ukraine, or in the geopolitics of our region, which means we have to change the technology to keep capability, then OK, you've got to get on with it."

And he said there was a level of frustration with the discourse around the Hunter frigates — that they were too expensive, too complex and too slow to build.

"Our contract was never just about building ships. It was never just about that," he said.

"Yes, ships were a catalyst, and yes, the navy needs our capability, but that was never the contract.

"The contract was to build ships and re-establish a capability, you know. Build an industry."

Rough waters for warships

Marcus Hellyer argued the world was becoming a more dangerous place to be operating warships, pointing to recent conflicts as evidence.

"The Ukrainians have hit numerous Russian warships in the Black Sea. Some Western navies were too scared to go into the Red Sea to take on the Houthis," he said.

"And we're also seeing that the US Navy won't actually run the Iranian blockade of the Persian Gulf. So all of that tells us that it's a very, very dangerous world for surface warships."

He said it raised questions about the place the Hunter frigates would hold — as large, crewed and complex warships — once they entered service in the 2030s.

"We are now spending $27 billion to get a vanishingly small number of exquisitely expensive warships whose sort of viability in modern conflict is increasingly questionable," he said.

And he said scrapping the project now — even if it meant forgoing the billions of dollars already spent — could still be the right call, if the remaining $20 billion or so was spent on additional Mogami frigates or autonomous systems.

Japan vows to give Australia first access to new Mogami warship Tokyo is stepping up its campaign to win a lucrative Australian naval contract by pledging to give "priority" to warship exports over its own navy.

But that argument is rejected by others like Alessio Patalano, a professor of war and strategy in East Asia at King's College London.

"In the age of missiles and drones, it turns out that the safest and most reliable place from where a competent professional organisation can project power is actually from the deck of a warship at sea," he said.

"How do we know this? Tell me, when was the last time that the Iranians, who worked the last 40 years to try to blow up an American warship, sunk, touched, or even scraped a large major surface combatant that is currently deployed?"

He said that while $27 billion was a lot of money, it was hard to see how they could have been built cheaper.

"No project is straightforward. No particularly complex project like an advanced warship is a straight line," he said.

"And frankly given the modifications, the changing requirements, the strategic conditions under which things were to be pursued, the availability of yards and manpower — I don't think there is any other cheaper solution to this."

Building towards AUKUS

The Osborne shipyards building the Hunter frigates sit amidst a massive, separate construction project — the enormous facilities that will eventually build Australia's first AUKUS-class submarine.

The Hunter shipyards sit beside what will eventually become the AUKUS shipyards, building at least five nuclear-powered submarines.

Two AUKUS submarine optimal pathways Scrutiny of AUKUS's delivery reveals two "optimal pathways" for Australia's submarines.

When the Hunter program was launched, Australia was still planning to build a fleet of diesel-electric Attack-class submarines with French shipbuilder the Naval Group.

But with those plans having now pivoted to the far more ambitious task of building an all-new AUKUS-class submarine, those working on the Hunter project hope they are laying the industrial foundations.

Andy Coxall said what they are working on pales in comparison to the scale and complexity of what is being attempted under AUKUS.

"Getting steelworkers used to delivering quality outputs to a very high level neatly dovetails into building the same level of output for submarines that are even higher, if you like, in terms of complexity," he said.

"So I think we're building a good position, certainly at Osborne, with that.

"But getting the nation's head around nuclear engineering and what that means is probably the challenge that Hunter isn't solving."

Defence Minister Richard Marles with his Japanese counterpart Koizumi Shinjiro, after signing a multi-billion-dollar agreement for Mogami frigates. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

Australia's naval fleet is undergoing its biggest transformation in decades.

Over the next two decades, aging fleets of Anzac-class frigates and Collins-class submarines will be replaced with new fleets of Hunter and Mogami frigates, along with Virginia-class and AUKUS-class submarines.

Mr Conroy said it was an undoubtedly expensive process, but worthwhile.

"We're more than doubling the surface fleet as well as acquiring the AUKUS submarines," he said.

"So they all go hand in hand, but this investment will be worth it."

World.title: The political pile-on that could be Pauline Hanson's best weapon
World.content:
In both Liberal and Labor research on how to meet the growing electoral threat from One Nation, one piece of advice does not change.

Do not go after Pauline Hanson personally.

Not because these parties don't want to. They do. But after hours of focus groups, one finding is remarkably consistent: a significant group of voters see Hanson as the victim of a political pile-on.

For her supporters, any attack on her risks reinforcing that perception — particularly because Hanson has positioned herself as the outsider exposing Canberra's cosy political club.

So the strategy has been simple — demolish the argument, not the woman.

You can hear it in Angus Taylor's reluctance to take Hanson on directly. He is trying to win back voters drifting to One Nation without sounding like he is judging them. Or worse, looking down on them.

Taylor's caution can look awkward and passive. But there is a reason for it.

Kos Samaras, director of Redbridge and a former Victorian Labor strategist, says the polling explains much of why.

"That applies to about half her base. So about 15 per cent of Australians who report to us they plan to vote for One Nation have a parasocial relationship with her and her party," he says.

"The other half is parked on her because they are sick of the two-party system, but they harbour some reservations about her views."

Samaras says about half of Hanson's vote is rusted on to her. The rest is softer. They are fed up with the major parties, but they still have reservations about the One Nation leader.

One Nation's Hastie strategy is risky

That makes One Nation's decision to go after Andrew Hastie particularly risky.

One Nation thrives on anti-establishment grievance. But branding a former SAS officer a traitor for evidence he gave under subpoena moves well past this terrain and into something much darker.

Samaras puts it simply: "This second half will mark her down for calling Hastie a traitor."

He is referring to One Nation's "Please Explain" cartoon, which was pinned to Hanson's X account. It called Hastie a "traitor" eight times and a "gutless maggot", seemingly in response to the deputy Liberal leader giving evidence under subpoena in the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation case.

When asked about the video, Hanson called it satire and refused to remove it.

As Hanson asks voters to treat One Nation as a party ready to govern, she will find it harder to stand only on a platform of grievance.

Hanson is formidable in telling people who to blame. She has built her brand and profile on being the lone straight talker prepared to call out politicians and a broken system letting hard-working families down.

Will One Nation supporters mark Pauline Hanson down for attacking Andrew Hastie? (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The stuff Hanson thrives on

And politics can provide her with pretty good material.

Coverage of a public golf club getting $6 million is usually reserved for suburban papers and community social media pages.

Last week, the Marrickville Golf Club found itself trending in Canberra as the government defended a grant made through its $560 million community infrastructure program.

The political storm was not whether the club needed the money; it was that Anthony Albanese had been made an honorary member and the club happens to be in his electorate.

The prime minister said he did not know the club had made him an honorary member and had not been in the clubhouse for years.

And in the kind of irony that only seems to fly in Canberra, Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie was leading the attack.

Labor tied itself in knots to say its program was different from the community grants that became known as sports rorts and resulted in Bridget McKenzie losing her job in the former Morrison government.

For voters dealing with the cost-of-living crisis, the fact that the schemes are not identical and the circumstances are different won't be the part of the story that cuts through.

They see one side of politics attack the other for the way it spends taxpayer money, then appear to do the same themselves.

This is exactly the kind of stuff Hanson thrives on.

McKenzie resigned in February 2020, after failing to disclose her membership of a gun club that received $36,000 of government funding.

Labor went hard at the time; then-deputy opposition leader Richard Marles said: "Politics shouldn't be the basis on which these decisions are made. This wasn't about community sport, this was about saving the Liberal Party."

Last week, when pushed on the Marrickville grant, Albanese said: "I make no apologies for my electorate being serviced by me as a good local member."

Grievance politics isn't enough

That is the problem for the major parties: every time they attack something in opposition, then do a version of it in government, Hanson gets another free kick.

But the closer One Nation gets to power, the harder it is to survive on grievance alone.

The irony is, Hanson has plenty of material without having to go for personal attacks.

Over the weekend, comments Hanson made earlier about the prime minister's mother, Maryanne Albanese, resurfaced. Albanese was raised by his mother in public housing in Sydney's inner west, where she relied on a disability pension, living with severe rheumatoid arthritis that crippled her joints.

"Housing commission houses should not be there for people to live in them for 30, 40 [years]," Hanson said. "You have been given a hand up, move it on to the next ones coming through."

Albanese on Sunday paid tribute to his mother for maintaining her kindness despite having a tough life.

"If Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that's fine. But my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson's league — way out of it," an emotional Albanese said at a press conference in Sydney.

He added: "I'm proud to be a 'houso'."

Political analysis that matters The ABC's politics podcast, Politics Now, dives into the biggest stories, giving you a balanced look inside the strategies and decisions behind the headlines.

This is not the first time we have had a parent brought into political debate. Back in 2012, Alan Jones said Julia Gillard's father had "died of shame". Days later, Tony Abbott told parliament her government "should have already died of shame".

Abbott at the time said he was ''absolutely oblivious'' to Jones's controversial remarks. Gillard's father had recently died; it is hard to imagine she thought much of the oblivious line.

The ugly episode was a cautionary tale on what should be off limits in politics. You would think talking about the dead or calling a former soldier a traitor would be clear, indisputable lines not to cross.

If One Nation wants to be treated as a party ready to govern — voters will see its judgement as fair game too.

Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

World.title: Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, gives first glimpse of family life in Britain
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, gives first glimpse of family life in Britain Victoria Ward September 14, 2026 — 5:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: The Duchess of Sussex has provided the first glimpse of her family’s new life in the British countryside. A video montage posted on the duchess’s Instagram page on Sunday (UK time) painted an idyllic picture of the early English autumn, with a roaring fire, muddy puddles, raincoats and wellies. The Sussexes are shown walking through woodland before the duchess turns towards the camera to shout: “Come on you, come on.” One of the children appears to be humming as they warm their feet by a log fire, while someone wearing a pair of wellies delightedly jumps up and down in a large puddle.



Princess Lilibet, five, is shown riding a bicycle fitted with stabilisers and decorated with pink tassels, with a doll on the back. Meghan and Harry walk through woodland in one of the scenes from the Instagram clip. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex Prince Archie, her elder brother, runs towards a herd of deer that crosses their path ahead as the duke shouts out “Archie!” Pula, the family’s labrador, is shown bounding down another woodland track as Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go by Wham! plays over the footage. The duke and the children are also filmed in a small rowing boat as he fixes up a hook on a fishing rod while the dog plays in the water. Prince Archie, seven, can be heard saying “I got this” in a distinctly American accent.



The video was accompanied by a Union flag and a heart emoji side by side. It marks the first time the Duchess has been seen since returning to the country. An image of the duke filming at Tower Bridge Studios emerged on social media last week. A recent Instagram post shows the duchess with her daughter, Lilibet, last month. Instagram The family moved back to Britain from California in late August, and last week the children started at their new prep school. A source close to the couple said: “They are happy to be back.” However, tensions with Buckingham Palace emerged after a letter was sent at the direction of the King to military and government figures, reminding them that the Sussexes remained “private citizens” who did not represent the monarchy.

World.title: ASX eyes gains, Wall Street rises; Fed meeting in focus
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX eyes gains, Wall Street rises; Fed meeting in focus Stan Choe September 14, 2026 — 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks rebounded and regained much of their losses for the week after oil prices eased off their recent spurt. An update on inflation across the United States that came in close to economists’ expectations, even if prices are still rising too quickly for everyone’s liking, also helped calm the market. The S&P 500 climbed 0.9 per cent and snapped a four-day losing streak, its longest since June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 509 points, or 1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1 per cent. The latest inflation data strengthened expectations among traders that the Federal Reserve will feel compelled to hike its main interest rate at its meeting this week. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to climb, with futures on Saturday pointing to a gain of 18 points or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.75¢. They got help from a pullback in oil prices, which had jumped to their highest levels since May because of the ongoing war with Iran. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, fell 2.8 per cent to settle at $US104.61 after getting near $US110 overnight.



That took a bit of pressure off inflation, which remains stubbornly high. A report on Friday showed that US consumers had to pay prices for gasoline, food and other costs of living that were 3.4 per cent higher last month than a year earlier. While still high, that was close to what economists expected and what Wall Street was prepared for. The data also strengthened expectations among traders that the Federal Reserve will feel compelled to hike its main interest rate at its meeting this week. Related Article Opinion

AI The economic puzzle behind AI giants’ doomsday warnings Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Such moves are the typical way the Fed tries to rein in high inflation, and they work by filtering through the bond market, making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, slowing the economy and hopefully removing fuel for further inflation. The rising expectations for an upcoming hike to rates drove up the yield of the two-year Treasury, which moves with guesses for upcoming Fed action, to 4.62 per cent from 4.56 per cent late Thursday.



Longer-term Treasury yields held steadier, though. That could be a signal that investors in the bond market see upcoming hikes by the Fed as helping to keep control of inflation over the longer term. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose more modestly to 4.97 per cent from 4.95 per cent late Thursday, while the 30-year yield eased to 5.36 per cent from 5.37 per cent. Economists say hikes could quiet questions about the Fed’s commitment to keeping inflation under control. Worries had risen earlier in the summer about its credibility and whether it would do what’s needed to bring inflation down, even if it causes pain for the economy in the near term. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has been adamant about not giving hints about where the Fed may take interest rates, though he did calm some concerns among investors at a speech late last month. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has been pushing for interest rates to go lower rather than higher. “Symbolism can trump substance, even when it comes to monetary policy,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. It’s all coming at a moment when confidence among Americans continues to sour. A preliminary report from the University of Michigan on Friday said US consumer sentiment is falling, with declines for both Democrats and Republicans.



Their expectations for inflation coming in the year ahead jumped to 4.6 per cent from 4 per cent last month. That’s the highest reading since June, and it’s concerning for the Fed and for economists because it can trigger a vicious cycle of behaviour that worsens inflation. On Wall Street, Kroger rose 2.7 per cent after the grocer reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It also held firm on its forecast for profit over the fiscal year, even though it trimmed its forecast for an important underlying measure of revenue growth. ACV Auctions, whose digital marketplace connects wholesale buyers and sellers of vehicles, soared 44.2 per cent after Copart said it would pay $US10.50 in cash for each of the company’s shares. Copart, whose online vehicle auctions sold more than 4 million units in the last year, fell 2.6 per cent. Related Article General insurance ‘Humans make mistakes’: Insurer offers discount to self-driving car owners An early jump for Oracle faded as trading progressed after the tech giant reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. After initially leaping 8.5 per cent, its stock swiveled between gains and losses and finished with a loss of 1.7 per cent.



Stocks closely tied to the artificial-intelligence industry broadly became shaky this summer on worries that the AI frenzy may have sent prices too high. All told, the S&P 500 rose 65.28 points to 7,656.98. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 509.19 to 52,573.29, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 251.31 to 26,333.04. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe as oil prices eased. London’s FTSE 100 added 0.4 per cent after a report said the U.K. economy was stronger in July than economists expected. Stock markets were weaker in Asia, where Japan’s Nikkei 225 lost 1.9 per cent and South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.8 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
