World.title: Reality check in the mail for Wallabies with scary Springboks up next
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion Reality check in the mail for Wallabies with scary Springboks up next Iain Payten Senior Sports Reporter September 14, 2026 — 5:22am

September 14, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Wallabies will be quietly hoping the brutal four-Test series between the Springboks and All Blacks has left both sides battered and bruised. Australia play South Africa in Perth, on September 27, and based on what we witnessed in the Greatest Rugby Rivalry, some fatigue in the legs and minds of the Bokke will be needed for the Wallabies to match them. It will be a major step up from Les Kiss’ first four games in charge. South African players celebrate after defeating the All Blacks in Baltimore. AP Photo/Stephanie Scarbrough South Africa were scarily good in beating the All Blacks 3-1 in the series, and they are now the red-hot favourite to win a third straight Rugby World Cup next year. The All Blacks were strong as well, but the Springboks physically dominated them, both in the set-pieces and in collisions. Throw in electric players such as Kurt-Lee Arendse on counter, and Malcolm Marx’s on-ball pestilence, and the Boks are a complete side.



Will they be knackered? Sadly for Aussie fans, probably not. Rassie Erasmus’ squad also has ridiculous depth, and they’re using their pitstop on the NSW Central Coast this week to rest up. South Africa’s Kurt-Lee Arendse, right, attempts to break the tackle of New Zealand’s Peter Lakai. AP Photo/Stephanie Scarbrough Super Hooper still on the scene Les Kiss will name his squad to meet the Boks on Monday, and the Wallabies will be particularly boosted by extended stays of offshore duo Tom Hooper and Taniela Tupou. Tupou, whose 145-kilogram frame will be vital at scrum time, had already indicated he would stay for this game before heading back to Racing Metro.



Hooper’s return date to Exeter was a little less clear. But informed sources say he’s also due to be named by Kiss, and the big back-rower will be a crucial player for the Wallabies. Tom Hooper passes during a Wallabies captain’s run in July. Getty Images The All Blacks showed in their first Test win in Johannesburg that defensive turnovers are vital to slowing the Boks’ roll, so poaching threats will be needed for the Wallabies at Optus Stadium. But you also can’t survive with the sheer size needed to go toe to toe in the contact zone. Hooper is one of the few Australian players who has both. At 199 centimetres and 123 kilograms, the Bathurst bulldog is abrasive in contact, but is also deceptively good for a steal or three. Super players press claims



The smile on Tom Lynagh’s face after a 40-minute return for Queensland on Saturday said plenty. After just 17 minutes all year due to injury, Lynagh emerged unscathed after a decent shift at Ballymore. That would have encouraged many, including Kiss. Tom Lynagh playing for the Reds against the Force. Erick Lucero/QRU Media Whether Lynagh is recalled to the Wallabies remains to be seen. It’s probably wiser to leave him playing for Queensland for a few more weeks, with an eye on games against the All Blacks in October. Harry McLaughlin-Phillips was also solid in the Force’s late win. Zac Lomax also returned to action at No.13, and if anything, he overplayed his hand. But the call to try him at No.13 is a smart one given it’s not a position of depth in Aussie rugby. The Tahs were too strong for the Brumbies in a scrappy game on Sunday afternoon in Bungendore, with Teddy Wilson influential and Max Burey strong on debut. Corey Toole showed his potent speed, and young Brumbies skipper Toby McPherson also stood out with some bone-crunching hits.



Wallaroos show potential against the world’s best On paper, the result of the Wallaroos’ 48-15 loss to England in Salford on Sunday morning was as expected. The English women are an even more dominant world No. 1 than the Boks men. But the Wallaroos showed enough to suggest a turnaround is under way in the new regime run by ex-Aussie sevens coach Tim Walsh. The Wallaroos led England 10-5 at half-time, which was the first time the Red Roses had trailed after 40 minutes since 2020. Considering England have won 67 of 68 games since 2020, that’s a decent confidence-builder. Faliki Pohiva of Australia celebrates as she goes over to score. Getty Images for Rugby Australia



You can’t get too carried away – England were clearly rusty early on. But steps forward, however small, are the name of the game for the Wallaroos. Professionalism can’t come quickly enough The biggest positive of a game like that for the Wallaroos is to be given painful lessons on where their game is lacking. Under pressure, the Wallaroos were unable to stay on task for more than a few phases, with and without the ball. Defensive connections in particular got very loose. All of that is perfectly predictable for a semi-professional side, up against full-time teams such as England and New Zealand. Staying on task is a trained behaviour.



“The reality is that even at our best, we’re probably not good enough,” Walsh said. “And we will be, but that’s where we’re at at the moment.” The sequence of phases that led to Faliki Pohiva’s try was a glimpse of what is possible. Strong carries from Amelia Whitaker, Pohiva and Waiaria Ellis and a lovely kick from Samantha Wood led to a stolen lineout from Michaela Leonard and a second powerhouse charge through traffic from Pohiva. The seeds are there, but they badly need an irrigation system. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: Key Trump adviser confident Australia would join US ‘in a good fight’
World.content:
Analysis NationalAUKUS Key Trump adviser confident Australia would join US ‘in a good fight’ Michael Koziol September 14, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington DC: A few months ago in Honolulu, the Trump administration’s point man for AUKUS – who rarely speaks publicly – gave a broad-brush appraisal of why Donald Trump strongly supports the agreement. AUKUS, which marks its five-year anniversary this week, was more than a one-off deal, Adam Korzeniewski told the audience. It was “a mentality”, a way of thinking that could be applied with other partners. “AUKUS is the spearhead, it’s the canary in the coalmine, it’s the future model of interoperability between different allies,” he said. “If we can’t figure this out with Australia and the UK, then what are we doing?” Trump believed AUKUS was “completely in line with his national security strategy”, Korzeniewski said. Marija Ercegovac Trump believed AUKUS was “completely in line with his national security strategy”, Korzeniewski said. That document, rewritten in November 2025, stipulates the US will build a military capable of denying aggression anywhere in the First Island Chain around China.



But it won’t do this alone. The strategy says America’s allies must step up: spend “much more” on collective defence, allow the US greater military access to their ports and other facilities, and invest in capabilities that deter aggression. AUKUS ticks all of those boxes. As for the question of what the US would expect of Australia in the event of a conflict with China, Korzeniewski had little doubt that Canberra would play its part. “Australia joined us in the Vietnam War,” he said. “I’m not really that concerned about Australia’s willingness to join in a good fight if one comes up.” Korzeniewski is an AUKUS liaison officer in the State Department, who moved to the role in February. A political appointee of the Trump administration, he is a bridge between the bureaucracy and the politicians. His previous job was White House liaison during the dismantling of USAID. Scott Morrison announcing AUKUS with Boris Johnson and Joe Biden in September 2021. AAP / Mick Tsikas His remarks to the Security and Defence Plus forum in Honolulu, which have not been previously reported, add context to Trump’s oft-cited declaration that AUKUS is “full steam ahead”.



Those three words, uttered by the US president when Prime Minister Anthony Albanese visited last year, have become gospel for both US and Australian officials. The phrase is repeated so often that it tends to invoke eye-rolls among Australian correspondents in Washington. But Trump has said little publicly about why he values AUKUS so highly. For opponents of the agreement in Australia, Korzeniewski’s remarks will bolster perceptions that the US is using AUKUS to establish a strategic foothold here. This was reinforced by the Pentagon baulking at recent suggestions that the presence of US submarines at HMAS Stirling near Perth might be limited to five years. In the view of AUKUS opponents, this is not in Australia’s interests. But all three AUKUS governments – in Canberra, Washington and London – believe their interests are aligned. And in the five years since it was announced at a virtual press conference (during which Joe Biden memorably referred to Scott Morrison as “that fellow down under”), AUKUS has survived a change of government in each country. The political consensus could not be clearer, even if there is lingering uncertainty among voters. Polling by the United States Studies Centre in May showed more Australians support the country acquiring nuclear-powered submarines than oppose the idea, and more people believe AUKUS will make Asia safer than not. Anti-AUKUS protesters outside the ALP conference in Adelaide in July. Dominic Lorrimer



But about 45 per cent of Australians felt the government had not adequately explained the need for AUKUS. A fifth said the pact should be cancelled. “This is moving forward,” Korzeniewski said in Honolulu. “There’s not going to be any great revisions. Things may change after first contact with the enemy – which may be our bureaucracies in this case – but this is a fact. This is going to be something that’s done at some point. People are welcome to criticise, but we’re not paying any heed to the critics.” Related Article September 11 attacks ‘May fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city’: CIA releases pre-9/11 Bin Laden briefings The Trump administration was not paying any attention to AUKUS critics, he added. “Everybody’s entitled to their own opinion. Oftentimes these folks that write these opinions have contrary interests, or maybe they get the facts wrong.” Sitting beside Korzeniewski on the Honolulu panel in May was Greg Wilcock, Australia’s consul-general for the US in Hawaii, formerly the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s assistant secretary for US policy. He made the point that the best way to arrest public doubts about AUKUS was to demonstrate tangible results.



Wilcock argued AUKUS did not undermine Australia’s sovereignty. “Any government, including in Australia, is going to reserve its room for manoeuvre in exercising sovereignty about how its country is used, about how its sovereign assets are used,” he said. “The good news for the United States and Australia … is that we have so driven – and we have driven very hard – our operational integration and our policy integration. And that makes it much less difficult to have an honest, outcomes-focused conversation about how we are going to exercise that sovereignty for joint effect.” The Albanese government stresses it has given no undertaking about participating in any conflict. “We’ve given no commitment publicly or privately,” Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy told this masthead in Washington DC in July. “A decision to enter a conflict will be a decision of a future sovereign elected government.” Rather than any lack of political will, the real impediment to AUKUS fulfilling the promises of five years ago is the dire state of the American and British defence industrial bases on which Australia will rely. As this masthead reported in July, the production rate of Virginia-class submarines has flat-lined at 1.1 to 1.2 boats a year, according to the Pentagon, and billions of dollars from US and Australian taxpayers have not yet made a difference. The rate needs to climb to 2.33 a year to meet AUKUS commitments.

World.title: From Moree schoolgirl to High Court trailblazer and human rights advocate
World.content:
Obituary NationalVale From Moree schoolgirl to High Court trailblazer and human rights advocate Malcolm Brown September 14, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mary Gaudron 1943–2026 When in 1951 Dr H.V. (Doc) Evatt, then federal opposition leader, stood in the back of a utility in Moree to campaign for a “no” vote in the coming referendum to outlaw communism, he encountered an eight-year-old girl who asked: “Please, sir, what’s a constitution?” The Doc must have had prescience, or astonishing insight, because he took the child seriously, and after a discussion relating the Ten Commandments to government, he sent her a copy of the Australian Constitution. The little girl, Mary Gaudron, was to grow up to become the first woman appointed to the High Court of Australia and rule on matters relating to that very constitution. Federal Justice Mary Gaudron in 1998. Fairfax Mary Genevieve Gaudron was born in Moree on January 5, 1943, the eldest of five children of a train driver, Edward Gaudron, and his wife Grace (Bonnie) (nee Mawkes). Mary’s working-class background later would open her up to criticisms that she was “Labor-oriented”. She did have a keen interest in the disadvantaged. But she needed drive, being born in those circumstances, decades before women’s liberation became fashionable. Through her life, Gaudron, feisty and plain-spoken, was to contribute to rectifying most of the problems she was exposed to in her early life, including Moree’s race relations.



Gaudron went to a local convent school, then got a bursary to St Ursula’s, Armidale. One nun recalled her as a “quick-witted girl … determined to make the best of her abilities”. Gaudron achieved a brilliant Leaving Certificate pass, which earned her a Commonwealth Scholarship to study arts/law at the University of Sydney, which she entered in 1959. She took an interest in speleology, the study of caves, and also played the mandolin. University friends remembered her as “brilliant” or “good fun”. She graduated in arts in 1962 and in February 1963 she married a fellow caver, Benjamin Sidney Nurse. She continued a law course part-time, supporting herself by working as a registration clerk in a legal office. Mary Gaudron, 31, at home in Sydney with daughter Danielle. Fairfax Gaudron encountered many obstacles. One of her lecturers said she should not take part in a moot court because women were not expected to take the practice of law seriously. But she was scarcely to be put off. Blackacre, the law students’ magazine, paid tribute to “a slight redhead with a temper to match”, and added: “Mary has all the attributes of a thoroughly disconcerting, accomplished debater. She has a keen analytical mind, a magnificent command of language and sheer audacity. Opponents are demolished by a few four-letter words.” Gaudron gave birth to her first child, Danielle, in 1964 and the following year she topped her final law exams.



Taking out the University Medal, and asked to comment on the award going to a female rather than a male, she said: “The only difference between us is that I sit down to pee!” She lectured for a time on succession law; she got articles despite prejudice among lawyers in favour of male graduates; and she was admitted as a solicitor of the NSW Supreme Court. She was admitted to the bar in October 1968, but she encountered more prejudice when she tried to get chambers on a barristers’ floor, and ended up sharing chambers with pioneering barrister Janet Coombs. But when she went into action, specialising in defamation, negligence and industrial law, Gaudron drew attention. On one occasion, High Court judge Sir Victor Windeyer admonished her on mispronouncing the name of one Lord Esher, she said: “If his Lordship were present, by whatever appellation, he would realise that I [was] relying on his pronouncement of the law, not the pronunciation of his name!” In the High Court, Gaudron acted on her own as counsel in an appeal in a defamation case, O’Shaughnessy v Mirror Newspapers, and won. In 1972, she became the first woman to be appointed to the NSW Bar Council. She was retained by the Commonwealth in the second equal pay case, where the Australian Council of Trade Unions, supported by the Whitlam government, challenged the restrictions of the original equal pay decision in 1969 and succeeded in having equal pay extended to work of equal value. In 1974, now with another baby, Julienne, she was appointed deputy president of the Commonwealth Conciliation and Arbitration Commission, her ceremonial welcome to the commission famously interrupted by daughter Julienne’s cry: “Mummy, Mummy!” In 1979, she sat on the maternity leave case that laid down award standards allowing for a year’s unpaid leave for all full-time and permanent part-time workers. Gaudron became foundation chair of the NSW Legal Services Commission. In 1980, she resigned from the Conciliation and Arbitration Commission over an issue relating to a colleague, Justice Jim Staples. She then briefly took up a position as visiting fellow at the University of NSW Law School. In 1981, she achieved another first for women by becoming NSW solicitor-general. She also became the first woman in NSW to be appointed a Queen’s Counsel. As solicitor-general, Gaudron had to deal with complexities surrounding Chief Magistrate Murray Farquhar, solicitor Morgan Ryan, magistrate Clarrie Briese and eventually Justice Lionel Murphy, and the fallout from The Age Tapes.



The Australian Law Journal commented on her “outstanding and ingenious advocacy”. Gaudron, having divorced Ben Nurse, married John Fogarty, with whom she was to have a son, Patrick. She took up a council position at Macquarie University and on a committee at the University of Wollongong dealing with technology and social change. When she was appointed to the High Court on February 6, 1987, her elevation was warmly welcomed by much of the legal profession. But she encountered criticism that she had been too close to Murphy and the Wran government. Prime minister Bob Hawke had to publicly defend her against opposition criticism of her “Labor connections”. The law profession gossip sheet, Justinian, attributed to her “a melancholy catalogue of sins of omission and commission” and said she had “an emotional disposition inappropriate in a holder of judicial office”. Mary Gaudron at a conference for women lawyers. Tanya Lake Undeterred, Gaudron pursued her passion for human rights and her zeal for justice and equality.



This was evident in the Mabo case, where in her joint judgment with Sir William Deane, she said the dispossession of Aboriginal people from their traditional lands was “the darkest aspect of the history of this nation”. Mabo, which found native title did exist in Australia, was followed by other outstanding judgments in human rights cases such as Wik and the Hindmarsh Island trial. Gaudron made a valuable contribution to the establishment of legal principles in a series of leading cases, particularly in the law relating to discrimination, and she identified equal treatment as a fundamental characteristic of the judicial process. In 1997, she was appointed foundation patron of the Association of Women Lawyers. In 2002, though only 60 and at one time considered to be in the running for chief justice, she announced her resignation from the High Court bench, effective from February 20, 2003, and the following month she became a judge of the Administrative Tribunal of the International Labour Organisation in Geneva. High Court chief justice Mary Gaudron, prime minister Julia Gillard, governor-general Quentin Bryce and attorney-general Nicola Roxon after federal ALP government swearing in ceremony in 2011. Wolter Peters In 2004, she was a member of an ILO Commission of Inquiry into trade union rights in Belarus. In 2006, the UN’s then-secretary-general, Kofi Annan, appointed her to the Redesign Panel on the N System of Internal Justice. In 2009, Gaudron became vice-president of the Administrative Tribunal of the ILO and in 2011 she became president. She resigned from the ILO in 2012 to care for her husband, who had suffered a cerebral haemorrhage. Governor-General Sam Mostyn paid tribute to Gaudron on Sunday afternoon, saying her distinguished career had transformed the country’s legal landscape.



“Justice Gaudron brought her fierce intellect, integrity, compassion and a deep commitment to justice to every role she held. Her legacy endures in the Australian legal system and in the many people who continue to follow the path she helped forge.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Why cereal and bread could actually be good for you
World.content:
Tips & adviceHealthy eating Why cereal and bread could actually be good for you Nutritional quality matters far more than processing level for long-term health, a new study has found. Sarah Knapton September 14, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Breakfast cereals and bread have been given a reprieve by nutritionists, who have admitted that some ultra-processed foods are not that bad for health after all. Harvard University has found that the nutritional quality of food is far more important than the processing level when it comes to long-term health. British experts said the results provided an important balance to the current “scaremongering” about ultra-processed foods (UPFs). The study of more than 200,000 people showed that quality of diet was important to lower the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and death, regardless of the level of food processing. Multi-grain bread has its health benefits. Getty Images



Processing ‘not inherently harmful’ The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up While many ultra-processed foods are high in sugars, salt and refined carbohydrates, others, such as fortified breakfast cereals, whole-grain bread and canned beans contain important nutrients, fibre and antioxidants, the authors argued. Conversely, many unprocessed foods, such as homemade cakes, fruit juice, potatoes, red meat and white rice can be unhealthy. Researchers said it was still important to limit processed foods with low nutritional value such as hamburgers, chips, pizza, doughnuts, fizzy drinks and biscuits. Dr Xiaowen Wang, of the department of nutrition at Harvard’s TH Chan School of Public Health, said “while many ultra-processed foods tend to be of poor nutritional quality and should generally be limited or avoided, processing itself is not inherently harmful.



“Focus on what you’re eating overall, not just whether it’s processed. A healthy plant-based diet rich in whole grains, fruits, vegetables, nuts, legumes and healthy plant oils is beneficial, even if it includes some processed foods.” Unprocessed food and drinks, like juice, can still be unhealthy. More nuance around UPFs In Britain, the average person consumes 56 per cent of their daily calories through UPFs, and previous research has shown they can have a detrimental effect on almost every organ of the body. Many UPFs are created from pre-digested ingredients, so the gut does not get the normal signals telling it not to overeat, leading to overconsumption. A study is ongoing to see whether UPFs could be behind the rise of bowel cancers among under-50s.



But recently, scientists have started to believe the truth about ultra-processed food may be more nuanced. For the new study, scientists examined the diets of people involved in three studies across three decades. Their diets were classed into one of four categories: healthy/ultra-processed, healthy/minimally processed, unhealthy/ultra-processed and unhealthy/minimally processed. Fortified yet ultra processed cereals such as Special K can still be good for you. iStock About half of the study participants had died or developed heart disease or type 2 diabetes in the intervening years, and healthy diets were associated with a lower risk, while unhealthy diets were associated with higher risk. However, the risks were almost identical regardless of whether the diet was ultra-processed or minimally processed.



“Advising people to universally avoid ultra-processed foods can lead to lower diet quality since healthy ultra-processed foods are beneficial and unhealthy minimally processed foods are detrimental,” added Dr Wang. “These are important findings because they may help people to feel less anxious about eating the processed foods that are affordable, perfectly healthy and part of everyday life.” Dr Beverley O’Hara Commenting on the research, Dr Beverley O’Hara, lecturer in public health nutrition at Leeds Beckett University, said “the study appears to be an important counterbalance to the large number of poor-quality studies that have led to widespread scaremongering about UPFs. “The results also showed that both processed and unprocessed healthy plant-based diets were protective against cardiovascular disease. “These are important findings because they may help people to feel less anxious about eating the processed foods that are affordable, perfectly healthy and part of everyday life.”



Dr Aisling Daly, senior lecturer in nutrition at Oxford Brookes University, added: “Advising people to blanketly avoid processed foods is not a helpful approach, so having a way to help consumers balance both processing level and nutrient quality would be a beneficial public health strategy, which would likely improve health outcomes. “We have placed too much emphasis on processing level, without recognising that some processing is beneficial to our health, and other processing is not directly harmful to our health.” The research was presented at Nutrition 2026, the annual meeting of the American Society for Nutrition. The Telegraph (London) Related Article Seven ultra-processed foods you probably didn’t know you were eating

World.title: ‘Tail, film, heckle’: Inside the Brethren’s secret election influence plot with the far-right
World.content:
Running the show behind the scenes were elders from a wealthy Christian sect formerly known as the Exclusive Brethren. Messages leaked from inside the secret operation, which this masthead can now publish, show the trail leading right to the top of the church – to Gareth Hales, one of the powerful sons of the sect’s world leader, Bruce Hales.

He was among a motley crew of far-right agitators paid to harass the prime minister and his ministers, as well as Greens and teal independent candidates, in nearly a dozen scripted stunts on the campaign trail.

But McIntyre had other associations, even more secret than Nazis.

The man, who was quickly bundled out by security, was a far-right influencer named Laurence McIntyre. Only months earlier, McIntyre had been pictured alongside neo-Nazis at a white supremacist gathering in Melbourne, and chat logs reveal he also appeared in private neo-Nazi groups on Telegram.

Albanese would later recall how someone suddenly “stormed” through the press scrum, “yelling out all sorts of aggressive” things about immigration.

From day one of the 2025 federal election campaign, the prime minister was being secretly tracked. When Anthony Albanese stepped up to speak at a press conference in Brisbane on March 29, a man was already lying in wait.

But one of the senior Brethren figures behind the operation, Lester Sharples, has now confirmed to this masthead “it was organised by a number of people, of which I was one”, though he denied knowing of money changing hands.

The church and elders approached about the revelations, which this masthead first reported last month, have repeatedly denied any involvement in the stunts, including when questioned by a recent parliamentary inquiry.

Six sources with knowledge of the operation, speaking anonymously for safety reasons, have told this masthead how the Brethren used information from contacts in Canberra to track the PM’s plane, then followed his protective detail from airports, at times driving agitators to his hotel for ambushes, and afterwards paying them in bundles of cash.

One elder even suggested one-liners to agitators heckling MPs – all designed to grab headlines and embarrass opponents of the Coalition.

Multiple Brethren leaders appeared in the chats alongside far-right figures like McIntyre discussing payment and logistics. Pictures were shared from successful stunts, which this masthead has now traced to more than a dozen disruptions splashed across social media during the campaign.

Chats on encrypted apps show Brethren figures tailed politicians and fed “private intel” on their locations to far-right activists with a history of white supremacist associations. They show how, the night before Albanese’s press conference, McIntyre was brought in to “tail, photo/video, heckle”.

This is the story of how an orchestrated “election influence operation” unfolded.

This masthead is not suggesting any illegality in planning or carrying out the stunts, but teal independent Monique Ryan, who was targeted by at least one, told this masthead: “Orchestrated, threatening interruptions by malevolent influencers and third parties will have a chilling effect on people running in politics. We have to fight back against groups looking to degrade our democracy.”

Albanese and a host of MPs have demanded answers from the Coalition and the church about the stunts and the wider campaign, as the church did not declare any political spending.

Key far-right figures were also paid tens of thousands of dollars to serve as middlemen in the church’s shadowy advertising campaign, this masthead can reveal, endorsing Brethren posters and buying ad space. Meanwhile, the sect’s rank-and-file members were pressured to turn out in their thousands to campaign undercover for the Liberals at polling booths.

The stunts were just one arm of the Brethren church’s multimillion-dollar, undisclosed effort to help elect Peter Dutton as prime minister.

The documents show Gareth Hales, the son of the church’s “Man of God”, was a member of at least one key coordinating chat as of March last year. Four sources say Hales was also at a secret meeting between the Brethren and their far-right helpers at a golf course in Sydney in the first days of the election, as the church’s plot to import aggressive, MAGA-style politics into Australia hit its stride.

Brethren often handled transport to the campaign events. But for the heckling, they used “guns-for-hire” outside the church – neo-Nazi associates, pro-Putin conspiracists and even an ex-Liberal staffer. All these men were notorious enough already, it was thought, that no one would suspect the hand of the church behind it. Not even their own flock.

The idea behind the stunts – which was known to only a few in the Coalition and not authorised by the Liberals’ head office – was to make it seem as if the public was turning on left-leaning politicians over issues like immigration.

Both were in a Signal chat with high-ranking Brethren church members, and for weeks it had been abuzz with discussion as the covert operation kicked off around Australia.

On the first day of the 2025 Federal election campaign, when McIntyre heckled Albanese and treasurer Jim Chalmers at a medical centre, a Brethren staffer waited at his side, helping him film the stunt for distribution online.

He thought people like McIntyre “were guys who would go out and ask bold questions”.

Sharples told this masthead that the stunt operation wasn’t directed by the church explicitly; it was run by “a group of mates and colleagues”. He “didn’t know the background” or the neo-Nazi connections of the agitators, he claimed, and didn’t expect things to ever turn violent.

Ahead of the PM’s Brisbane press conference, Sharples had asked if a far-right figure helping coordinate nationally could get “his guys” to show up and ask questions, and then “intervine [sic] if it turns negative”.

“We’ll have to keep a close eye on Albo any time he’s in [south-east] Queensland”, Sharples told organisers in the weeks before the key March 29 stunt. He handed out scripted lines for hecklers. “I voted Albo and all I got was a lousy tshirt” was one that did not make the final cut.

In Queensland, one of the operation’s main coordinators was local Brethren businessman Sharples. He confirmed to this masthead he was also at the Brethren’s Sydney golf club meeting with far-right figures, and did not deny Gareth Hales was in planning chats.

This masthead does not suggest Bruce Hales was directly involved. Gareth Hales, who was also photographed campaigning in a blue Liberal t-shirt during the election, was approached for comment.

The leaked chats show McIntyre, who goes by WhatsNews?! online, was brought in for the March 29 stunt by another far-right influencer, Chris de Bruyne or “Chriscoveries”, who was helping the church coordinate the operation.

De Bruyne was also involved in the Brethren’s unofficial ad campaign. His wife and their lobbying firm Australian Firebrand endorsed multiple Brethren posters, including the mysterious “Make Australia happy again” signs that popped up during the campaign, reflecting a line coined in a church meeting by Brethren leader Bruce Hales.

The night before Albanese’s press conference, De Bruyne told a go-between for the Brethren and the Coalition campaign that he had arranged for McIntyre, “WhatsNews”, to rock up to “tail… video, heckle” Albanese the next day.

His contact, who was working with church elders, confirmed that “they [the Brethren] want hecklers primarily” but “they have drivers” to do the tailing.

After the stunt, footage was quickly passed to De Bruyne, who circulated it online. Soon the story of the PM and Chalmers facing down “the mystery local” concerned about immigration had hit the headlines.

Only the most fleeting glimpse of the Brethren staffer by McIntyre’s side made the TV news bulletins that night.

Police tails and money trails

Not all Brethren disruptions went so smoothly.

Less than two weeks earlier, a stunt planned for another Albanese stopover in Brisbane had to be abandoned because the PM’s protective police detail had noticed a Brethren car, with far-right agitators inside, following Albanese’s entourage from the airport.

Sources say Sharples was in that car. They’d planned to ambush Albanese at the Stamford hotel. Sharples told this masthead, “We wanted to ask him some questions that were genuine and we wanted answers on … I wanted a good government”.

“I think at one stage I was in a car that was headed in the same direction as a politician (we were going to the same event),” he added, but denied being stopped.

The Brethren businessman admitted he poured many hours of his own time into “volunteering” for the clandestine operation, often after hours.

Loading

Later on, serious questions about security on the campaign trail were raised when Albanese was twice ambushed in his Melbourne hotel lobby by two far-right agitators. The men had also been sent by the covert Brethren operation, and both were former associates of neo-Nazis.

One was Harrison McLean, an ex-member of the extremist group The Proud Boys, who, as this masthead revealed at the time, had boasted in a livestream of being given “private intel” on Albanese’s location as part of a close-knit “team” running an influence campaign.

McLean was also involved in another Brethren-organised stunt targeting Monique Ryan.

Home Affairs minister Tony Burke later described the ambushes as “physical intimidation”, saying, “Australia hasn’t had that before, and we shouldn’t.”

The going rate for each stunt was between a few hundred dollars and $1000 per person, according to sources and financial records. The money came from the Brethren, five sources say – at first handed over in cash from duffel bags or in clandestine meets in car parks, and later through a web of middlemen, pay points and shell companies.

When one heckler involved in the early stunt with McIntyre was recruited by elders to perform another in April – this time targeting Greens MP Elizabeth Watson-Brown at a community picnic – he asked: “Do you guys need bank details for payment transfer after or do you guys work on a cash system as well?”

After this job was done, he sent a picture of McIntyre at the event as proof – it matched footage of the stunt that De Bruyne circulated the same day.

But this time there was a hitch with the new “method of disbursement”. Sharples asked another far-right figure to chase it up, and payment went through the same month.

“I did not ever pay anyone, and don’t know anyone who did, nor any sum or money involved,” Sharples told this masthead.

Last month, church spokesman Lloyd Grimshaw told the parliamentary inquiry examining the 2025 election that “the … Plymouth Brethren Christian Church never funded one cent to any political cause or party”. It had no involvement in the election at all, he said.

Grimshaw told this masthead he wasn’t involved himself in the stunts or coordinating chats, which he claimed to have no knowledge of as a Brethren operation. “I made the decision not to be involved in the election campaign,” he said.

McLean refused to answer questions but did not deny being paid for the stunts.

McIntyre also didn’t deny being paid but denied knowing the Brethren, even though he was in chats with multiple elders. “You’re told a lot of shit it seems mate. Good luck with it all,” he said in response to questions.

Guns for hire

At the heart of the operation was a small, trusted group of far-right middlemen. These men had deep connections to the radical edge of politics, including to neo-Nazis, and they were paid considerably higher “fees” than the guns-for-hire hecklers they helped recruit for the Brethren. They were also helping organise the church’s secret ad spends on posters and billboard trucks then being rolled out across the country. “And of course,” says one source. “Part of their job was to keep the whole thing under wraps.”

Word of this lucrative opportunity had trickled down to the far-right from connections who had worked security for the Brethren, two sources said.

On April 1, just days after Albanese was heckled by McIntyre in Brisbane, Brethren elders gathered with them at the Ryde-Parramatta golf club in Sydney to discuss the ongoing campaign.

De Bruyne was among those invited. He did not answer questions from this masthead but has since boasted online of being given a budget of around $15,000 for distributing footage of the stunts in “the operation with links to … the Exclusive Brethren”. His company still showcases clips of the stunts on its website among the campaigns it has been hired for.

Two other middlemen were paid tens of thousands of dollars each, three sources with knowledge of the payments say. One was given a 2 per cent cut of all s booked by the Brethren, but the arrangement was later reversed because of concerns about the optics of money from the sect going offshore through an overseas business account.

Any spending over $250,000 would require the church to declare itself a “significant third party” in the election, which would threaten its lucrative tax-free charitable status. The sect, backed by the Coalition, is fighting any finding of this nature by the parliamentary inquiry.

They say the effort was entirely voluntary and not backed by the church – despite evidence, obtained from within the sect, that its meetings were shifted for election activity, and hundreds of young Brethren were put up in hotels.

During the stunt operation, the church was often referred to as “the client” and frequently acted through a company, Sante Global, owned by Gareth Hales. Sante was also the name on some payments, and this masthead has confirmed it booked the room for the April meeting at the golf club.

Brethren elder Arne Proctor was another senior Sante executive identified in the trove of leaked communications. He declined to answer questions on the record but has denied any knowing involvement with far-right figures.

In early March, messages show Proctor told a go-between connected to the Coalition campaign that those involved in the stunts were simply “concerned businessmen that can see the country going the wrong way if the wrong people make it in”. It was the Brethren cover-story for the whole campaign.

One of the Brethren’s earliest recruits for the stunts was an ex-Liberal staffer Barclay McGain, who gatecrashed forums in March to heckle Greens MP Watson-Brown as well as teal donor Simon Holmes à Court. McGain, who now heads CPAC Australia, was previously involved in gatecrashing drag storytime events.

Communications obtained by this masthead reveal Brethren elders, including Sharples, held meetings with McGain about the stunts in March. Messages between middlemen discuss McGain happy to accept payments of about $400 at a time, and show McGain approaching those in the operation about events they were looking to crash from his personal phone number.

McGain has repeatedly denied being paid or knowing that the stunts were part of a co-ordinated Brethren operation, though he confirmed he handed his footage over to De Bruyne to distribute.

In Melbourne, fringe anti-lockdown politician Morgan C Jonas was a key figure behind the scenes, helping distribute content and performing a stunt himself, this time targeting Foreign Minister Penny Wong. He endorsed unofficial campaign posters that Brethren members in Liberal t-shirts were seen putting up.

A Brethren member in shorts and a Liberal Party t-shirt puts up a poster endorsed by Morgan C Jonas.

Jonas denied being paid for the stunts and endorsements on the posters, which drew the scrutiny of the Australian Electoral Commission. He told this masthead “they were my messages that I wrote, signed and authorised, and fully stand by”.

Though the secret operation was run by church elders, most Brethren members – including the many thousands who turned out to campaign in Liberal party t-shirts that April – had no idea.

It is also unclear how much the Coalition knew about the full story behind the stunts, though some people connected to the campaign were aware of them at different times, and senior party sources confirm rumours of the dirty tricks campaign were circulating.

Ordinary members of the church have since told this masthead they are horrified at the revelations. In his evidence to the parliamentary committee, Grimshaw denied any church involvement with far-right figures, insisting, “the church completely rejects anti-Semitism, which is completely antithetical to our views”.

Grimshaw also told the committee that everyone who participated was a volunteer, and that he did not know about the message from world leader Bruce Hales, that the Brethren needed to “make Australia smile again,” that kicked off the church members’ activism.

The committee is scrutinising Grimshaw’s testimony, and is now considering calling Bruce Hales to give evidence.

World.title: It’s the world’s largest city, but you won’t see many tourists
World.content:
InspirationSouth-East Asia It’s the world’s largest city, but you won’t see many tourists Anthony Dennis September 14, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each Sunday the central streets of the world’s largest city are closed to its relentless traffic between 6am and 11am. It’s a once-a-week opportunity for residents to breathe easy, or at least a little easier, and to enjoy some open space in a place chronically deprived of such a thing. Bundaran HI roundabout, with Hotel Indonesia Kempinski (bottom left), is the city’s most photographed landmark. iStock This Sunday is special, however, as it’s the occasion of the urban behemoth’s 499th birthday, with the usual roar of vehicles replaced by a mass celebration complete with a raucous on-stage ceremony. You could be forgiven for presuming that the city in which I find myself is Tokyo. Or perhaps Delhi. Maybe even Cairo. Think again. This is Jakarta. As a kind of surprise birthday gift, the United Nations crowned the Indonesian capital as the world’s newest most populous city, with nearly 42 million residents. It was followed by Dhaka, Bangladesh, with almost 40 million people, and Tokyo with a comparatively meagre 33 million (presumably falling due to Japan’s rapidly declining population). Why am I here? It’s a good question. Gertrude Stein, the American novelist, poet and playwright, could have been thinking of Jakarta, rather than Oakland, California, her childhood home, when she coined the immortal line: “There’s no there there.”



True enough, Jakarta remains one of South-East Asia’s least visited and appreciated cities, at least by Westerners, and true again, I’m literally the sole Caucasian I notice among the throng at its birthday party. But what Jakarta does offer is an authenticity largely untainted by mass tourism. 



Visit I do. But for me, there’s another compelling personal reason to visit. I’ve long been a fan of The Year of Living Dangerously, both the 1978 Christopher Koch novel and the 1982 Peter Weir film on which it is based, starring Mel Gibson and Sigourney Weaver. The most notable performance in the underrated film – set in 1960s Indonesia, during the overthrow of President Sukarno – is by actress Linda Hunt, who won the 1983 best supporting actress Oscar for her portrayal of the diminutive character Billy Kwan, becoming the first actress to win an Oscar for playing a man. Jakarta’s eccentric 25-room House of Tugu hotel is a living museum you can stay in. One of the most dramatic scenes in the film is when the idealistic Kwan hangs a sign, “Sukarno feed your people”, from what doubles as the Hotel Indonesia, as a public protest against the controversial inaugural Indonesian president, who served in the role between 1945 and 1967. The Hotel Indonesia is still there, complete with a huge black-and-white photograph off the lobby of President Sukarno with Marilyn Monroe, in which he appears to be admiring her breasts. Now rebranded as the 289-room Hotel Indonesia Kempinski and directly linked to the gargantuan Grand Indonesia shopping mall, it opened in 1962, becoming Indonesia’s first five-star property.



Some of the 1000 antiques on display in House of Tugu, Jakarta’s most unusual hotel stay. Symbolising the emergence of the former Dutch colony as a modernising, forward-thinking independent nation, the hotel sits immediately opposite Bundaran HI, a massive roundabout with the welcoming bronzed Selamat Datang Monument as its centre. The roundabout is among Jakarta’s most photographed landmarks, and one that’s particularly impressive illuminated after dark. So difficult is it to negotiate on foot, with its incessant multi-lane traffic, there’s a government plan to build an underground pedestrian tunnel as a safer link to the five-star hotels huddled around it. In a city full of stellar and affordable accommodation, the retro Hotel Indonesia Kempinski, where I appear to be the only Western inhouse guest, is itself a worthy reason for visiting Jakarta, though there’s an even better excuse. One of the colourful Peranakan heritage-style guestrooms inside the House of Tugu. Named as one of TIME magazine’s “world’s greatest places” for 2026, the 25-room House of Tugu is a living museum in which you can stay. Its historic eight-storey facade almost entirely enveloped in vegetation, the hotel is located in Old Jakarta (Kota Tua), where architectural remnants of the Dutch colonial rule survive.



Opened last year after two decades of planning and development, the hotel is a repository of Peranakan heritage in the form of 1000 or so antiques, each collected over nearly 60 years by Anhar Setjadibrata, co-owner of Indonesia’s Tugu Hotels & Restaurants group, his wife Wedya Julianti and daughter Lucienne Anhar. Nusantara’s imposing Plaza Kusuma Bangsa monument surrounded by newly constructed government buildings. Alamy This is calculated and considered hoarding on the grandest scale; so much so that the House of Tugu team is building a new museum wing, due to open early next year, to house and exhibit yet more items that are now in storage. “Jakarta is still misunderstood as a destination,” says Lucienne Anhar. “For many foreign visitors, Indonesia means Bali. And Bali is wonderful, but Indonesia is much bigger and culturally much more complicated than Bali alone.” Sunda Kelapa, Jakarta’s old port, is replete with surviving 18th century whitewashed Dutch colonial-era buildings. iStock



True enough. What little many Australians do know about Jakarta is that it’s to be largely replaced by a new capital, Nusantara, which is rising, rather slowly, but impressively, in the jungles of East Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo. Another known fact is that Jakarta’s traffic is even worse than Bangkok’s. In fact, the Hotel Indonesia Kempinski dedicates a whole page on its website advising ways to cope with traffic in a city largely starved of public transport. Then there’s the fact that Indonesia’s largest and low-lying city is sinking, probably faster than its replacement’s construction, which Indonesia’s incumbent president seemingly doesn’t support with the same vigour as his predecessor. Jakarta’s imposing Catholic cathedral, located near the city’s Merdeka Square. Getty Images I witness the sinking problem myself when I visit Sunda Kelapa, Jakarta’s old port. It’s still replete with 18th-century whitewashed Dutch colonial-era maritime administrative buildings, but seawater is visibly inundating the immediate wharfside area where classic wooden sailing ships, known as pinisi, are moored. Ominously, by 2050, parts of Jakarta are predicted to be submerged. One area, North Jakarta, has sunk 2.5 metres in the past decade. “Jakarta is not an easy city in the conventional tourist sense,” says Lucienne Anhar, in something of an understatement. “It is huge, busy, chaotic and sometimes exhausting. But that is also what makes it interesting. It is the place where so many different Indonesians meet.



“As a capital city, it hosts performances of the most talented artists representing cultures of the different islands. We know Jakarta also has extremely exciting nightlife, fantastic restaurants, really great food and very welcoming people.” Related Article Air travel Free flights on offer to spread Indonesia tourism beyond Bali I have to agree. Indonesia is known for its friendly people, but the citizens of Jakarta are even friendlier still, and this among the stresses and strains of the biggest city in human history. Jakarta’s not for everyone, but I have nary a scintilla of regret in spending five intriguing, and, yes, at times, challenging, nights here. In fact, I can’t wait to return for the grand opening, if they’ll have me, of the House of Tugu’s new museum. I gave it a go, and I’d give it a go again. THE DETAILS



STAY

Rooms at the Hotel Indonesia Kempinski, Jakarta, are from $190 a night; at the House of Tugu, Jakarta, rooms are from $224 a night; at The Legian Seminyak, Bali, rooms are from $617 a night. Additional taxes and fees may apply. See tuguhotels.com; kempinski.com; lhm-hotels.com Related Article Travel tips No jet-lag required: The 10 greatest short-haul holiday destinations FLY

Garuda Indonesia operates six flights a week between Sydney and Jakarta, and four flights a week between Melbourne and Jakarta. Connect to Denpasar, Bali, from Jakarta on regular domestic services that take under two hours. See garuda-indonesia.com MORE

indonesia.travel The writer travelled with the assistance of The Legian Seminyak, Bali resort and paid for his accommodation in Jakarta.

World.title: Petone Beach's leopard seal dies
World.content:
A leopard seal which hundreds of spectators visited has died, A Hutt City Councillor says.

The female leopard seal was spotted two weeks ago lounging on Petone Beach, with some concerns members of the public were harassing the animal.

Councillor Brady Dyer said the seal died on Sunday night, and will be removed by the Department of Conservation (DOC) on Monday.

Conservationists echoed the news on social media, saying they suspected the seal looked unwell.

A leopard seal on Petone Beach garners keen public interest, 6 September, 2026

DOC has been approached for comment. Staff had previously expected the seal to return to the water when it was ready.

"[In] the last few years, this is probably the third one that I've seen. We had a massive, huge leopard seal in Oriental Parade by the boat sheds for a time," DOC ranger Melody McLaughlin told RNZ a week ago.
