World.title: 'Imitation' or 'perfect solution' - Labour's KiwiSaver policy
World.content:
Barbara Edmonds discusses Labour’s new KiwiSaver policy Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Labour has been "ankle tapped" by National on KiwiSaver according to the managing director of Simplicity, but the wife of Sir Michael Cullen, who got the scheme going, says the party's found the "perfect solution."

It comes as Nicola Willis calls the policy a "watered-down version" of National's.

Labour announced on Sunday it would up employer contributions to 6 percent, in line with National's proposal, but wouldn't make employee contributions compulsory to ease the pressure during a cost of living crisis.

Anne Collins, wife of Sir Michael and lifetime Labour member, said she was "absolutely delighted" with the result, after "a lot of" discussion about KiwiSaver during party conferences.

Labour announces Kiwisaver policy Morning Report Download MP3 3m

"This is just a perfect solution because it's such a very, very successful policy," she told RNZ, but noted the current government had "repressed our wages", referencing public sector job cuts and keeping minimum wage below keeping up with inflation.

"So people's wages are not where they should be.

"It's making it hard for people to save for their future, which is so important."

This policy was a solution because Labour would "love to have made it mandatory", she said, but the party realised making payments at a time when people were struggling was "too ideological."

"It's just not practical enough. And Michael was always very pragmatic. I mean, he has great ideals, but he wanted things that would work for people."

She still wasn't sold on total compulsion, and described Sir Michael as incentivising the scheme when he brought it in.

"Everyone got given $1000, and then they got a good tax rebate, and the employers got a good tax rebate. So there was a lot of incentive, not just straight compulsion."

National's Nicola Willis said the policy was just a "watered-down" version of her own party's announced in June. RNZ/Nick Monro

Collins said Labour's policy would re-incentivise people after a range of cuts and changes to the scheme because they will see their employer's contribution growing, their own fund growing, and be encouraged to get in and "help it when they can."

She said Sir Michael would be "disgusted" with what's happened to wages and to working people in New Zealand at the moment.

"He would want everything to be done to help them."

But Simplicity KiwiSaver managing director Sam Stubbs, said National had "ankle-tapped" Labour on its own policy.

"This is the policy that Michael Cullen invented, and I would say that National at this stage seem to have a slightly more comprehensive set of policies for Kiwis rather than Labour do."

Stubbs said he was pleased with most of what Labour was proposing, but that he was expecting the party to do more.

"I was actually sort of personally disappointed that their policy wasn't everything that National have promised and a little bit more."

He said KiwiSaver was Labour policy, and the history of National has been "nothing other than chipping away at it."

"But now, to be honest with you, National sort of ankle tapped Labour on the KiwiSaver policy."

He described moving toward compulsion as "good", along with employer only contributions, and getting rid of total remuneration contracts where employer KiwiSaver contributions are included in the salary rather than an additional sum.

But he said the overall amount Labour wants Kiwis to save for their future was "not going to be nearly enough." And the "real disappointment" he added was a lack of policy for children.

"They need to seriously look at kids. We should be having KiwiSaver accounts at birth."

Both New Zealand First and National are proposing compulsory contributions for all workers, but have also both announced policies that would automatically enrol babies and children.

On Sunday, Labour leader Chris Hipkins explained automatic enrolment wasn't something Labour was currently considering.

"Right now we have to make different choices, and we made different choices."

National's Nicola Willis said the policy was just a "watered-down" version of her own party's announced in June.

"While imitation is a sincere form of flattery, their attempt falls short. It's less ambitious than National's and won't help Kiwis saving for their future anywhere near as much."

New Zealand First used the same line in June about National's policy, having already proposed automatic enrolment in May.

World.title: MSD's one failure after another on payments
World.content:
MSD has made a litany of mistakes over botched benefit decisions and more - but apologies in contrast are thin on the ground.

What's going on at the Ministry of Social Development (MSD)?

A review last Thursday revealed more than 30,000 social welfare payments totalling more than $2 million were wrongly suspended after a law change last year.

MSD officials had failed to identify during the policy and legislation development process that winter energy payments for pensioners and veterans needed to be excluded from suspension before the Government approved the bill and passed it under urgency. More than 16,000 pensioners were affected.

Days earlier, on Monday, 1News broke the story that MSD had declined food grants to thousands of beneficiaries, saying food was non-essential. MSD refused to apologise.

In June, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon was extensively quizzed about revelations that MSD staff have performance targets to reduce emergency housing numbers.

In May, hundreds of sexual abuse survivors were told they could soon lose access to counselling. This came just a few months after MSD published online the names of five people making compensation claims for sexual abuse in state care.

Their lawyer described the privacy breach as the worst of its kind.

And this is just a snapshot of the damning headlines over the past year. Finally, on Friday, Minister Louise Upston said sorry. "I'm the minister. I accept responsibility," she told RNZ.

"Over the past 12 months or so, the Ministry of Social Development has let people down across the board... and something has to change, and they have to do better," RNZ field correspondent Jimmy Ellingham tells The Detail.

He's covered many of the ministry's recent botch-ups and spoken to the victims for RNZ, including the mistaken publication of names of people making compensation claims for sexual abuse in state care.

"So the lawyer, Lydia Oosterhof, said these clients, particularly one of them, was a very, very, very high risk.

"She said that if this client of hers were to see his name published online in connection with being the victim of sexual abuse, that he was at real risk of self-harm."

Another pensioner Ellingham spoke to "has been hauled in, not just about this [winter energy payments], but over various issues, six times in the past year to MSD officers, just always to reconfirm his details".

"So six times in just over 12 months. You can imagine the stress that that causes, because there's also the disability payments and various other payments that he gets."

And a Lake Alice survivor he interviewed was denied an accommodation supplement "which he needed to pay his rent" because he had received a $150,000 redress payment and bought a boat.

"Now the compensation money you get as a Lake Alice survivor should not count when you're being assessed for the accommodation supplement, nor should any assets you've bought from it because it's illogical that it would just sit in the bank," Ellingham says.

MSD did eventually correct the error, but "he went for months without that accommodation supplement. The problem is there".

Retired judge and former chief ombudsman Sir Peter Boshier has a long history of examining whether government agencies are acting fairly, reasonably and lawfully, and tells The Detail that MSD's recent performance is "regrettable", saying it leaves people "really agitated and upset".

"We are creatures of habit, and so when something doesn't happen when it should, it pays us to really understand the effect on someone personally. And I think with MSD, the particular business that they're in, when something doesn't happen, it causes real, real grief.

"And part of my job as chief ombudsman was really trying to instil into agencies, such as MSD, that getting it right is what matters so much because the agitation and anxiety cannot be understated."

When asked if the standard of accountability should be higher for MSD, compared to other government departments, Sir Peter replied: "Yes, I do. And the reason is that MSD is dealing with utter sensitivities.

"Some government departments, who are dealing with building consents or a pothole in a road or whatever it happens to be, if something doesn't happen on time, so be it.

"But I think with MSD, look, the challenge they've got, I would accept this, is that they're dealing with some of our most vulnerable people.

"And they're dealing with an awful lot of transactions and a lot of money. But really what that says to me is that you just can't underestimate the importance of getting it right."

The winter energy payment botch-up came down to legislation being rushed through, and it required many beneficiaries to confirm their circumstances annually to remain eligible for their payments.

But the WEP payment should have been exempt from that process; since it wasn't, thousands of pensioners missed out on payments they should have received.

So who is responsible?

"Well, I suppose from the purest point of view, it's the government of the day that ensures that legislation gets through," Sir Peter says. "And it's the responsibility of the agency to implement that government decision. So really, the purest answer is, the minister who sees a bill through to become an Act takes responsibility for its implementation."

Sir Peter says apologising and taking ownership of mistakes is often the best course of action.

"So when here something goes wrong, to acknowledge and to say that you're sorry means just so much.

"What I most wanted as the chief ombudsman was to say to an agency when they got it wrong, ' Would you please own this? Would you please not just give a superficial regret, but actually apologise and say that you're really sorry for anything that's happened to that person that's caused them grief?' It just means so much to put things right in that way."

He says, "I can't stress enough how important it is that it's a no-holds-barred: where did we go wrong in this, and what should we have done to ensure that there is no gap and no way in which a mistake could occur. To try and get something mistake-free is the ultimate for me."

Check out how to listen to and follow The Detail here.

World.title: Christchurch golf course 'devastated' by golfer's racial abuse
World.content:
A Christchurch Golf club is shocked that a golfer racially abused and assaulted a man in Hagley Park next to the golf course.

The president of Hagley Golf Course said on Saturday afternoon it had received a number of reports of a golfer acting aggressively and pushing a man who was with his wife and a young child.

Stuff reported that the golfer yelled at the Indian couple's child for coming near the golf course, but then became racially abusive and pushed the father.

Course president Hamish Galloway said the club totally condemned the racist and violent behaviour.

"We're a community golf course. We have a real range of people that belong to our club and we pride ourselves on that. There's a real ethnic diversity that's important to us. So for something like this to happen is devastating for us."

He said he had been in touch with the victim to express his regret that it happened and his desire to support the family.

Galloway said they did not know who the perpetrator was, but had seen photos and did not believe he is a club member.

He said they did have issues with people playing golf without signing in and paying at the club house, and that may be the case on this occasion.

The club was continuing to try to identify the man.

A police spokesperson said police received a report at about 1.45pm on Saturday of an assault in Hagley Park, with a person allegedly pushed twice.

World.title: Vanuatu ferry disaster: 'It's a miracle anyone survived,' rescuer says
World.content:
An Australian pilot who helped locate survivors after a ferry disaster in Vanuatu says "it is a miracle anyone survived". After the ferry MV Matui sank in rough seas on Friday morning, more than 30 people remain missing.

The ferry departed from Santo at 6am on Friday for Ambae, approximately 96 kilometres away. However, it capsized in large waves. According to Luganville MP Matai Seremaiah, the vessel sank at about 9:30am.

Tragically, confusion around the vessel's status and misinformation meant that it was over 30 hours before help arrived. Reports suggest 15 people survived the sinking.

Although the current confirmed death toll stands at two, more than 30 people remain missing. One body was recovered over the weekend but another could not be brought back due to bad weather.

Mark Turnbull, a pilot and doctor based on Gaua Island in Torba Province, was one of the first people in the air looking for survivors. Turnbull said he was contacted by an individual to help start the search for survivors:

"The government is pretty slow, even the shipowner was very slow, but there was one individual who was particularly motivated to help," he said.

"The weather was rough and it wasn't possible for very small boats to go out, and so they had to send fairly substantial looking 'smallish' ships."

Turnbull would conduct an aerial search, return to refuel, and then resume the search.

From the air, he was able to see debris and objects floating, which had obviously come out of the vessel.

"We saw drums of fuel, we saw flotation stuff, lots of these lifejackets that had been separated from the people somehow, then this big tank they were hanging onto, and some wheels [and] inner tubes some people had been holding onto as well."

He told RNZ Pacific about the "big black tank", a 1000L agricultural tank that had fallen off the ferry.

Turnbull said that a group of survivors told him that they had been clinging to the tank, and during the first night 5 people had died. Apparently, the second day they were in the water, the survivors let go of the tank and went separate ways to seek rescue.

The survivors Turnbull spoke to were weak and extremely dehydrated from their ordeal. Almost all of them had swollen eyes from exposure. One of the survivors had very swollen lips and had been attacked by fish "he was feeling wounded and weak."

Turnbull said that one of the survivors had swum all the way from where the ferry sank to Santo to raise the alarm that the vessel had sunk. Until then, it was believed that it was merely adrift. This raised the urgency level of search and rescue efforts.

He said that the terrible weather conditions would have made survival in the water very difficult.

"It was a dire situation, terrible weather, hard to do search and rescue because the wind was so horrific, up to 30 knots and sometimes gusting to even higher than that"

After talking to survivors, Turnbull said that the vessel was probably hit broadside by a large wave.

This had happened very suddenly, so there was no time to evacuate properly before the passengers and crew found themselves in the water - without proper survival gear.

He said without a working liferaft people were scrambling for "little bits and pieces" to hold onto to stay afloat.

"It's amazing that anybody survived that, for them to travel such a long distance was incredible, it was truly incredible, the distance they travelled was massive, it was huge."

"Those conditions through the night, with the waves pounding at them , it's really amazing that anybody survived."

Turnbull said he hopes this will be a turning point for search and rescue procedures in Vanuatu because the initial effort to locate and rescue survivors in this instance was very poorly coordinated. Private citizens had to step forward and coordinate the rescue attempts before official rescue efforts were organised.

"I hope this is an opportunity for the leadership of that area of Maritime search and rescue. That they will come up with a much more coordinated plan. We were not sure exactly who reported the ferry's GPS coordinates, as things were poorly organised."

World.title: 'Flawed assumptions' behind Immigration NZ's bungling of tech upgrade
World.content:
Immigration New Zealand overestimated the benefits from its newest transformation project by $134 million because of "significantly flawed assumptions".

The new head of INZ said it was virtually unheard of to get the productivity savings the project had forecast, and it had paused the programme.

The overestimate amounts to more than a quarter of the $453 million savings that Our Future Services (OFS) was forecast to save.

It means if the $336 million project goes ahead, it will now cost more than it saves - and its financial credentials had been a key drawcard when ministers chose it.

A report to Cabinet shows the project's productivity boosts and overhead savings from staffing cuts were both overstated.

New head of Immigration New Zealand Andy Milne was not pulling any punches when he spoke at the Association for Migration and Investment conference in Auckland.

"One of the questions I asked at our last OFS board was, how do we get those benefits so wrong? So even my new programme lead coming in has looked at it and said, look, if you were aiming for a 50 percent productivity uplift from a process improvement - that's pretty much unheard of.

"So there's some pretty hard questions that we have to answer around those benefits. And overhead benefits ... I think it was $50,000 per FTE saving was the estimate.

"But you don't get those kind of overhead [cuts] as you reduce by fives and 10s. They're usually sort of big organisational costs that are shared across the whole of the organisation.

"So there's some lessons for us there in terms of how we've calculated those benefits."

The Cabinet paper shows moving visa types onto the new Adept system has taken longer than expected, meaning plans had to be rescheduled and old technology was still being used.

"The productivity gains that we expected and the overhead savings that we expected have not been realised or they've been smaller than we anticipated," Milne said.

"So now is a really good time to take stock of that programme. When I first read the business case, the thought that it was going to take us another seven or eight years to migrate all products onto Adept just seemed a staggeringly long time. And in the world of fast-moving technology, it's hard even for me to imagine where we'll be in eight years' time."

The demise of the Biometric Capability Update (BCU) also affected the OFS project, as it was due to deliver an identity capability that the newer project relied on.

At the time Cabinet first signed off OFS, it was told legacy platforms that were at the end-of-life stage carried significant risk and required high maintenance costs, estimated at $224m over the next 13 years.

The BCU rose in cost over time and took seven years before it was axed, with Parliament's privileges committee ruling MPs had been deliberately misled over its axing.

Immigration Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Immigration Minister Erica Stanford said she and other ministers were also kept in the dark about its progress but she did not believe the benefits of OFS were deliberately inflated.

"Of course it's disappointing that they haven't got some of their figures right. But as I say, the most important thing now is that we stop, pause and do what we have done and make sure we are getting that right and that we are getting more productivity and better efficiencies out of the visas that we have already moved on so we can see some of the benefits and take a breath and make sure we get the next part right.

"From what I understand, it's a genuine error. I'm not sure that it was done to look better, but look, these are questions that need to be put to MBIE and probably to the chief executive."

Officials had pointed to higher productivity seen when permanent resident (PR) visas were on the Adept system, automating some tasks and allowing each immigration officer to process 20 visas a day compared with five previously. But PR is simpler, has a lower decline rate, and is processed by a small team at one site, meaning its results should not have been extrapolated to future productivity gains.

The Cabinet paper shows Our Future Services went through an independent quality assurance review and a Treasury review in 2024 before it was given the go-ahead.

It said the $134 million in forecast benefits were now unlikely to happen "in the way, amount or timeframe assumed in the detailed business case".

Both OFS and BCU - which cost about $36 million - are now the subject of a Public Service Commission review.

World.title: Piastri hit twice on first lap, Antonelli wins thanks to safety car luck
World.content:
Oscar Piastri and George Russell made contact with each other twice before the first corner in a Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix won by Kimi Antonelli, who took full advantage of a fortunate safety car.

Piastri finished eighth in the maiden grand prix at the brand-new Madring circuit, driving most of the race with a damaged front wing.

The Australian started seventh on the grid and got a fair start off the line. Russell, starting sixth, cut across Piastri and made contact with the Australian's front wing.

The pair made contact again while braking for the first corner, with Piastri's front left colliding with the rear of Russell's car.

Part of Piastri's damaged wing flapped in the breeze as the Australian tried to finish as high as he could.

Piastri went deep into the race before pitting, emerging back on track in 11th.

The Australian battled back in the final laps to climb up to eighth.

Norris cruelled by safety car, Antonelli tightens grip on title with win

An ill-timed safety car cost reigning world champion Lando Norris the chance of victory in Spain, as Kimi Antonelli's win gave the young Italian an 81-point lead in the drivers' championship.

Kimi Antonelli has now won eight grands prix this season. (Reuters: Albert Gea)

Norris, who started on pole, had a healthy lead over Antonelli on lap 14 of 57 when misfortune struck the McLaren driver.

Aston Martin's Lance Stroll went off the track, leading to a virtual safety car being called.

Norris had passed the entrance to the pit lane moments before the VSC was deployed, meaning he had to drive at 40 per cent speed while others behind him, including Antonelli and Max Verstappen, took a cheap pit stop.

As Norris approached the pit entrance on lap 15, the VSC ended and he pitted while his rivals were able to race at full speed.

McLaren also had a slow stop thanks to an issue with changing the front right tyre, meaning he dropped from first to sixth.

"Tough race, one that just got away from us," Norris said.

"I felt like we deserved it today, but that's racing. We'll take it on the chin and try again next time."

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc did not pit and led the race from Antonelli.

Leclerc stayed out until lap 48 of 57, and with the Madring proving hard to pass on, Antonelli, Max Verstappen and Norris were bunched up behind him, setting up a tense finish.

Once Leclerc pitted, Antonelli was able to drive in clean air and pulled away from Verstappen, who was able to hold off Norris for second place.

"It was a very difficult race, not straightforward at all," Antonelli said post-race.

" It's good to win, but it doesn't feel as good because I think Lando deserved the win. "

While Antonelli claimed his eighth grand prix win of the season, his nearest rivals in the championship were off the podium.

Mercedes teammate Russell placed fifth, while Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton retired early with a brake failure.

Antonelli's lead in the drivers' championship is a big 81 to Russell, and 101 points to Hamilton with either eight or nine race weekends remaining, depending on whether F1 can race in the Middle East at the end of the year.

World.title: Kangaroos survive Blues scare to keep AFLW record alive
World.content:
Ash Riddell racked up 39 disposals as North Melbourne survived a scare to keep its record AFLW winning run rolling with a 10-point victory over Carlton.

In other results on Sunday, Melbourne defeated Port Adelaide 11.8 (74) to 2.11 (23) at Casey Fields, Richmond beat St Kilda 9.4 (58) to 6.7 (43) at Windy Hill, Sydney got past cross-town rivals GWS 13.9 (87) to 8.8 (56) at Henson Park, and Fremantle downed Essendon 5.7 (37) to 3.4 (22).

In front of more than 3,500 supporters at Arden Street, a boilover was on the cards after the Blues kicked back-to-back goals against the breeze in the second quarter to take a three-point lead.

The match was still in the balance in the dying minutes, with Carlton's Lily Goss having the chance to close a 10-point deficit to four after taking a mark 35 metres out.

But not realising there was a player behind her, Goss played on and was immediately tackled, with the moment proving Carlton's last chance to fire a shot as the Kangaroos held on to win, 4.9 (33) to 3.5 (23).

Riddell was unstoppable throughout, while Jasmine Garner (30 disposals, five clearances, one goal) was also a significant contributor for the victors.

The Kangaroos have a 5-0 win-loss return this season.

They have won a record 32 straight matches since drawing with Geelong in round two of 2024.

Riddell said her team embraced the challenge thrown down by the Blues.

"We love it, and we had that against Brisbane a couple of weeks ago," Riddell told the Seven Network.

"We get excited by that. You could see the girls smiling as they came in at three-quarter time. We want that challenge, so it's great."

Although Carlton dropped to a 4-1 win-loss record, the strong display against the Kangaroos has fuelled their belief.

"We would have loved to have won, so we're a little bit disappointed, but also super proud," said Blues captain Abbie McKay following her 27-disposal, five-clearance effort.

"We lost by [53 points] last year, so it shows we're really growing as a team.

"We're here to win, and we're here to win a grand final. Although we lost, it shows we're improving."

Riddell was everywhere in the first term on the way to 15 disposals and four inside 50s.

Goals against the breeze to Nell Morris-Dalton and Lila Keck thrust Carlton into a shock lead early in the second term, but a 40-metre set-shot from Tahlia Randall followed by Blaithin Bogue's goal on the run ensured the Kangaroos entered the long break with a nine-point advantage.

Randall suffered a scary moment in the third quarter when she hyperextended her left elbow, but she was able to return after receiving treatment.

The stand-out moment of the third quarter was a two-bounce, tackle-busting effort from Carlton speedster Goss that helped set up a goal to Erone Fitzpatrick.

Garner's late major ensured the Kangaroos headed into three-quarter time with an eight-point lead, and there were no goals scored in a frantic final term.

AAP

World.title: Cleary plays hero and villain in NRL finals thriller
World.content:
Nathan Cleary is at risk of being rubbed out of Penrith's preliminary final after booting the Panthers to a thrilling 19-12 finals win over the Sydney Roosters.

In a cracking Sunday afternoon qualifying final, Cleary was sin-binned for collecting Hugo Savala's leg before breaking a 12-12 deadlock with a late field goal at Parramatta Stadium.

Brian To'o then iced the win with a 77th minute try after pouncing on a spilled Roosters pass.

The result means the Roosters will host Cronulla in a do-or-die semi-final on Saturday night, while Penrith are one win away from their sixth grand final in seven years.

But all eyes will be on the NRL's charge sheet on Monday, with Cleary anxiously awaiting what sanction he will face for crashing into Savala's leg after the Roosters player kicked in the first half.

The Panthers star immediately gave a worried look, before referee Gerard Sutton told him his action had "force", was "very dangerous" and "carried a high risk of injury".

If Cleary was to receive a grade-two dangerous contact charge on Monday, the game's best player would be facing a ban from the preliminary final with an early plea.

If he elected to challenge the charge, he would then risk being rubbed out of the grand final if found guilty.

A grade-one charge would only attract a fine for Cleary, and prove a massive boost in Penrith's bid for a fifth premiership of their dynasty.

Panthers coach Ivan Cleary was adamant the challenge was not worthy of a suspension.

"God no, of course not," said Cleary.

"He was just trying to make a play and he was thinking the right thing but he got the angle wrong.

"I must say though, the same thing happened to him earlier in the game, but anyway.

Cleary's challenge on Savala could have huge implications in the premiership race. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"We just had to manage our way through that period and then it was a dogfight for most of the second half, like a real semi-final.

"You could tell he was disappointed. Hugo (Savala) is not injured, it's just a black and white thing we've brought into the game."

The Roosters failed to make use of Cleary's absence, with Savala missing the ensuing penalty goal and being denied a try for a double movement after the break.

That was one of the few chances during a scoreless opening 32 minutes of the second half, before Cleary stepped up as the game's ultimate ice man.

To'o iced the game with a late intercept try. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Sat in the attacking line after a searching Moses Leota run, Cleary was able to slot over the one-pointer with no pressure from Roosters defenders.

Daly Cherry-Evans then attempted to reciprocate moments later, but sprayed a shot from 20 metres out to the right before To'o's sealer under the posts.

"Execution of moments (cost us). It was a good contest, both teams were in there fighting," said Roosters coach Trent Robinson.

"You're looking for those little opportunities where can take advantage. Cleary took his with the one-point and we had some that we missed.

"We missed them and they got them. That's the tale of the tape really."

Cleary's boot had also wreaked havoc early on Sunday, with the Roosters unable to handle three of his bombs and Liam Martin leaping to score off one of his shallow cross-field kicks.

The Penrith halfback also changed the point of attack and went back inside to Dylan Edwards for the Panthers' second try, with the fullback swerving his way over to make it 12-12 after 38 minutes.

Mark Nawaqanitawase's freakish ability had kept the Roosters in the match in the first half, with two key intercepts.

The Roosters winger first helped deny a Penrith try when he reached out and held onto an Isaiah Papali'i ball in the third minute.

He then gave the Roosters a 12-6 lead when he stretched out to stop a Penrith break, juggled the ball three time as he fell, got up and ran 45 metres to score.

AAP/ABC

World.title: I'm ready to be Swans captain, says Gulden
World.content:
Sydney superstar Errol Gulden says he is prepared to step up as captain to help the Swans pursue an AFL premiership bid without the injured Callum Mills.

The 24-year-old has thrown his hat in the ring to deputise for skipper Mills after his midfield performance led the Swans to a stirring qualifying final win over Brisbane.

Sydney coach Dean Cox also has an experienced leader in former co-captain Dane Rampe, as well as fellow veteran Jake Lloyd, midfielder James Rowbottom and Tom Papley at his disposal.

Whoever Cox lands on could also play a key leadership role next year, with Mills facing the possibility of missing the entire 2027 season after tearing the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee.

Swans vice-captain Isaac Heeney is among five players serving club-imposed bans after last month's post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

Star defender Mills had earned significant praise for leading the Swans through the turmoil, which past players said shattered the club's famed "Bloods culture".

Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice are the other Swans who will not play again this season.

Gulden rallied the Swans after Mills went down late in the first quarter against the back-to-back reigning premiers, finishing with one goal, 34 disposals and eight clearances.

"If it [the captaincy] was offered to me, I would love to," Gulden told AAP.

"I would feel like I'd be ready. I wouldn't change anything that I'm doing. I don't think any of us need to change anything that we're doing.

"But you're just so shattered for the person. He's [Mills] just an amazing leader.

"He is the best human being at the club. It's just not fair.

"We've just got to keep going, and it's going to be next man in."

Gulden said the 53-point qualifying final win left him with the most pride he has ever felt in the Swans across six seasons at the club.

The two-time All-Australian has played in two losing grand finals (2022, 2024), with last year's 10th-placed finish the first time he had missed finals in his career.

"I love playing with this team. The last couple of games have been so fun as a player to be a part of," Gulden said.

"There's something in having your back against the wall and trying to fight your way out of it.

"The weekend [against the Lions] was easily the most rewarding game.

"The most pride I've felt to be a part of this team in my career.

"There was obviously some respect lost for the club. It's completely fair enough.

Scans confirm ACL rupture for Swans skipper Callum Mills will be sidelined for the remainder of Sydney's finals campaign and possibly all of next season after scans revealed an ACL tear in his right knee.

"All we can focus on as players is what we can control, and that's going out there and representing the club the best way we can on and off the field.

"I'm really proud of the club and the team, everyone involved, because the last few weeks have been really difficult."

Sydney will continue its unlikely flag push by hosting minor premiers Fremantle at the SCG on Friday.

"A premiership would mean the absolute world to me," Gulden said.

"Even if what happened hadn't happened, it still would mean the world to me."

AAP

World.title: Warriors moved to Eden Park for Knights finals showdown
World.content:
The Warriors will make history when they host their first NRL final at Eden Park after the governing body announced the venue for the club's elimination final.

The NRL confirmed the Warriors would play Newcastle at Eden Park next Sunday at 6:05pm (4:05pm AEST) in week two of the finals.

The Warriors' first preference is to play at Mt Smart Stadium where their support is through the roof.

Eden Park holds 50,000 people, however, and is a more modern stadium compared to Mt Smart, where a sold-out crowd of 26,131 created a cauldron-like atmosphere in the Warriors' 26-16 loss to the Dolphins in Saturday night's qualifying final.

The Warriors have hosted five finals in their history in Auckland, but all at Mt Smart.

The Warriors have injury concerns ahead of the clash with the Knights, who they beat 46-32 in Auckland in round 25.

They lost strike centre Leka Halasima in the warm-up to the Dolphins clash with the Tonga international clutching at his right leg.

Trindall returns from shoulder dislocation to lead Sharks in finals win Four weeks after dislocating his shoulder, Braydon Trindall has returned to lead the Cronulla Sharks to a 26-16 win, advancing to the second week of the NRL finals while knocking out the North Queensland Cowboys.

"It was a hamstring in the warm-up, nothing related to what he's been having, which was an ankle injury," coach Andrew Webster said.

"He just felt his hamstring in the first stride out and reported it straight away. Yeah, couldn't go.

"I don't know any more than that right now."

Halasima is set to miss the Newcastle clash amid fears that prop Jackson Ford's injury comeback will be short-lived.

Ford, on return after a 12-week pectoral tear lay-off, limped off against the Dolphins with an ankle complaint.

"Not good," Webster said, when asked about the nature of the injury.

"We don't know much more."

The Warriors were never in full cry in attack against the Dolphins, with five penalty goals edging them to a 16-8 lead, but also denying them the chance near the opposition tryline to perhaps put the game to bed.

"We didn't get the opportunity to get a flow in to our attack," Webster said.

"That's the negative side of taking the penalty goals. But to stretch the lead out to eight points, we had to do it. It's a no-brainer.

"The negative side is there, but the eight-point gap is what every team should take."

Webster said the Warriors were in a strong position when leading 12-8 at half-time, but were unable to contain Dolphins centre Herbie Farnworth in particular as their tackles failed to stick.

"We were trying so hard … chasing contact and collision, and they were pinballing. We have to be more efficient next week."

AAP

World.title: Root says England's back from 'chaos' after Pakistan series sweep
World.content:
Joe Root admits England descended into "chaos" before he returned as the Test captain and believes things are back on track after sealing a cricket series whitewash over Pakistan on Saturday.

England survived a scare before Root and Jordan Cox scored unbeaten half-centuries to knock off the target of 130 and win the third Test at Edgbaston by eight wickets with five sessions to spare.

The dramatic retirement of Ben Stokes in June followed by coach Brendon McCullum being stripped of his red-ball responsibilities briefly left the Test side with a worrying leadership vacuum.

Root, who served as skipper for five years before standing down in 2022, accepted the captaincy again and, in concert with interim coach Marcus Trescothick, brought a hat-trick of comfortable wins at Leeds, Lord's and now Edgbaston.

The partnership steadied the ship ahead of Stephen Fleming's arrival as McCullum's long-term successor.

The Kiwi is due to arrive in the country in the coming days and Root believes he will find a team that has put its turbulent recent past to one side.

"There's been a lot of chaos around this series before a ball was bowled," Root said.

"The way we've handled it on and off the field, the way everyone understands what is expected of them, both as a player and how we want to carry ourselves, is a really good thing.

"It's been a very unusual summer, hasn't it? We had a resignation mid-series, there has been a few off-field incidents and we've got a new coach. Whether you call it chaos, whether you call it unusual, whether you call it unsettling, all of those are fair.

Root fuming after Carse nightclub incident England captain Joe Root opens up on his disappointment after finding another teammate involved in an alcohol-fuelled off-field incident.

"But ultimately, the thing that I care about and the most important thing is what happens from that. The way that we've responded to that has been excellent. And the fact that there's now clarity in what is expected of the group moving forward is quite evident. We build on that now."

Pakistan finally put England under some pressure in Birmingham after flaccid efforts in the first two games.

A stunning 81-run cameo from debutant Razaullah Khan on Friday left England chasing 130.

In Saturday's first over, the host was reduced to 2-2 when Mohammad Abbas got Ben Duckett to edge behind and Emilio Gay lbw.

"We thought this morning that anything is possible," Abbas said. "My specialty is taking wickets with the new ball … and we tried our best."

England could have been 3-35 when Root dragged on but Mohammad Ali overstepped.

Root and Cox shared an unbeaten stand of 128 with Root finishing on 62 and Cox 59 when they won at 2-133 just before lunch.

Seam bowler Ollie Robinson was named the player of the series for taking 21 wickets at an average of 8.76.

AP

World.title: New world number one Rybakina dethrones Sabalenka in US Open final
World.content:
Elena Rybakina has won her first US Open title, ending Aryna Sabalenka's hopes of a hat-trick of wins at Flushing Meadows in New York.

Rybakina controlled the first set, then was put in danger in the second, defending two set points before losing a third to allow Sabalenka back into the match.

However, the Kazakh player held her nerve, taking an early break in the third set and holding on for her third major title win, 6-4, 5-7, 6-2.

The win marked a second major triumph for Rybakina this year, after her Australian Open final victory over Sabalenka in January.

Sabalenka's loss ended her hopes of winning a third US Open crown in a row, emulating tennis great Serena Williams, who was undefeated between 2012 and 2014.

Sabalenka was increasingly frustrated through the match, smashing a couple of racquets as she struggled to find a way past her opponent.

Aryna Sabalenka's inability to crack Elena Rybakina left her frustrated at the US Open final. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

Rybakina stopped Sabalenka's 19-match winning streak at the US Open, where she had not lost since falling to Coco Gauff in the 2023 final.

The WTA Tour leader in aces got less than half of her first serves in but instead put Sabalenka under constant pressure with a strong return game, racking up 12 break chances and converting three, which was all she needed.

Rybakina earned $US5.5 million ($7.67 million), the largest prize in grand slam history, and tied Sabalenka and French Open winner Mirra Andreeva with a tour-high three titles this season.

Sabalenka took home $US2.8 million ($3.9 million) but it was clear how little that meant to her, as she smashed her racquet after a brief hug with Rybakina at the net.

A devastated Sabalenka found it hard to talk at the trophy presentation.

"That's the last thing I want to do now is giving a speech," she said.

"Obviously, I'm disappointed but I want to say congratulations Elena, it's a great win.

"I wish I could perform a little better, but maybe next year," she said as tears fell.

Rybakina was overjoyed and a little overwhelmed.

"It's tough to find words right now," she told the crowd.

"I didn't expect anything like this coming to this tournament. I've been dealing with an injury but somehow everything aligned together on my side.

"I want to say to Aryna, you are a great champion. It's so difficult to play you. I was diving around on court trying to get balls [back]."

Rybakina also thanked the crowd for their support, adding: "I'm falling in love with New York more and more."

It was celebration time for Elena Rybakina at the US Open after she won her second major title of 2026. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

The second seed drew first blood to go ahead 3-2 following a Sabalenka double ⁠fault, with the frustrated Belarusian earning a code ‌violation immediately afterwards for launching ‌a ball high into the stands of the main showcourt.

A sudden drop-off in Rybakina's level midway through the second set gave the 28-year-old Sabalenka hope, and she produced a delicate drop shot and a stunning backhand crosscourt winner en route to forcing a deciding set.

However, Rybakina's quality ‌shone through as she took a commanding 5-2 lead and then ​closed out a famous triumph to leave her Belarusian rival without any major silverware in 2026.

ABC/wires

World.title: Wallaroos scare England but fail 'mission impossible'
World.content:
Australia's rugby women have given England's world champions a run for their money by leading sensationally at half-time, but the Wallaroos' dream of downing the Red Roses crumbled as they ended up losing 48-15 in Salford.

The English were stunned in the first 40 minutes of their WXV Global Series opener on Saturday (Sunday AEST) as the Australians went in to the break with a 10-5 lead but any hopes of handing the hosts their first defeat after 38 straight victories was buried after the break.

The John Mitchell-coached world champs, initially rusty in their first outing since being crowned European grand slam champions in May and struggling to adapt to the new smaller size 4.5 ball being trialled, ran in eight tries in total as their set-piece finally began to tick over to their normal high efficiency.

But Australia could be proud of their efforts, deserving their half-time lead as they controlled the breakdown and defended stoically even after being reduced to 14 for 10 minutes in the first period when halfback Samantha Wood was sin-binned for a deliberate knock-on.

Still, they went in to the break with the lead thanks to barnstorming prop Faliki Pohiva rumbling her way over for a try after Michaela Leonard's stolen lineout on England's five-metre line, but the world champions were hardly inconvenienced, despite their initial rustiness.

"It is an absolute joke if you are worried about being down 10-5," said Mitchell afterwards and the response of his team demonstrated they were surely never really concerned.

"More important is how we worked our way back into it."

In front of a crowd of 9,251, England did indeed begin to turn it on, with May Campbell, captain Meg Jones, Bryony Field, Mia Venner and Sadia Kabeya all crossing for tries in a 20-minute spell to add to player-of-the-match Abi Burton's first-half score.

Lucy Packer and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald also then went over, with Asoiva Karpani scoring a second for the Wallaroos late on in a show of defiance amid the hammering.

Loading Instagram content

Tech.title: Apple is reportedly working on iPhone game controllers
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says Apple is developing two game controllers for the iPhone and will likely sell them under the Beats brand. Rumors that Apple might enter the game controller business have circulated for some time. But last week, MacRumors reported finding two references in macOS 26.7’s code to two game controllers identified as first-party devices.

Despite the code being found in macOS, not iOS, Gurman says the controllers are designed for iPhones. Additionally, he says that it is Beats executives leading the charge on this product. Apple sometimes uses its subsidiary brand to experiment with new product categories and compete at lower price points without sullying its more premium Apple lineup. As Gurman notes:

For example, Beats now sells a range of iPhone cases and USB-C cables that don’t necessarily fit Apple’s usual approach to design. A controller makes sense in that context. To reach a broad audience, it has to be relatively affordable, which means avoiding some of the more expensive materials and finishes typically associated with Apple products. The culture and lifestyle around gaming controllers also could fit naturally under the Beats umbrella.

Tech.title: The Units’ Digital Stimulation is synthpunk perfection
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

The Units are a band I discovered in part thanks to No Dogs in Space. During their miniseries on The Screamers (another incredible band worth checking out), they mention synthpunk.org as one of their sources. And there’s no better way to get my attention than to combine two of my favorite things — punk rock and synthesizers. The site was down that day (it appears to be back up now), but I was able to access a version from July through the Wayback Machine. What greeted me was a bare-bones site with links for six bands, including The Screamers. But at the top was The Units, a band I’d never heard of and, after tracking down their 1980 record Digital Stimulation, I fell in love.

The production, especially on the Devo-esque vocals, feels distinctly of its time. But the sound palette and arrangements are more aggressive, dancier, and generally just more modern-sounding. Ignoring the vocals, album opener “High Pressure” could pass as an MSPAINT song. The title track, with its sped-up disco stomp, could have been released by DFA in 2003. And many of the later tracks would be at home on a Single Frame record.

The Units weren’t the first punk band to dabble with synths. Nor were they the first act to largely replace guitars with keyboards and lean into technology as a core theme of their songwriting. The Talking Heads offered a cleaner, artier take on punk, incorporating keyboards, non-Western percussion, and even tape loops. Devo’s first single, “Mongoloid,” has a distinctly punk edge that would have been right at home alongside The Units. But the band still leaned heavily on traditional guitar and bass, and always felt more at home in the art-rock and new wave scenes.

Husband-and-wife duo Scott Ryser and Rachel Webber, the primary songwriters of The Units, had a sharper edge to their sound. They were firmly grounded in the West Coast punk scene that made its DIY ethos a core part of its identity. Their contemporaries were the Dead Kennedys, The Mutants, and The Avengers. You can hear it in the lean arrangements that prioritize raw energy over perfection. That’s not to say songs like “Cannibals” and “Bugboy” are simplistic. Their bleak, slightly humorous critiques of an uncaring world are models of efficiency — unfussy and infectious.

Like a lot of Bay Area punk bands, there’s a melodicism to The Units’ work that is hard to shake. “Warm Moving Bodies” feels like a dancefloor anthem waiting to happen, and “High Pressure” is an undeniable earworm.

The band did record a second album in 1981, Animals They Dream About, but it remained unreleased until 2016. It’s also an excellent document of the under-represented synthpunk scene of the late ‘70s and early ‘80s. Though, it is far more polished and leans into poppier new wave arrangements that are a step removed from their bootstrapped punk roots.

The Units’ Digital Stimulation is available on Bandcamp and via streaming on Apple Music, YouTube Music, and Deezer.

Tech.title: Waymo pulls over, calls cops on riders with a ghost gun
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Two people were arrested in San Fransico while riding around in a Waymo robotaxi after the cab pulled over and called the cops on them. The riders were juveniles in possession of a loaded AR-style ghost gun and were taken to a juvenile hall. While the police report did not specify who was operating the autonomous car, Waymo later confirmed it was one of its vehicles to the Los Angeles Times.

A spokesperson told the LA Times that a “violation of our terms of service involving a firearm” was detected. At which point the car pulled over and alerted the authorities.

Earlier this year, a Waymo faked having mechanical problems to pull over when two passengers were drinking alcohol and firing a toy gun out of the back of the car. In that instance, the riders Waymo snitched on were also juveniles. So let this be a lesson to teens: if you’re gonna do dumb stuff, don’t do it in the back of a robotaxi.

Tech.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother will make you forget all about Marvel’s Blade disaster
Tech.content:
Marvel’s mishandling of its Blade reboot will likely go down as one of the studio’s biggest mistakes. There was a great actor in place to play the vampire hunter (Mahershala Ali), and a promising director set to take over the reins (Bassam Tariq). In retrospect, though, the disappointing demise of Blade might not be such a bad thing, because Tariq and Ali have collaborated on something much more interesting than a superhero reboot: the powerful hitman thriller Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.

That was one of five movies I was able to cram into a very hectic third day at the Toronto International Film Festival (you can see my previous reports here and here), and it was one of those days that drives home why events like TIFF can be so special. Each film I saw was drastically different from the last — there was everything from a drama about drifting cars to a throwback horror flick based on a famous Japanese ghost story — which was a great reminder that there are still plenty of new ideas left in the world of film.

So let’s get to it. Here are some rapid-fire reviews of everything I saw on day 3 at TIFF.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

In theaters in October

Latif (Ali) lives a life of contradictions: he’s a devout Muslim and loyal father, but he also works as a hitman, albeit one who works under a specific moral code (only kill bad guys; never use a gun). But both his faith and his code are tested when his wife dies and he’s forced to become a single father to three kids, including a newborn baby. At the same time, his blood-soaked past comes back to haunt him, putting everyone at risk. We’re in a great moment for pure action flicks like Furious or the John Wick franchise, but Your Mother offers something very different. It’s a powerful character study, one where the action is comparatively fleeting, but all the more powerful and impactful because of it. It’s a film that always left me guessing just how Latif was going to get through this, and, despite being very serious and often solemn, the story also has plenty of laugh-out-loud moments. Ali is excellent as the morally questionable righteous killer, but I was also really impressed by John Cho as the villain, a charismatically unhinged leader of a right-wing church group.

In Alaska

No theatrical date yet

A slow-burning crime thriller, In Alaska, co-directed by Jaap van Heusden and Vinnie Karetak., follows a suicidal teen named Woody (Leo Matthew Temela) who, after a tragic mishap, finds himself wanted by the FBI for causing millions of dollars worth of damage to an oil pipeline. It’s a film of two sides: Woody’s desperate attempts at survival, and veteran agent Susan (Noomi Rapace), the only who realizes the damage wasn’t caused by eco-terrorists. In Alaska is a moodier take on the genre, and one that asks some difficult and important questions about both its leads, particularly Woody, who constantly grapples with whether he even wants to live at all. What starts out bleak ends on a much more hopeful note.

Image: TIFF

The Face of Horror

No theatrical date yet

Conceptually, Anna Biller’s The Face of Horror is a mishmash of styles and influences. It’s based on the influential Japanese ghost story Yotsuya Kaidan, but adapts the tale for 14th century England. It then renders the whole thing in the style of Technicolor horror classics. That curious combination works, though, as the film has a campy sense of theatricality to it, with over-the-top performances and classic-style special effects — including some truly memorable make-up work — that lend its grisly tale of murder and betrayal a distinct vibe. And it’s all held together by two strong lead performances: Eleanor (Kristine Froseth), the jilted wife-turned-nightmare of Edward (Jonah Hauer-King), a smarmy and morally-dubious knight who is the kind of asshole you can’t wait to see get what’s coming to him.

Image: Image: Roadside / Vertical

Babies

No theatrical date yet

A film that explores that nagging question many long-term couples are forced to answer repeatedly: when are you going to have a baby? Written and directed by Lauren Miller Rogen, Babies is centered on Annie (Anna Kendrick) and Aaron (Seth Rogen), the only childless couple in their social circle. But Annie can’t stop thinking about the question — there’s a lot of her internal monologue debating the pros and cons of having kids — and the couple are forced to really confront the idea when a close friend and her young daughter come to stay with them, providing a taste of parenthood. Babies works for two reasons. First, it’s hilarious: Kendrick and Rogen have a blast together, and the supporting cast includes the likes of Issa Rae, Zach Cherry, and Ed Helm. But it also feels grounded in a way that makes it very relatable, whether you have kids or not.

Drifter

No theatrical date yet

If Good Will Hunting and The Fast and the Furious were smushed together, you might get something like Drifter. The film is directed by longtime Fast star Sung Kang, who also plays the lead role of Tree, the janitor of a smalltown race track who moonlights as a driver for a drug kingpin. But all he really wants to do is drift, and events conspire to bring him to an event where he’ll go up against the best drifters in the world. The challenges are much more than just on the track, though; Tree has spent most of his life alone, so he’s forced to learn to open up to others, and he also has to contend with extracting himself from the world of crime. Unfortunately, Drifter leans too heavily on the established formula of underdog sports stories, which makes most of its beats feel predictable, with the exception of its completely improbable ending. Worse still is that, with the exception of Tree, none of the characters feel developed at all, and the crime thriller aspect doesn’t gel well with the feel-good story. At least there are some beautiful sequences that make drifting a car feel like an artform.

Tech.title: Your car is selling your data
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on cars, data privacy, and autonomous vehicles, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

Earlier this year, the Federal Trade Commission issued an unprecedented penalty against General Motors: a five-year ban on selling customer data to consumer reporting agencies and third-party data brokers.

For years, GM had been collecting all sorts of data on its customers — such as how often they sped or whether they drove at night — and selling it to brokers to generate risk profiles for insurance companies. More often than not, drivers were unaware of the degree to which their data was being collected. Many had unknowingly consented to it by signing up for an OnStar connected services plan, which activated a feature called Smart Driver that collected their driving data.

GM was then turning around and sharing that data with two data brokers, LexisNexis and Verisk, both of which work with the insurance industry. In a 2024 blockbuster investigative report by The New York Times, some drivers said their insurance rates went up as a result of the data collection. The enrollment process was so confusing that many vehicle owners had no idea their data was being shared. Under the settlement with the FTC, GM has to make it easier for drivers to turn off location tracking, as well as enable them to access and delete their data collected by the automaker.

But GM isn’t the only automaker vacuuming up data on its customers. A team of researchers from the Mozilla Foundation spent months examining the privacy policies of all the major car companies for a report they were working on in 2023. Their conclusion: Every single one had “horrible privacy and security,” said Jen Caltrider, who helped author the study. Not only that, but customers were forced to accept overlapping policies for the car, the connected services, the smartphone app, and the financial services through which they received their loan — all of which included data collection provisions.

“And so it was really overwhelming trying to understand what was going on,” Caltrider said.

There has been plenty of corroborating evidence for this. Consumer Reports published its own investigation last year that concluded “nearly every automaker that sells cars in the U.S. is similarly collecting and sharing so-called ‘driver behavior data’ with other companies and continues to do so.”

Cars are particularly problematic compared to phones because the privacy controls are less intuitive. A smartphone owner can generally find and tweak their privacy settings. With a vehicle, the data collection is spread across multiple systems and policies, making it much harder for consumers to understand what is happening. It feels like a free-for-all because automakers are collecting enormous amounts of information without much public scrutiny.

How it’s going

After GM was penalized as a result of the Times investigation, the issue of data privacy and cars appears to finally be getting some scrutiny. But as is often the case, policymakers may be missing the mark on how to address it.

Last December, a trio of House Republicans introduced the Data Rights for Information and Vehicle Electronics in Real-time, or DRIVER, Act. According to these lawmakers, the bill “reaffirms a basic principle: if you own the vehicle, you should own the data it generates.”

But while the bill would give vehicle owners a bit more control over their data, it would also allow automakers to continue gathering and selling it to third-party data brokers, which makes it a nonstarter for privacy advocates. As Caltrider notes, access and deletion rights are not the same thing as preventing excess collection in the first place. If an automaker can collect enormous amounts of information and the consumer must then go through an arduous process to discover what was collected and request that it be deleted, the burden remains on the individual. Most privacy advocates would rather see a system in which automakers simply do not collect so much information to begin with.

The issue has even risen to the level of MAGA World. Last July, Donald Trump’s Transportation Secretary, Sean Duffy, sent a letter to Congress outlining the administration’s policy priorities for the upcoming surface transportation reauthorization bill. Tucked in the letter was a new concept called “the Freedom Car,” which Duffy described as Americans’ right to “drive disconnected and non-automated” vehicles. The proposal would ban the government from requiring that vehicles be equipped with automated driving systems or have the capability to transmit data wirelessly — which, to my knowledge, no one is trying to do.

What happens next

It’s unclear whether the DRIVER Act or the Freedom Car will ever clear the hurdles in Washington to become real policies. What is clear is that there is significant demand for simpler vehicles. People are asking why they can’t just buy a car without all the sensors and data collection. They look at new concepts like the Slate Truck and wonder whether they could also use something more bare-bones.

Sure, consumers may accept useful safety equipment such as backup cameras, but many don’t want their vehicle tracking everything they do — and they definitely don’t want to see ads on their vehicle screens. (BMW, I’m looking at you.) Nor do they want Flock cameras tracking their every movement while they drive down the street.

But automakers have every incentive to keep collecting data because there is money to be made from it. As long as the broader data economy rewards companies for gathering and monetizing information, there’s little reason for automakers to voluntarily abandon the practice.

By the way

Every automaker has its own privacy page where vehicle owners can submit requests, including opting out of data collection. Of course, they’re all buried under mountains of legalese, so good luck finding it.

Same goes for all the smartphone apps for connected car services. Changing your privacy settings in those apps is generally a little easier.

Read this

The New York Times ’ investigation into GM’s data collection program is worth a read, if just for the flabbergasted reactions from drivers who couldn’t understand why their insurance rates were going up.

Edmunds and Consumer Reports both did the work to ask every automaker for their data collection policies. There’s a lot of variety across the industry.

These Redditors are crowdsourcing a list of new cars (from 2019 onward) that aren’t digitally connected and/or transmitting data to the car company’s servers. Spoiler alert: It’s a pretty short list!
